Lane battlers: autoBuild, waveClock + waveSpawn, upgrades, victory: score. Dungeon Keeper: diggable rock and gold veins, imps with digs + claimer, territory.buildOnlyOwned, reinforced walls (territory.fortify), painted rooms (lair supply, hatchery food income, library work), neutral portal with claimedByTerritory, creatures with attractedBy + needs, flies that follow the tunnels (movement.airOverRock: false), hand, possession, victory: keyUnits (dungeon heart). Knights and Merchants / Settlers: "storage": "buildings", storehouses, recipe chains (woodcutter → sawmill, farm → mill → bakery), carrier serfs, roadNetwork, materials delivered to sites, trainFrom recruits, inn food needs with starve. The editor saves corners inline up to 256x256 cells and as cornersFile (maps/<map name>.r16, next to the map) above that; loaders (game, headless, editor, MCP) read the file through the content reader, so it also works from packs.

Presentation only (modules/rts/view/RtsTerrainRender.*). Optional keys in the same terrain block as the overlays (rules.json or game.json; game.json wins per key). Without them every game looks exactly as before (vertex colours per cell kind, plateaus with sharp cliff walls, ramps, soft colour transitions, apron, one water sheet). "terrain": { "layers": [ // up to 4 tiling splat layers (world-space, mipmapped, wrap) {"id": "snow", "texture": "textures/terrain/snow_repeat.png", "normal": "textures/terrain/snow_n_repeat.png", "scale": 6, "tint": [1, 1, 1]}, {"id": "earth", "texture": "textures/terrain/earth_repeat.png", "scale": 4} ], "cells": {"grass": {"layer": "snow", "color": [0.9, 0.93, 0.97]}, // layer id, or {layer, color (vertex colour override)} "sand": "earth", "ramp": "earth", "rock": "earth", "blocked": "earth", "lakebed": "earth", "shallows": "earth", "dug": "earth"}, "cliff": {"texture": "textures/terrain/rock_repeat.png", "normal": "textures/terrain/rock_n_repeat.png", "scale": 3, "tint": [1, 1, 1], "slope": [0.3, 0.55]}, // blended in where 1 - normal.y is in that range "splatStrength": 1, // 0..1: mix of the textures over the vertex colours "water": {"mode": "auto", "color": [0.22, 0.45, 0.62, 0.78], "offset": -0.12}, "lod": "auto", "lodRange": 128 // heightfield maps: CDLOD on above 256 cells per side ("on"/"off") } key meaning layers splat layers (≤ 4): texture albedo (sRGB), optional normal (tangent-space, +Y up), scale world units per repeat, tint. Loaded with TextureCache::resolve(path, …, tiling): never taken from an atlas page (name them *_repeat.png so the packer skips them too) cells cell kind → layer id or index; kinds: grass (.), sand (, no-build), ramp (/), rock (R), blocked (#), lakebed (~), shallows (=), dug (diggable rock floor). color overrides the vertex colour of the kind on every tier cliff texture on cliff walls and steep slopes (Medium: one projection, High: triplanar + normal map) water.mode sheet = one plane under the whole map (classic, default for cliff-level maps), bodies = each connected water area gets its own surface just below its lowest shore (lakes on plateaus, valleys of heightfield maps; default for heightfield maps), auto lod, lodRange big heightfield maps: chunks drawn with 2^k cell steps (k ≤ 4) by camera distance, geomorphing in the vertex shader, skirts against cracks Map key terrainMaterial (optional, visual): rows of 0..3 (layer index) per cell, other characters = by cell kind. Painted with the editor's Рельеф window or terrain_material. Quality tiers (pause menu Ground textures, Renderer3D::materialQuality(), capped by the device default; AIVERSE_TERRAIN=low|medium|high overrides for testing): Low = vertex colours (weak Mali / Adreno / PowerVR, also every game without layers), Medium = splat textures + cliff texture, High = + normal maps and triplanar cliffs. Shaders: engine/view/game/GameTerrainShaders.h (GLSL + MSL, sun + soft shadows + point lights + clouds as the lit shader). Performance: the terrain is cut into 32x32-cell chunks, frustum-culled; the editor rebuilds only chunks whose cells changed; during a match nothing is rebuilt: resource fields, creep and (heightfield maps) fog of war are read by the shader from small per-cell textures. AIVERSE_TERRAIN_STATS=1 prints chunks / triangles / frame time. Sample: templates/frostcrown (generated CC0 textures, tools/terrain/make_textures.py). Editor / MCP (heightfield maps, apps/editor/core/TerrainOps.cpp, window Рельеф): terrain_sculpt {op: raise|lower|smooth|flatten|noise|set, x, y | points, radius, strength, seed} (the first sculpt creates corners from the visible surface: cliff levels, ramps, fine heights), terrain_heights {points | grid}, terrain_material {layer, x, y, radius}, heightmap_export {file, scale?} / heightmap_import {file, scale, offset} (16-bit grayscale PNG, (w+1) x (h+1) pixels, height = offset + value / 65535 * scale). Corners are visual unless rules terrain.model is heightfield (see below).

"terrain": {"style": "smooth"} in rules.json / game.json draws the terrain from a visual heightmap with several samples per cell instead of one height per cell corner: bevelled cliffs with organic outlines, rounded plateaus and ramps on cliff-level maps, bicubic relief with fine noise on heightfield maps, per-pixel lighting, materials blended at sub-cell resolution with automatic rock on steep slopes. Default "classic" keeps the old look. A map can carry its own painted detail: terrain.detail = {"scale": 4, "file": "maps/<name>.detail.r16", "splat": "..."} (int16 LE, 1/16 units, (w*k+1) x (h*k+1)). Tuning keys terrain.detailLook. Editor / MCP: terrain_detail, terrain_sculpt (sub-cell, erode, stamp), terrain_paint_material, heightmap_import/export {detail: true}. Full description and numbers: docs/terrain.md § Detail surface. Samples: starfall (cliffs), metaltide (relief), frostcrown.

rules.terrain.model: "heightfield" + a map with terrain.corners / cornersFile (without corners the map plays like "levels"). Corner (x, y) is the top-left corner of cell (x, y); heights in 1/16 world units. Everything is integer / fixed point and deterministic. Surface: ground height at any point is bilinear between the 4 corners of its cell; ground units (and the y of every mobile unit) stand on it; projectiles start at the shooter's ground + 0.6 and aim at the target's ground + 0.4. Slopes: per cell steepness = max(gradient length, steepest cell edge), in height units per cell. A unit can't enter cells steeper than its move.maxSlope (or terrain.maxSlope of its layer; sand for layer: "sand"); pathfinding, local avoidance and spawning follow the same rule. Cliff/ramp rules (levels, /) are replaced by slopes. Structures need cells no steeper than terrain.buildSlope. Speed: speed * (1 - uphillSpeed * climb) going up, * (1 + downhillSpeed * descent) going down, where climb/descent = height change per cell along the move; clamped to 0.25..2. Vision: line of sight from eyeHeight above the unit's cell to targetHeight above each cell in sight range; a cell behind a ridge is hidden (heights.blockVision: false turns this off, air units see over). Targeting only picks enemies in a cell the player sees. Cliff level of a cell = floor(cell height / levelHeight) (0..9), so level-based rules and triggers keep working. Range / damage / miss bonuses use the exact height difference (see heights). Checksums: corners and the model are part of the state hash only for heightfield games. Big maps (256x256 cells and more): long paths use hierarchical pathfinding (16x16 clusters with border entrances, refined with A*), built at match start and rebuilt only around structures that block cells. aiverse_headless --project DIR --bench-paths N times path queries; python3 tools/templates/mapgen.py --big 1024 <scratch>/maps/big.json writes a 1024x1024 test map (keep it out of templates/). MCP: map_info.heightfield (corners, min, max, storage, model), map_heightfield {"enabled"} adds a flat heightfield or removes it, map_validate warns when the model is heightfield but the map has no corners and flags units/structures standing on slopes too steep for them. Sculpting: terrain_sculpt, heightmap PNG import/export (see Terrain materials). The view draws the relief from the corners (two triangles per cell, diagonal (0,0)-(1,1)); GameView::heightAt follows the same triangles, so models and overlays sit on the drawn ground.

The bodies themselves are described in docs/planets.md §1-2 (world.bodies, kind, radius, faceSize, seaLevel, orbit, terrain.faces / terrain.corners, nereid = the sea as a NEREID water body for buoyancy and currents, §1). What only the view reads: {"id": "terra", "kind": "planet", ..., "visual": {"color": [255, 220, 160], // stars: light colour and glow; others: far-away tint "atmosphere": {"color": [110, 170, 255], "height": 0.08}}} // or false; default: on for planets, off for moons visual.flora: TerraWeave trees and rocks on the body (one site per land cell, species from the sphere climate): {"density": 0..1, "scale": world units per metre} or false; default density 0.22 on planets, none on moons, scale 0.06. visual.atmosphere.height: shell thickness as a fraction of the radius (0.005..0.5). The shell and the haze use the colour; the shell is drawn from the Medium material tier up. terrain.faces[f].material: rows of digits 0..3 per face (. = by cell kind), like the flat map's terrainMaterial; painted by terrain_material with body. Ground look on planets = the visual terrain block of the game (layers per cell kind, cliff texture, water colour). Ground overlays on planets use the same visual terrain.territory / dig / roads / lanes blocks as flat maps (territory fill and borders, rock blocks with veins / gems and dig marks, road cells, lanes and map roads between buildings draped on the surface). Territory, diggable rock (diggable characters in terrain.faces[f].rows), rooms, claims, capture and lanes work on planets with the same rules keys (docs/planets.md §3). Editor / MCP: planet_info; terrain_sculpt / terrain_paint / terrain_material with body + face + x, y (cells on that face) or dir [x, y, z] and radius in cells (3D brush, crosses face seams).

A map with a world block is a planet map: the bodies replace size / terrain / fields (docs/planets.md). Flat maps are untouched (same checksums). "world": {"start": "terra", "bodies": [ {"id": "sun", "kind": "star", "radius": 40}, {"id": "terra", "kind": "planet", "radius": 16, "faceSize": 24, "orbitAltitude": 4, // shell of move.layer "orbit" "orbit": {"around": "sun", "radius": 400, "period": 1200, "phase": 0.1}, // seconds, turns "terrain": {"faces": [{"rows": [...], "levels": [...], "fields": {"metal": ["..19.."]}}, ... 6 faces], "corners": [ ... 6 * (N+1)^2 ... ] | "cornersFile": "maps/x.terra.r16"}}]}, "players": [{"name": "Blue", "start": {"body": "terra", "face": 4, "x": 12.5, "y": 12.5}}], "entities": [{"type": "metal_spot", "at": {"body": "terra", "face": 4, "x": 7, "y": 8}}], "waves": [{"at": {"body": "terra", "face": 0, "x": 3, "y": 3}, ...}] kind: planet, moon (surface: faceSize 2..512), star (no surface). radius 2..1200, radius + orbitAltitude <= 1500; orbitAltitude default 0.15 x radius. orbit.around must name an earlier body. At most 16 bodies. Visual detail per body (docs/terrain.md "Planets"): terrain.style (smooth / classic, default the game's), terrain.detailLook {scale, roughness, craters}, terrain.detail {scale, file} (int16 LE 1/256 units, 6 x (faceSize*scale+1)^2, written by the editor). Presentation only: the simulation and checksums ignore them. Positions on planet maps are {body, face, x, y} (cell coordinates on that face, 0..faceSize); [x, z] is an error. Fields per face (fields in a face: digit rows per resource) or fields: [{center: {body, face, x, y}, radius}]. Per-face rows / levels use the flat-map characters; rules terrain.model: "heightfield" makes corners drive slopes (rise per world unit), speed and line of sight, exactly like flat heightfield maps. cornersFile: raw int16 LE, faces 0..5 each (N+1)^2 row-major; the editor writes it for bodies above 257² corners. Seam corners must be equal on every face that stores them (map_validate warns; the loader averages). Units: move.layer: "orbit" (flies on the orbit shell, free great-circle moves, sees the surface below, can be hit only by weapons whose targets list "orbit"), move.transitSpeed (world units/s for transfers; default 10 x speed). Command kCmdTransit (units = orbit units, param = target body index): timed transfer computed from the body positions at departure, arrival on the facing side of the target's shell; events kEvTransitStart / kEvTransitEnd. Rules movement.planetHpaCells (default 65536): bodies with at least that many cells (6 x faceSize²) use hierarchical pathfinding for long trips (0 = every body). Structures stand inside one face (a footprint crossing a seam is not buildable). Units on different bodies only meet through the orbit layer. Sample: templates/planets.

A map can be generated by the engine instead of (or before) being drawn by hand: deterministic integer code (modules/rts/gen/), so the same request gives a bit-identical map on every platform. It runs at match start (lockstep multiplayer, server arbiter, headless, replays: every peer regenerates the same map from the match seed), in the editor (window Генерация) and over MCP (map_generate, gen_presets), where the result can be baked into a static map. "generate": { "preset": "continents", // gen_presets: built-in + rules "mapgen.presets" "seed": "match", // "match" = the match seed (a new map every match), or a number (fixed map) "players": 4, // 1..8; the map's players array is resized to it (names/factions/teams kept) "symmetry": "auto", // auto | none | point | mirror | mirror-y | mirror4 | rot4 | rotational "template": "maps/valley.json", // optional: map whose player-1 objects are the start kit and whose neutral objects decide what is placed "params": {"water": 0.3, "trees": 1.5} // overrides of the preset's params } Flat maps: top-level generate. Planets: world.bodies[].generate (presets rocky, ocean, moon; see docs/planets.md §4). What the generator writes: size, terrain.rows (. ~ # , = / R, diggable characters for caves), terrain.levels (rules terrain.model levels), terrain.corners (heightfield), fields, entities, regions (if the template has them), roads (garrison games), terrainMaterial (from the biome and the game's visual terrain.layers ids: grass / forest / sand / dirt / earth / rock / snow / mud ...), players' start, and a summary block generated (preset, seed, symmetry, starts, path lengths between starts measured with the engine's A*, connected, pathSpread in per mille, object counts, warnings). Every other key of the map (victory, triggers, waves, lighting, ...) is kept. Objects come from the game's own types: player 1's objects of the template (or of the map itself) are the start kit, placed for every player in the symmetric frame (rotated by quarter turns so footprints stay aligned); neutral objects are counted near the template's bases / far / at the centre and placed the same way (mines and metal spots near each base, forests in forest biomes, creep camps away from bases, garrison buildings, portals...). Without a template the rules decide: a structure that produces workers + 4 workers (or a key unit, or the biggest garrison), resource nodes, structure.on spots, field spawners, neutral creeps. Resource fields of the template are reproduced (near ones keep their offset). Fair starts: the start of player 1 is chosen in the fundamental domain of the symmetry and copied to every image; base areas are flattened (one cliff level / gentle corners, never water); starts are connected (ramps cut through cliffs, shallows = through water, a graded road on heightfields, the cheapest route through diggable rock); objects never block the route between starts (an unblock pass removes them); the result is validated with the pathfinder. "connect": "none" keeps islands separate (naval / air games). Determinism: integers / Fixed only (no float), seeded hashing, ordered containers; the generator runs inside GameCore::setup before the map is loaded, so replays and the server arbiter regenerate identically. Golden hashes of the presets are in tests/tests.cpp (gen_golden_maps and friends): a change of the generator's output shows there. Same seed + params + engine version = same map.

A planet preset as the map's generate builds the whole world block: the bodies (and their orbits, visuals) come from the template map's world (e.g. templates/planets), else a sun + planet + moon. Every surface body gets per-face rows, corners, material; players get start: {body, face, x, y}; objects are written with at. layout: "shared" (default): all players on the start body, rotational symmetry about the polar axis: exact for 2 and 4 players (half / quarter turns map the cube-sphere onto itself, heights are symmetrized corner by corner), averaged over the rotations for 3, 5+ (generated.symmetry: polar-exact / polar). Starts near the equator in the middle of each longitude sector, away from face seams and rough ground; base areas flattened; graded causeways where the ground doesn't connect. layout: "separate": every player on an identical planet of its own (same terrain, same objects), orbiting the star at equal phases; players meet through orbit-layer units (warning when the rules have none). Objects: the template's player-1 objects (offsets measured on its body, across face seams) are the kit; neutral objects near the template bases / far / on moons are counted and reproduced (objects[].moon, objects[].pole); moons get moonResources (default 2) x their share. generated.nearResources lists the resource objects within nearRadius of each start (equal by construction; a warning otherwise). Fairness: the generated map is loaded into a simulation and the engine's MapGrid::findPath measures the ground path between every pair of starts (generated.paths, connected, pathSpread = spread of each player's distance to the nearest rival, per mille). One body only: world.bodies[].generate (terrain + reported start sites, no objects), as before. aiverse_headless --project templates/planets --generate rocky --seed N --players 3 [--gen-params '{"layout": "separate"}']. Optional blocks that make the sample games play like their originals (modules/rts/RtsOriginals*.cpp). A game that uses none of them keeps its exact checksums. These blocks are the single implementation of their mechanic: the agent-mech spellings of the same mechanics (armorModel, type shields, upkeepResources, resourceNode.maxWorkers, "crew": {"accepts"}, upgradeGarrison) are aliases parsed into them (see the agent-mech sections above). block where meaning armor (alias armorModel) rules {"model": "subtract" | "percent" | "classes", "perPoint": 0.06, "minDamage": 1, "minShare": 0.2, "negative": "linear" | "exponential", "base": ["melee", "pierce"]} — the one damage pipeline of every game: weapon bonus, shields, then the model. subtract: StarCraft / AoE with a floor (no block at all: damage - armor, at least damage / 5); percent: Warcraft III (reduction = a·k / (1 + a·k)); classes: AoE II class attacks / armors (type armors, weapon attacks, see the agent-mech aliases above) health.armor object type {"melee": 1, "pierce": 2} (or health.pierceArmor): two armors; weapons pick one with "armorClass": "pierce"; stat pierceArmor / armor2 for techs weapon bonus type {"cavalry": 15, "armored": 10} extra damage vs types with the tag, added before armor (AoE / SC2 bonuses) health.shields (alias type shields: {max, regen, delay, armor}) type shields soak damage first (after the damage table and weapon bonuses; minus shieldArmor, at least the armor floor), the share that breaks through goes on to armor and hp; they recharge shieldRegen per second (default 2) after shieldDelay seconds (default 10) without a hit on the shield (StarCraft) heroes rules {"skills": true, "max": 3, "freeFirst": true, "tiers": ["hall", "keep", "castle"], "revive": {"costShare": 0.4, "perLevel": 0.1, "timeShare": 0.6, "maxTime": 110, "maxCost": {"gold": 700}}} — skill points (one at start, one per level; command kCmdLearn), ability "learnAt": [1, 3, 5] (default) / [6] (ultimate); hero n needs a structure from tiers[n-1..]; a dead hero is trained again as a revive (its level and skills, cheaper) upkeep[].resources, incomeMult (alias upkeepResources) rules upkeep only on some resources (WC3 gold) and / or on per-second income (CoH manpower); rules "upkeepResources": ["gold"] is the default resources of every tier without its own resourceNode.maxGatherers (alias maxWorkers) type workers harvesting at once (WC3 mine 5, SC patch 1); the others wait or take a free node nearby powerField / structure.needsField type {"id": 0, "radius": 6.5} on pylons; structures with needsField are placed and work only inside an own field queueSlots type items produced at once (reactor) cost.garrison (alias upgradeGarrison) type upgrading / converting into this type costs units of the garrison (Mushroom Wars 2) garrison.onCapture, garrison.keep type type it drops to when captured (loses a level); units that always stay home when sending (State.io) clash type units in transit fight hostile units they meet playerMods type {"max": 4, "mods": [{"tags": [...], "stat": "damage", "mul": 1.08}]} — every completed one modifies the owner's types (forges); a mod with "byCount": [1.5, 1.75, 1.9, 2] multiplies by the entry for the number owned (capped by the list) instead of mul^n (Bunker Wars armories) resource gain, perUnit, min rules "gain": {"kill": 1, "capture": 0.3, "captured": -0.4, "upgrade": 0.2, "lost": 0.45, "defended": 0.01}; "perUnit": [{"tags": [...], "stat": "damage", "mul": 1.06}] per whole unit held (morale suns) crew / crews / weapon killsCrew type "crew": "grunt" (or {"unit": "grunt"}): vehicles and guns with a driver; killsCrew (chance per non-lethal hit) empties them (owner 0); units with crews man any empty one (Z). "crew": {"accepts": [tags]} / true (agent-mech alias): units with one of the tags (any mobile unit) may man it too infect type {"by": ["infected"], "spawn": "walker", "count": 3} — killed by a unit with the tag: rises as the spawn type for the killer (They Are Billions)

"foundation": {"startHp": 0.5, "decay": 0.25, "floor": 0.5, "lostWithBuilding": true}, // or just true "types": { "concrete": {"structure": {"footprint": [1, 1], "terrain": "rock"}, "foundation": true, "cost": {"credits": 5, "time": 2}}, "wall": {"weathers": false, ...}, "gas_trap": {"structure": {"footprint": [1, 1]}, "health": {"max": 200}, "trap": {"radius": 0.8, "charges": 5, "rearm": 8, "armTime": 0, "hidden": true, "revealFor": 4, "removeWhenEmpty": true, "layers": ["ground"], "tags": ["hero"], // trigger filter (effect filter keys; or "trigger": {...}) "effects": [{"type": "area", "radius": 2, "lifetime": 5, "trigger": "periodic", "effects": [{"type": "damage", "amount": 18}]}]}}, "queen": {"abilities": [{"id": "inject", "target": "unit", "energy": 25, "smart": "ownProducer", "effects": [{"type": "status", "status": "injected", "duration": 29, "affects": "own", "kind": "structure"}]}]} }, "statuses": {"injected": {"onExpire": [{"type": "addCharges", "amount": 3, "limit": 19, "affects": "own"}]}}, "playerAbilities": [{"id": "chronoshift", "target": "pointPair", "effects": [{"type": "teleportGroup", "radius": 1, "maxTargets": 1, "tags": ["vehicle"], "affects": "own", "duration": 180}]}] Concrete (Dune II): a placed foundation structure turns its cells into the owner's concrete (MapGrid::foundation, drawn by the view's terrain.concrete block: color, seam, alpha, texture) and goes away (event kEvPaved). Concrete doesn't block anything. A structure finished with b = share of its cells not on own concrete gets at most 1 - b·(1 - startHp) of its hp and weathers by decay·b of its max hp per minute down to 1 - b·(1 - floor) (repairs raise it, the weather keeps going). weathers: false exempts a type. Structures of the starting map stand on concrete; a destroyed structure takes its concrete with it (lostWithBuilding). Flat maps only. The AI keeps a few free paved cells near the base and places its buildings on concrete first. Traps: a structure with trap fires its effects at the nearest unit passing the trigger filter (enemy ground and air units by default) within radius (target = the victim, point = its position, caster = the trap), then waits rearm seconds; charges (0 = unlimited) run out and the trap disappears (removeWhenEmpty). hidden traps are invisible to enemies (not targeted, not drawn) except for revealFor seconds after firing and to detectors. Event kEvTrapFired (a = trap, b = victim). The AI builds a few traps at the front of its base, more as the match goes on. Group teleport: see the teleportGroup effect; pointPair player abilities take two clicks (from, to); the second point travels in kCmdPlayerAbility param bits 16..48 (GameCore::packPoint2). Event kEvGroupTeleport (a = unit, value 1 = return trip). The AI shifts its biggest matching group next to the nearest enemy structure. Smart rule ownProducer: autocast / AI target: an own structure without the payload's status that has larva charges (when the payload, or the status it gives, adds charges) or something in production (chrono boost: a status with {"stat": "productionSpeed", "mul": 1.5}).

Still the 3D engine, seen through an orthographic camera; objects can be sprites and the ground a tile map. Two flavours, both pure data (samples: templates/tiles2d, templates/km2d; their placeholder art is generated by tools/art2d/make_samples.py): Tile 2D (Red Alert, Dune II, Warcraft II): camera straight down (pitch: 90), a map tiles layer drawn from a tileset, sprite units and buildings ("mode": "ground"). 3D terrain + sprites (Knights and Merchants): the normal terrain (levels, ramps, heights), camera at a fixed angle (pitch: 50), billboard sprites standing on the ground.

key meaning projection "ortho" or "perspective" (default) pitch, yaw, fov degrees; pitch 90 = straight down, yaw 0 = north up zoom, zoomMin, zoomMax start/limits: visible map cells vertically (ortho) or camera distance (perspective); without zoom the game frames the map pixelsPerCell ortho: start zoom so that one world unit is that many screen pixels (pixel-perfect sprites drawn with the same pixelsPerCell) rotate allow camera rotation (default: false for ortho) The editor uses the projection and angle for its Scene and Game views.

"tank": { ..., "sprite": {"sheet": "sprites/tank.png", "frame": [32, 32], "facings": 8, "mirror": false, "mode": "billboard", "pixelsPerCell": 32, "anchor": [0.5, 1.0], "offset": [0, 0], "team": "magenta", "filter": "nearest", "depthBias": 1.0, "lift": 0, "shadow": {"size": [0.8, 0.45], "alpha": 0.35}, "corpseTime": 4, "actions": {"idle": [0, 1], "move": [1, 4, 8], "attack": {"start": 5, "count": 2, "fps": 6}, "work": [5, 2, 4], "build": {"start": 1, "count": 4, "loop": false}, "die": [7, 3, 6]}}} key meaning sheet image (PNG/JPEG/TGA), required. Rows = facings (row 0 faces east/+X, then clockwise on screen: SE, S, SW, W, ...), columns = animation frames frame frame size in pixels (default: whole sheet width, square — give it for single images that are not square, otherwise the frame reaches past or stops short of the image) facings 1, 4, 8, 16, 32... rows; mirror: true stores only north → east → south (facings/2 + 1 rows) and flips them for the west side actions column ranges [start, count, fps] or {"start", "count", "fps", "loop"}. idle, move, attack, work (gathering/building workers), build (structure under construction; non-looping = frame follows the progress), die (played where the object disappeared, then the last frame stays corpseTime s). Missing actions fall back to idle (work → attack → idle) mode billboard (faces the camera; default), upright (vertical quad), ground (lies on the terrain; top-down games) rotate ground mode with one facing: the quad turns with the object, the top of the image is its front (cars seen from above) size / pixelsPerCell / scale world size: [w, h] cells, or frame pixels / pixelsPerCell; default width = footprint width (structures) or 1 anchor pivot in the frame, 0..1 from the top-left (default [0.5, 1], ground mode [0.5, 0.5]) offset [right, front] cells from the object centre; default for standing structures: the front edge of the footprint, so a 3/4-view drawing stands on its footprint team "magenta" (default): pixels in shades of magenta (r = b, g = 0) become the player's colour times their brightness; "none" shadow "cast" (real sun shadow, see below), "blob" (soft ellipse under the sprite), "none"; true = blob, false = none; the object form {"mode", "size": [w, h], "alpha"} is a blob unless mode says otherwise (size/alpha also shape the blob that replaces a cast shadow on low tiers). Default: the game's sprites.shadow; with the default "blob" only units get one (as before), ground sprites never cast castHeight world height of the shadow caster (default: the drawn height). 3/4-view buildings whose drawing includes the roof seen from above cast a long shadow with the full height: give the real wall + roof height shadowOffset [right, front] cells added to the sprite's offset for the caster (default: the caster stands where the sprite is drawn — for buildings the front edge of the footprint) castDepth buildings cast like a box: a second caster this many cells behind the first (default: the footprint depth for structures, 0 for units) lit override of the game's sprites.lit for this type depthBias, lift pull towards the camera so hills don't cut the sprite; air units float lift cells (default 1.2) above their shadow Sprites are batched (one draw call per sheet), alpha-tested, depth-tested against the 3D scene and painter-sorted; textures are read with platform::readContentFile. Types without sprite keep their 3D view, so a map can mix both.

Game-wide defaults in game.json (wins) or rules.json: "sprites": { "shadow": "cast", "lit": true } key meaning shadow default shadow of every sprite type: "blob" (default, the classic look), "cast", "none" lit sprites take the scene light (default false: painted colours, pixel-art purists): sun and sky colour, day/night and presets, point lights, cloud shadows and (Medium/High) the sun shadows of other objects falling on them. In full default daylight a lit sprite keeps its painted colours Cast shadows: the sprite is drawn into the sun shadow map as an upright alpha-tested quad standing at its foot, facing the camera's yaw (turned towards the sun when the sun shines almost along it), current animation frame and facing; the shadow then falls on the terrain, 3D models and other lit sprites with the sun direction, softness and PCF tiers of the 3D games. AIVERSE_SHADOWS / shadow tier sprites with "shadow": "cast" Off blobs only (the classic look, no shadow pass) Low buildings cast, units keep blobs; sprites don't sample the shadow map Medium / High everything casts (units keep a faint contact blob); lit sprites receive shadows Where shadows fall is the sun's direction: "lighting": {"sunDir": [x, y, z]} (game.json or the map, towards the sun at noon; the day cycle swings around it). Flat drawings hide shadows that fall straight behind them, and a sun behind the scene leaves camera-facing cliff walls unlit, so sprite games usually want it from the side and a little in front (km2d: [-1.0, 1.2, 0.45], shadows to the right). "shadowSoftness" (world units, default 0.22) is the maximum penumbra radius. Medium/high sun shadows harden at contact and widen with caster/receiver separation (PCSS); pixel-art games look cleaner with a tight one (km2d 0.07): kernels of a few shadow-map texels are filtered without the per-pixel noise rotation, so they stay smooth on every tier. Blobs and ground sprites are projected: a blob (and any "mode": "ground" sprite) is cut from the ground triangles under it — the exact triangles of the terrain mesh or the tile map — and drawn with a depth bias, so it bends over slopes and cliff edges and never z-fights or hovers. Sprite types get no extra contact-shadow decal from the lighting system (their blob does that job).

"tiles": {"tileset": "tilesets/desert.json", "rows": ["sssrrr", "..."], "fixed": [[x, y, tile]], "seed": 0} When a map with tiles is loaded (game, headless, editor play), the tile terrains' gameplay is written into terrain.rows, terrain.levels and a fields entry ("fromTiles": true) before the simulation starts — deterministic and idempotent; the simulation itself knows nothing about tiles. The editor also bakes it while painting, so saved maps carry valid terrain anyway. fixed places exact atlas tiles (autotile off). Optional block "environment" in rules.json (defaults) and in the map (map keys win, key by key). Code: modules/rts/RtsEnv*.cpp. A game without the block has no environment state and keeps its checksums and saves. State: the EnvState world resource (hashed, saved after the grid fields, rolled back with the world). The environment system runs before death (only with the block), environment3 after vision (only with fog). Flat maps only (planets are not supported). Units: positions are world coordinates; every distance / speed key (lightningKillRange, wind forces, spline velocity, ...) is divided by "scale" (authored distance units per world unit, default 1), so an importer copies source values verbatim and sets scale. Times are seconds. Skills are rules playerAbilities ids cast for the neutral player without cost. "environment": { "scale": 30, "season": "winter", "weather": ["rain", "snow", "lightning", "blizzard"], "weatherParams": {"puddlesFillSpeed": 20, "puddlesDrySpeed": 20, "rainWaitTime": 60, "noRainWaitTime": 30, "snowRestoringSpeed": 0.005, "snowWaitTime": 30, "snowFillRandomFactor": 0.6, "snowFillTimeRange": [40, 60], "blizzardWaitTime": 30, "blizzardFillTime": 40, "blizzardUnitKillSpeed": 5, "blizzardUnitSpeedFactor": 0.5, "blizzardUnitKillFactor": [1, 2], "blizzardVar": "blizzard", "lightningKillTime": 2, "lightningKillFactor": 70, "lightningKillRange": 80, "lightningPointKillValue": 10, "lightningTime": 30, "lightningWaitTime": 30, "lightningBurn": {"field": "fire", "value": 100, "radius": 40}, "grassRainBurnRandomFactor": 0.5}, "wind": {"minIdleDuration": 5, "maxIdleDuration": 10, "minBlowDuration": 5, "maxBlowDuration": 10, "minForce": 40, "maxForce": 80}, "zones": [{"id": "pond", "kind": "water", "poly": [[x, z], ...], "slowdown": 2}], // water | road | any other tag; "rect" / "circle" "splines": [{"id": "lava", "points": [[x, z], ...], "loop": false, "skill": "moving_flame", "velocity": 100, "emitPeriod": 10, "firstEmissionCooldown": -1}], "trample": [{"field": "snow", "perSecond": 0.1, "speed": [[1, 1], [0.9, 1], [0.7, 0.9], [0.4, 0.75], [0.1, 0.5]], "snowRestore": true}, {"field": "grass", "perSecond": -0.2, "lerpSpeed": 0.6, "killField": "fire", "hideStatus": "in_grass", "hideAbove": 0.3}], "fog": {"memory": false, "startFowSize": 3000, "startDuration": 3} } // rules.json "fogOfWar": {"ellipse": 2} // sight discs dx^2 + (2 dz)^2 <= r^2 (isometric fog) block behaviour weather rain: puddles fill / wait / dry / wait; water zones slow by lerp(slowdown, 1, 1 - puddles) (no rain: full slowdown; winter: never). Snow (winter): wait, then with snowFillRandomFactor a restore phase that lowers every snowRestore trample field. Blizzard: walkers on lanes lose blizzard health dt / killSpeed / resist (resist random per unit), slow down by blizzardUnitSpeedFactor and die; the trigger var blizzardVar is 1 while it blows (bots, scripts). Lightning: every lightningKillTime with lightningKillFactor % a random unit and everything in the ellipse (range, range / 2) around it dies, or a building loses lightningPointKillValue garrison units; lightningBurn sets a grid field there wind idle, then blows in the next of 8 directions (angle = dir * 45 degrees from +z toward +x) with a random force: speed + dot(facing, force) zones speed / slowdown in the first zone containing a ground unit; road zones skip the trample speed tables. kind is kept as the zone's tag, so a game's native module can give its own kinds a meaning splines paths (Catmull-Rom through the points). With skill: the ability is cast at the first point every emitPeriod and its areas ride the spline at velocity (moving hazards); on multiscreen maps only while the whole spline is on the screen trample moving ground units add perSecond to a grid field (docs/fields.md); speed table (last row with value <= first wins), lerpSpeed, killField (units on burning cells die; with rain its spread kernels succeed with grassRainBurnRandomFactor, GridFields::setSpreadScale), hideStatus fog

Visual keys of rules.json "fogOfWar" (game.json "fogOfWar" overrides key by key; editor window Туман войны, or rules_merge {path: "fogOfWar", value: {...}} over MCP): "fogOfWar": { "mode": "full", // simulation: full | explored | none (see rules table) "show": true, // false: no fog drawn (enemies outside sight stay hidden) "color": [8, 10, 14], // 0..255 or 0..1 "unexplored": 0.92, "explored": 0.47, // opacity over never-seen / seen-before ground "style": "smooth", // smooth | cells | grid (cells + lines) | pattern (dithered edge, classic) "softness": 2, // blur radius in cells (smooth, pattern) "fade": 0.3, // seconds for a cell to clear / fog over "noise": 0.0, // 0..1 cloudy moving edges "height": 1.3, // sheet height above the ground (covers units and low buildings) "grid": {"show": "fog", "color": [255, 255, 255], "alpha": 0.15} // none | fog | all } Weak GPUs (shadow quality off/low) draw smooth as cells without noise. Heightfield maps draw the fog in the terrain shader (colour, transparency, cells, grid; pattern and noise are sheet-only).

With "fogOfWar": {"lineOfSight": true} (always on for heightfield maps with heights.blockVision) each ground unit sees a cell only if the straight line from its eyes to the cell clears every cell in between. Heights: heightfield surface, or cliff level × levelHeight on level maps; plus dynamic occluders, recomputed every vision pass (5 ticks): Source Key Height above the ground Unit or structure type (walls, forests, tall buildings) type "vision": {"blocks": 3} over its footprint (structures) or its cell; gone when it dies Smoke, dust, wall-of-fog skills delivery {"type": "area", "radius": 2, "lifetime": 10, "blocksVision": 4} disc of the area while it lasts Undug rock fogOfWar.rockHeight (2, 0 = transparent) every rock cell Eyes: terrain.eyeHeight + type "vision": {"eye": 6} (watchtowers see over walls and hills); targets count terrain.targetHeight. Air units and types with "vision": {"seesOver": true} see the full circle. Integer math, deterministic; editor: Туман войны → "3D: линия видимости".

h: Overlays (helper elements on screen and in the world)
x: Optional list "overlays" in rules.json; game.json "overlays" adds entries or overrides them by id. An overlay is a condition (when), a place (anchor), a shape and a style, optionally spawned by simulation events. Presentation only: overlays never change the simulation. Editor: window Оверлеи (list, templates, JSON, preview); MCP: overlay_templates, overlay_list, overlay_get, overlay_set, overlay_delete, overlay_preview (+ view_screenshot). "overlays": [ { "id": "build_grid", "when": "placing", "anchor": "ghost", "shape": {"type": "grid", "radius": 4, "predicate": "buildable"}, "style": {"colors": {"true": "#3cff6450", "false": "#ff3c3c60"}, "lineColor": "#ffffff38", "outerAlpha": 0.55} } ] Built-in overlays are ordinary entries (the look the engine always had); override any key by id (objects are deep-merged, "replace": true replaces the whole entry), or hide one with {"id": "health_bars", "enabled": false}. A game without the block looks exactly as before. id what selection ring under selected objects (#78ff78e6; neutral objects #ffffa0e6) hover ring under the hovered object when it is not selected move_markers small ring where a move order was given placement footprint of the structure being placed, green / red (predicate: "ok") garrison_count garrison number in an owner-coloured pill health_bars hp bar of selected / hovered / damaged objects (26 px units, 46 px structures) build_progress construction bar Entry keys: id (required, unique), enabled (default true), order (draw order, default 0, then list order), when, anchor, shape, style, event; name / description are free text. Unknown keys, types, tags, statuses, colours or impossible combinations are errors (overlay 'x'.anchor.types: unknown type 'dragon'); at game start a broken entry is skipped with a warning, overlay_set refuses it.

A string, a list (all must hold) or an object (every key must hold). Strings: always, never, placing, selected, hovered, cursor, playing, paused, over. key holds when always true / false placing true: a structure is being placed; "id" / ["id", "tag:x"]: one of these types selected entity anchors: this object is selected (false: is not); other anchors: something selected. A filter object / type list narrows it: {"selected": {"owner": "own", "flags": ["ranged"]}} hovered the same for the object under the cursor entity entity filter on the anchored object (other anchors: any visible object matches) types, tags, owner, flags, status, hp shorthand for an entity filter at the top level key keys held: "Alt", ["Shift", "Q"] (A–Z, 0–9, F1–F12, Shift, Ctrl, Alt, Super, Space, Tab, Enter, arrows) state "playing" / "paused" / "over" or a list var / flag trigger variable: "alarm" (non-zero) or {"name": "alarm", ">=": 3} (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=) zoom camera distance in [min, max] cursor the cursor is over the map (true / false) mode client input mode: normal, attack, patrol, place, rally, ability, claim any / all / not combinations Entity filter (when, entity anchors): types (ids or "tag:x"), tags, owner (own, ally, friendly, enemy, neutral, any, or a list), flags (all must hold, ! negates: structure, unit, constructing, damaged (hp < 99.9%), garrison, moving, producing, idle, hero, worker, invulnerable, air, carrying, attacking, resource, energy, ranged (a weapon with range > 1.5), aura), status (any of these statuses active), hp ([min, max) fraction).

"hit" or {"on": "hit" | [...], "lifetime": 1.2, "rise": 0, "grow": 0, "spread": 0, "by": "own", "owner": "enemy", "types": [...], "max": 32}: every matching simulation event spawns a popup at its position for lifetime seconds, rising rise units / s, rings / icons growing grow / s. by = relation of the player who caused it, owner = of the object it happened to, types = its type. Events: hit, died, spawned, attack, gathered, delivered, produced, ability, cast, impact, miss, built, placed, trained, researched, levelup, captured, sold, upgraded, alert (under attack), status, area, claimed, wave, message, ping (pings of the client / editor). Popups never appear in cells the local player cannot see. Quality tiers (renderer material quality; AIVERSE_OVERLAYS=low|medium|high for testing): game overlays are capped per overlay (48 / 192 / 1024 elements), per grid / cells shape (600 / 3000 / 12000 cells) and in live popups (24 / 96 / 256); low halves ring segments. Built-in overlays are never capped.

game.json and maps can have a "postfx" block: a list of full-screen effects (bloom, colour grading, LUT, vignette, tilt-shift, sun shafts, FXAA, grain, ...) with quality tiers and a frame-cost model. Format, parameters, tiers and MCP tools: docs/postfx.md.

Optional map initialVars is an object of integer trigger variables loaded before user scripts. Example: "initialVars": {"loadout_support_1": 2}. At most 128 keys, ASCII letters/digits/underscore/dot/hyphen, length 1–128; integers −1000000..1000000. Values enter ordinary trig.vars hashing. Client UI can pass overrides with game.start(..., {initialVars=...}); see docs/ui-scripting.md. Saved map/replay setup retains the options, and omitted options preserve old behavior.

The bot reads the state and submits commands like a player (replays don't re-run it). Generic for every template; knobs in rules ai (above). What it does with the terrain: Analysis at match start (RtsAITerrain.*, integer, rebuilt identically after loading a save): per cell the elevation in height-advantage units (cliff level, or heightfield / planet height divided by levelHeight), the walkable mask of the ground layer (terrain only), corridor width (steps to the nearest wall: chokepoints), over (how far higher ground within 4 cells rises above the cell) and crest (prominence). Flat maps, heightfields and cube-sphere planets (neighbours across face seams) alike. Routes: weighted Dijkstra from our base to the nearest enemy base: climbing into the enemy and cells overlooked by higher ground cost extra (climbWeight, exposureWeight), so waves come through saddles and ramps instead of up a ridge under fire; an alternate route avoids the main corridor (used on odd waves when stalemated). Posts on the route: rally point on the highest well-covered ground 9-14 steps out of the base (the army waits there, producers rally there); the narrowest cell on our side (towers after a raid); a watch post on the most prominent ground in the middle of the route for a scout (vision over ridges). Idle units are not re-sent to the rally point (a unit walking back would not count as ready for the next wave). Waves follow waypoints every 12 cells, stop at a siege spot on high ground short of the target, then attack; they hold up to 30 s instead of charging uphill into a stronger enemy (and pull in reinforcements), retreat to the rally point below 25% of their start size without a kill (until stalemate level 3), launch early with what is at home when our army is twice the enemy's whole armed force, stop at a stuck-wave watchdog (30 s without moving), retarget the next structure, attack construction sites by name. Economy guards: own build spots (lanes between dropoffs and resources kept free, the rally area kept free, random tie-breaks), stuck builders released and their spots avoided, the first army producer early, converters (metal makers) only with a surplus, one more producer when resources float, expansion (a dropoff at the next node) when the near nodes are gone, workers spread over crowded nodes and spawned on the side of their resource. Breaking stalemates: an enemy without armed units is finished by the whole army (its weakest structure that counts); at stalemate level 1+ a smaller strength edge launches a wave and at level 2+ waves are capped at 3/4 of firstAttackArmy; the bot builds / researches what unlocks units clearly better against the enemy's toughest building (damage table, bonuses, armor) and saves for it; garrison play sends from full garrisons first, funnels them to the front and after 10 min lets every garrison join a push; settlers economies build the main building material chain first, then what the army costs; a stock the population eats running dry stops housing; regions that must be seen first get a scout; slow gatherers (no workersPerBase in the rules) get more workers. Planets: an orbit fleet (invasionSize + 2 per invasion) transfers together to the body with enemy structures and fights there until the body is clear, then the next body; more orbital yards when the enemy can be reached only through orbit; towers that hit the orbit when attacks come from there. Per-slot styles: map players[i].ai (see "Maps") gives one slot a preset and its own knobs; applied before the first think (and again identically after a load), so thinkTicks from the slot is used from the start. Save states: ComputerPlayer::saveState() / loadState() (headless --save F writes F.ai next to the sim state, --load F reads it): a restored bot plays on exactly like the saved one.

Rules block topDown (one directly controlled hero per player: stick movement with acceleration and wall sliding, aim snap cone, auto-fire policy, abilities along the aim, respawn) and game.json block topDown (virtual joystick, aim stick, ability buttons, keyboard / mouse / gamepad, follow camera). Keys, defaults and behaviour: docs/topdown.md. Sample: templates/topdown_arena.

Optional rules block progression: the match-progression library format (stats, perks, units, deck, xp with toNext / curve / kill, offers with default / levels / variants / preferNewRecruitAtLevel / recruitWeight / recruitAiPriority, summonPoints with id / team / position / radiusMilli / progressTicks / cooldownTicks / singleUse / action; perks with key, hook, scope, bearer, effects (stat, op, value, stage), maxSelections, minLevel, weight, requires, excludes, tags, upgrades, offerable, aiPriority, aiPriorityLowHealth) on real units, plus engine keys: units[].type, perks[].bullet (modifiers: split / ricochet / flyThrough / damage / speed / radius appended to the bearer's projectile programs), perks[].onHit / onHitChance (effects payload on hit: burn, stun, ...), players, killXp, orbs, orbOwner, autoOpen, offerAt, offerChoices, offerRerolls, rerollAvoidsRepeat, maxLevel, xpGrowthPerLevel, maxRecruitsPerSlot, maxSquad, pickups (radius, magnetRadius, grabRadius, attractSpeed, attractAccel, maxSpeed, landing, lifetime, maxOrbs), summons (progress, cooldown, maxAllies, charges, chargeRecharge, resetOnExit), squad (follow, lifetime), critDamage, decks, defaultDeck (battle deck payloads: player, techLevel, choiceCount, enforceUnlocks, slots with slot, unit, level, opened, inTeam, perks). Map: progression.summonPoints, players[i].deck (the match start payload). Hero xp from kills and xp orbs, seeded level-up offers chosen with kCmdProgression (UI, bot, Lua, MCP), perk stats on damage / incoming damage / speed / fire interval / range / max health / splash / crits / regen, summon circles and recruits as real units. Full reference: progression.md; sample: templates/perk_arena.

Rules block encounters (boss-encounters library on real units; reference docs/encounters.md, sample templates/boss_arena). Map players with "monsters": true and hostile creeps (owner 255) are driven by it (the computer player skips them). attacks.<id>: shape (circle / cone / line / ring), radius, inner, angle, length, width, anchor (source / aim), offset, windup, active, recovery, interval, cooldown, damage, damageMin, falloff, damageType, statuses (rules status ids or {"status", "duration"}), statusDuration, oncePerTarget, trackAim, sweep, cancelOnDeath, friendlyFire, minRange, maxRange, ability (a unit ability starts it). bosses.<unit type>: engageRange, loseRange, approach, immune, archetype, phases[] (hpBelow, after, damage, speed, cooldown, globalCooldown, transition, mode byRange / sequence / weighted, pattern[] (attack, alternate, minRange, maxRange, weight), adds[] (unit, count, every, maxAlive, minRadius, maxRadius)), enrage (after, hpBelow, damage, speed, cooldown). mobs.<unit type>: aggroRange, loseRange, stopDistance, switchMargin, wanderMin, wanderMax, arriveRadius, leash, wanderDelay, wanderLeg, wanderAttempts, fleeBelow, fleeRecover, fleeRange, fleeTime, wander, spacing, correction, lookAhead, neighbours, attack, think, flowDistance. schedule: personal, rotation, archetypes, spawnDistance [min, max], windows[] (start, end, breather, excludePrevious, pauseWaves, variants[] (boss, weight, archetype)). Lua events boss_engaged, boss_phase, boss_enraged, boss_adds, boss_defeated, boss_window, telegraph_start, telegraph_strike, telegraph_end (statuses: status_start); table encounters.

Rules block traffic (with topDown + driving): computer-driven cars on lanes built from the map's tile characters, signalised junctions with light props, pedestrians on the sidewalks who cross on "walk" and panic at gunfire; map "traffic": false switches it off. Keys, defaults and behaviour: docs/traffic.md.

Weapons and projectile deliveries accept an optional flight object with ordered Split, Ricochet, Fly Through and scalar modifiers. See Projectile programs for the schema, inheritance rules, collision boundaries, save version and executable example. Legacy projectiles are unchanged when this block is absent. Source on GitHub: docs/game-format.md

h: Packages: optional content from the catalog
x: The engine repository carries code and a minimal set of assets. Heavy optional content — PBR material libraries, their source images, project templates, model packs, sound, effects — lives in the package catalog AIVERSE-PACKAGES. A project downloads only what it uses. Piece Where Catalog: packages by category (materials/, textures/, templates/, models/, audio/, vfx/, ui/, scripts/, plugins/, tools/) AIVERSE-PACKAGES, <category>/<id>/aiverse.package.json Archives <id>-<version>.zip GitHub releases <id>@<version> of AIVERSE-PACKAGES Index index.json on its main: {id, category, path} per package; the package folder has aiverse.package.json and versions.json (written by the publish workflow) Client tools/pkg/aiverse_pkg.py (stdlib Python; --json on every command) Cache on this machine ~/.aiverse/packages/<id>/<version>/ (AIVERSE_PACKAGES_HOME), downloads verified by SHA-256 Website page Catalog (catalog.html): previews, description, minimum engine version, download

python3 tools/pkg/aiverse_pkg.py search terrain # also --category materials, --kind content python3 tools/pkg/aiverse_pkg.py info terrain-pbr python3 tools/pkg/aiverse_pkg.py add terrain-pbr --project ~/Games/MyGame python3 tools/pkg/aiverse_pkg.py status --project ~/Games/MyGame python3 tools/pkg/aiverse_pkg.py install --project ~/Games/MyGame # fresh clone: restore from aiverse.lock python3 tools/pkg/aiverse_pkg.py verify --project ~/Games/MyGame # exit 1 when installed files changed python3 tools/pkg/aiverse_pkg.py remove terrain-pbr --project ~/Games/MyGame python3 tools/pkg/aiverse_pkg.py fetch terrain-pbr-sources # authoring sources: prints the cached folder python3 tools/pkg/aiverse_pkg.py create <template-id> ~/Games/New # new project from a template package content packages are copied into the project at install.mount (for terrain-pbr: materials/terrain); install.mergeJson merges their material library into the project's materials.json. Ids the project already uses with another value are never overwritten (add fails; --force overrides). The project ships the files like any of its own, so a build needs no network and aiversebuild packs only what the project holds. game.json → "packages": {"terrain-pbr": "^1.0.0"} lists the wanted ranges; aiverse.lock next to it pins the exact version, archive hash and every installed file's hash. Commit both. source packages (bake inputs) and other tool data are never copied into projects: tools call aiverse_pkg.package_dir('<id>') (Python) and get the cached folder, downloading it once. template packages are whole project folders: create copies one and installs the packages its game.json lists. templates lists them: the official ones (made by the AIVERSE authors, marked official in the catalog) by default, every template package with --all, filtered by words; --cached answers from the cache without the network. Dependencies: add installs the content packages a package depends on first (a model pack uses the textures of terrain-pbr / vegetation-pbr through a relative path instead of copies). Version ranges: exact 1.2.3, ^1.2 (same major), ~1.2.3 (same minor), >=1.0.0, *. Every package declares minEngine; add prints a note when this checkout is older. Offline: AIVERSE_PACKAGES_OFFLINE=1 uses only the cache and the last downloaded index. C++ host tools and the editor find cached packages with engine/pack/Packages.h (aiverse::pack::cachedPackageDir("vegetation-pbr")). A game never reads the cache. Editor: the Studio window Catalog (Look and Publish workspaces, or "Catalog" in Search or run) searches the catalog, shows a package and installs or removes it in one click; it warns when the project's packages have missing or changed files and restores them from aiverse.lock. Agents use the same through MCP: package_search, package_info, package_status, package_add, package_remove, package_install, package_skill (they run aiverse_pkg.py on the open project).

h: Project templates come from the catalog
x: The engine's sample games are official template packages (templates/<id> of AIVERSE-PACKAGES, "official": true, authors ["AIVERSE"]), so a template can grow with its own textures, models and code without growing the engine. The start screen of AIVERSE Studio lists the official templates first (it opens from the package cache instantly and refreshes the list from the catalog in the background); More templates from the catalog… searches every template package, community ones included. A project made from a template package is downloaded, checked against its hash and unpacked into the folder you pick, then the packages its game.json lists are installed. MCP and the ImGui hub: list_projects returns the same list (ids pkg:<package> for catalog templates); create_project {template: "pkg:skirmish"} creates a project from a package. The engine repository has no templates/ folder any more. Tests, CI, the default client content and the game wizard read the official templates from one installed folder, named by engine id (skirmish/, mushrooms/, ...): AIVERSE_TEMPLATES_DIR, default ~/.aiverse/packages/templates. python3 tools/pkg/fetch_templates.py [--out DIR] [--only skirmish,...] installs or updates them (a second run is offline) and prints the folder; CMake runs it at configure time when the folder is missing (-DAIVERSE_FETCH_TEMPLATES=OFF to skip, target aiverse_fetch_templates to update). Changing a sample game: edit it in a checkout of AIVERSE-PACKAGES (generators in tools/templates/ edit the installed copies), bump the package version and open a catalog pull request; determinism baselines in tests/checksums/baseline.txt follow the package versions.

apps/catalogview (CMake -DAIVERSE_BUILD_CATALOGVIEW=ON, target aiverse_catalogview) shows a package's materials or its glTF / GLB models through Renderer3D with an orbit camera. A package opts in with a viewer block in its manifest; the catalog's pages workflow builds view/<id>/<version>/ (view.json + the files exactly as published, textures at their own size) and the WebAssembly viewer from this repository, and deploys both to the catalog's GitHub Pages. The website's Catalog card gets a 3D preview button that opens viewer/?src=../view/<id>/<version>&lang=ru|en in the card. Materials: a shape switch (sphere, cube, cylinder, plane) over a tiled slab; texel density is the same on every shape (one repeat per repeat metres, whole repeats around closed shapes so the seams meet). The info panel lists every texture map with its size in pixels and its file size. Models: Auto LOD (the level the renderer picked is highlighted), a fixed LOD 0…n, or STRATA (clusters built from the model on first request; Clusters colours them). Wireframe shows the edges of the shown level. The panel lists triangles per level, whether the engine generated the LODs, STRATA cluster count and build time, and the model's textures. Every loading state shows the animated AIVERSE mark (the same one as the site, Studio and web builds; tools/branding/logo/loader.py keeps the copies in sync, CTest branding_loader). URL parameters: src, item, shape=sphere|cube|cylinder|plane, lod=auto|strata|N, wire, clusters, lang. Desktop check: aiverse_catalogview --src <view folder> [--item N] [--shape S] [--lod auto|strata|N] [--wire] [--clusters] [--yaw deg] [--pitch deg] (AIVERSE_SCREENSHOT works as in the client; every change prints a catalogview-info: {...} line, the same JSON the page receives).

h: Packages that left the engine repository (2026-11-22)
x: Package Was Now in the engine terrain-pbr (materials, 14 PBR ground materials) engine/assets/materials/terrain checkerboard only (empty projects) vegetation-pbr (materials, bark + leaf atlases, bark projection, winter) engine/assets/materials/vegetation — terrain-pbr-sources (textures) tools/terrain/pbr_sources — vegetation-pbr-sources (textures) tools/vegetation/pbr_sources — The tools that used those folders now take them from the catalog: tools/terrain/install_pbr_pack.py (= add terrain-pbr), bake_pbr_pack.py --root <payload copy> (sources from the catalog), build_detail_materials.py, bake_landscape_pbr.py, tools/vegetation/*. The editor's TerraWeave forest preview reads vegetation-pbr textures from the project, else from the cache.

A repository skill lists the packages it needs in its frontmatter: --- name: aiverse-terra-vegetation description: ... packages: vegetation-pbr, terrain-pbr --- python3 tools/skills/catalog.py search|plan shows them (contentPackages, with ready install commands in plan), and python3 tools/pkg/aiverse_pkg.py skill <skill-id> --project P installs them. Agents: before following such a skill in a project, install its packages; never copy package files into the engine repository.

h: Adding your package to the catalog
x: Anyone can offer a package; the owner reviews every pull request. What you need: content you may redistribute under a permissive licence (MIT, BSD-2/3, Apache-2.0, Zlib, CC0, CC-BY-4.0, OFL-1.1), a real engine frame or the asset itself as a preview, and a GitHub account. Fork AIVERSE-PACKAGES and create the folder <category>/<id>/ — category one of templates, materials, textures, models, audio, vfx, ui, scripts, plugins, tools; id of lowercase letters, digits and -, unique in the catalog. Write aiverse.package.json. Texts are English; translations are optional <key>-<lang> fields (ru, zh-CN, ja, ko, es, pt-BR, de, fr): json { "schema": 2, "id": "my-rocks", "version": "1.0.0", "kind": "content", "category": "models", "title": "Desert rocks", "title-ru": "Камни пустыни", "summary": "Eight sandstone rocks with three LODs each.", "summary-ru": "Восемь песчаниковых камней, по три LOD.", "license": "CC0-1.0", "minEngine": "3.1.0", "authors": ["Your Name"], "tags": ["rocks", "desert"], "dependencies": {"terrain-pbr": "^1.0"}, "install": {"mount": "models/my-rocks"}, "viewer": {"kind": "models", "items": [{"model": "rock-0.gltf", "title": "Rock 1", "title-ru": "Камень 1"}]} } kind: content is copied into a project at install.mount, template is a whole project, source stays in the cache for tools. All fields: docs/manifest.md of the catalog. Add README.md (what it is, how to use it, licence and origin) and at least one preview.jpg (640..2400 px wide, up to 1 MB, up to 6 previews). Put the payload into files/, laid out as it should appear under install.mount — up to 2 GB in total. Git takes files up to 100 MB; for a bigger single file run python3 tools/catalog.py upload <id> --repo <you>/AIVERSE-PACKAGES (zips files/ into a release of your fork and writes "archive" into the manifest) and remove files/ from the pull request. Textures another package already has are not copied: depend on that package and refer to its files with a relative path from your mount (../../../materials/terrain/textures/…); aiverse_pkg.py add installs dependencies first. Check: python3 tools/catalog.py check must print 0 errors. To try it in a project, copy files/ into the install.mount folder of a test project and open it in the editor. Open a pull request. CI repeats the check. The owner accepts it with the label accept, not the Merge button: the files become the release archive <id>@<version> and the package lands in main without them (its manifest gets "archive"), so uploaded files never enter the repository history. versions.json, the line in index.json, the website card and the 3D preview follow within minutes. Updating: change the files, raise version and open a pull request. A published version is never replaced (projects pin the archive hash in aiverse.lock). How the catalog stores it: index.json at the catalog root lists only {id, category, path} of every package (and the category names); the package folder holds aiverse.package.json (written by the author) and versions.json (written by publish: versions, archive URLs and SHA-256, previews, the 3D preview URL). Heavy assets are never committed to the engine repository again. Source on GitHub: docs/packages.md

Mechanics that the data blocks of rules.json can't express are written as Lua 5.4 scripts in the game folder. Scripts are content: they are read when a match starts, packed into content.rpak like any other file, edited in the editor with hot reload, and the engine never has to be rebuilt. There are two kinds of scripts: simulation scripts view scripts listed in rules / map "scripts": ["scripts/x.lua"] rules / map "viewScripts": ["scripts/view/x.lua"] runs inside the deterministic tick, on every machine of a match, in replays on the local machine only, every frame numbers integers and fx (fixed point); no floats normal Lua numbers may read and change the game (game.* actions) read the game, show notices / effects / sounds A game without "scripts" runs only the engine's standard library (below): no "scripts" system, no budget, identical checksums. // rules.json { "scripts": ["scripts/rules.lua", "scripts/abilities.lua"], "scriptBudget": 1000000, // optional: VM instructions per tick for all simulation scripts "types": { "archer": {"abilities": [{"id": "mend", "target": "none", "cooldown": 20, "autocast": true, "effects": [{"type": "script", "fn": "chain_heal", "jumps": 3, "amount": 60}]}]} } } Sample: templates/scripted (Iron and Gold + a war chest, veterans, a scripted chain heal and a custom defeat condition).

-- scripts/rules.lua local util = require("lib.util") -- scripts/lib/util.lua (only files of the game) function on_start() -- global on_<event> functions are handlers state.kills = {} -- persistent data lives in `state` game.message(0, "Hold the bridge!") -- 0 = every player end -- every 30 seconds the player with the most units gets 50 gold every(30, function(tick) local best, most = nil, -1 for _, p in ipairs(game.players()) do local n = game.count{owner = p, kind = "unit"} if game.player_alive(p) and n > most then best, most = p, n end end if best then game.give(best, "gold", 50) end end) on("unit_died", function(e) state.kills[e.owner] = (state.kills[e.owner] or 0) + 1 if state.kills[e.owner] >= 50 then game.defeat(e.owner) end end)

Lockstep multiplayer and replays re-run the same scripts on every machine and must get bit-identical results on Windows, macOS, iOS, Android and the web. The engine enforces most of it; the rest is a small contract.

Lua 5.4 has integers and floats. Floats can differ between platforms, so a simulation script never sees one: Float literals are rejected when a file loads — x * 1.5, 1e3, .5, 0x1p4 give scripts/x.lua:12: float literal 1.5 - use fx("1.5") or an integer. Float arithmetic raises an error — / and ^ always produce floats in Lua, so 7 / 2, n / 2, 2 ^ 3 fail with "float arithmetic is not allowed in simulation scripts (use fx() numbers, or // for integer division)". Use 7 // 2 (integer division, = 3) or fx(7) / 2 (= 3.5). The guard sits inside the VM (third_party/lua/aiverse_luaconf.h), so it also catches floats made from strings ("1.5" + 1). Every API function that takes a number accepts only integers or fx; a float gives "got a float - use fx() or integers". fx is the engine's fixed-point number (Q47.16, engine/core/Fixed.h), the same type all gameplay math uses: local a = fx(3) -- 3 local b = fx(3, 4) -- 0.75 (3 / 4) local c = fx("1.25") -- 1.25 (decimal string, parsed with integers only) local d = a * b + 2 -- fx mixes with integers: + - * / // % unary - if d >= 4 then ... end -- < <= > >= work between fx and integers print(d, tostring(c)) -- "4.25" (formatted without floats) fx.sqrt(d) fx.abs(x) fx.min(a, b) fx.max(a, b) fx.lerp(a, b, t) fx.floor(d) fx.ceil(d) fx.round(d) fx.int(d) -- -> integers (also d:floor() ...) fx.is(v) math.type(v) == "fx" Pitfall: fx(1) == 1 is false — Lua only calls __eq when both values are tables or userdata. Compare fx with fx (v == fx(1)) or use <, <=, >=. Values from the game are fx when they can be fractional (positions, hp, resources, time) and integers when they can't (ticks, counts, players, levels, handles). math keeps abs, min, max, floor, ceil, sqrt (→ fx), tointeger, type, maxinteger, mininteger and math.random (simulation RNG: math.random(n), math.random(a, b) integers, math.random() an fx in [0, 1)). tonumber("12") works; tonumber("1.5") is an error (use fx("1.5")).

h: IEEE floats as bit patterns: f32, f64
x: A script that must reproduce another program's floating-point results exactly (a port of a game that simulates in float) keeps each value as its IEEE bit pattern in an integer: binary32 as 0..0xffffffff, binary64 as the signed 64-bit reinterpretation (BitConverter.DoubleToInt64Bits). The f32 and f64 tables do one correctly rounded IEEE operation per call (round to nearest even; NaN results are the canonical quiet NaN 0x7fc00000 / 0x7ff8000000000000), so results are identical on every platform: f32.add/sub/mul/div(a, b), f32.sqrt(a) binary32 arithmetic f32.dot2(a, b, c, d) a*b + c*d rounded once (fused two-term dot product) f32.fromint(i), f32.tof64(a) integer → binary32 (rounded); binary32 → binary64 (exact) f32.lt/le/eq(a, b) IEEE comparisons (NaN unordered, -0 == +0) f32.fdot2(a, b, c, d) dot2 of finite operands (a non-finite operand is an error) f32.sqdist(p, q) fdot2(x, x, y, y) of x = p.x - q.x, y = p.y - q.y (tables with x, y; each difference rounded) f32.floorint(a) floor as an integer; a finite with |a| < 2^31, otherwise an error f32.atan2(y, x), f32.sincos(a) binary32 atan2 / sine and cosine: an exact series in 96-bit fixed point rounded once (sticky bit), as an integer-only port computes them; |a| <= 2^33, finite operands, otherwise an error f32.segment(walkable, burning, owners, w, h, first, second, from, to) four-connected grid walk from point from to to (corner crossings check both cells): true when every cell is inside, walkable[c] == true, not in burning (may be nil) and owned by first or second (may be nil); the crossing parameters are binary32 operations; more than w + h steps is false f32.cellat(p, w, h) grid cell y*w + x of x = floorint(p.x), y = floorint(p.y), or -1 outside 0..w-1 × 0..h-1 f64.add/sub/mul/div(a, b), f64.sqrt(a), f64.fromint(i), f64.tof32(d), f64.lt/le/eq(a, b) the same for binary64 Arguments must be integers (f32 ones in range), otherwise the call is an error. Both tables exist in simulation and view scripts. (Built on the host's IEEE operations with one operation per call, no FMA contraction and a check of the default floating-point environment: engine/game/ScriptIeee.cpp.)

Everything a script remembers between ticks must be in the global table state, in an entity's own table game.data(h), or in trigger variables (game.set_var). The engine writes them into the simulation canonically (sorted keys) when the world is observed — before a checksum, a rollback snapshot or a save — not after every tick: they are hashed into the checksum (desync detection), copied by rollback snapshots, saved, and read back into the VM when the netcode rewinds or a save is loaded. A tick that only changes Lua tables costs nothing until then. game.data(h) returns the entity's own table (created on first use, gone when the entity dies, kept by transform). Only tables handed out since the last write are serialized again, and only changed ones are re-hashed, so per-unit records belong here, not in one big state table: lua local d = game.data(h) -- {} the first time d.morale = (d.morale or 10) - 1 for _, h in ipairs(game.units{has = "morale"}) do ... end -- entities whose table has the key game.has_data(h, "morale") game.clear_data(h) View scripts get a read-only copy of the stored table. The editor shows these tables too (Inspector «Детали» → «Данные скрипта»; Hierarchy search d:); with game.json editor.hierarchy a key can name the row (label) or group the tree (data:<key>), docs/editor-world-tree.md. Allowed in state and game.data: integers, fx, strings, booleans and nested tables whose keys are integers or strings. A value that can't be stored (function, float, table key, cycle) is left out of the saved state and logged; keep such values out of persistent tables. Globals are read-only after loading: assigning a new global in a handler is an error, reading an undefined one too (typos show up immediately). Define functions and constants at the top level. Don't change file-level local variables from handlers (local count = 0 ... count = count + 1 in a handler): such state isn't part of the snapshot, so a rollback can't restore it. Use state. Constants and helper functions as locals are fine. Don't keep references to state sub-tables or game.data tables in locals across ticks (a rollback replaces them); call game.data(h) again.

pairs() iterates in sorted key order (booleans, integers, then strings), never in hash order, so loops over tables are deterministic. sorted_pairs is the same function. next is not available (iteration order would leak). Keys of other types can't be iterated with pairs. table.count(t) is the number of entries of t (no walk in key order needed just to count). game.units{...} returns handles sorted by entity index. Randomness only from math.random / game.random (the simulation RNG). tostring never shows addresses ("table", "function"), string.format("%p") is refused. String hashing and table.sort pivots use constant seeds (identical on all machines). Not available: os, io, debug, package, load, loadfile, dofile, collectgarbage, string.dump; setmetatable refuses __gc and __mode (they depend on garbage collection).

All simulation scripts together get scriptBudget VM instructions per tick (default 1,000,000). An endless loop is stopped with "instruction budget exceeded" — even inside pcall — and the game goes on; handlers that didn't get to run in that tick are skipped once. Any error is logged with file:line (headless output, editor Console and Скрипты windows, MCP play_status.scriptErrors, script_check) and disables that handler for the rest of the match (deterministically: the flag is simulation state). Functions called from data ("fn" of effects and trigger hooks) are disabled the same way. Loading errors (syntax, float literals, a missing file) skip that file; the match still starts. Script cost per tick: aiverse_headless --tick-times FILE writes the wall time of every simulation step (tick microseconds per line).

Handlers are registered at the top level of a file (while it loads): registration called argument on("start", fn) / function on_start() once, first tick — on("tick", fn) / on_tick every tick tick every(seconds, fn) every N seconds (seconds: integer or fx) tick on("unit_died", fn) / on_unit_died a unit or structure died e.unit (dead handle), e.owner, e.unit_type, e.x, e.z, e.killer (last damage source, may be dead too), e.killer_owner (when the killer lives) on("spawned" | "built" | "trained" | "upgraded", fn) created / construction done / trained / upgraded e.unit, e.owner, e.unit_type (trained: e.producer) on("researched", fn) a tech finished e.player, e.tech, e.producer on("captured", fn) changed owner e.unit, e.owner, e.old_owner, e.by on("player_defeated", fn) a player is out e.player, e.surrendered on("ability", fn) a unit used an ability e.caster, e.player, e.ability, e.index, e.target, e.x, e.z on("damage", fn) damage dealt e.unit, e.source, e.player (source owner), e.amount (fx) on("level_up", fn) a hero levelled e.unit, e.player, e.level on_area(name, "enter" | "leave", fn) a unit entered / left a map area (map "areas", checked every 5 ticks) e.unit, e.owner, e.area, e.x, e.z game.after(seconds, "fn_name", arg) once, later (a timer kept in the simulation state) arg (storable like state) Every event table also has e.event, e.tick, e.player. Scripts run in the scripts phase at the end of the tick (after triggers) and see every event of that tick. Every other simulation event works with on(name, fn) too and gets a generic table {event, player, tick, x, z, unit (a), other (b), value} plus unit_type (spawn / train / build / upgrade events), status (status_start, status_end), resource (gathered, delivered, produced), amount (damage), text (message). Names: attack hit miss train_started build_placed gathered not_enough ready_to_place sold region_claimed wave low_power message dug territory room_painted recruited creature_left picked_up dropped slapped possessed payday player_ability produced delivered road_built lanes_changed status_start status_end area_start area_trigger area_end projectile_launch impact chain_jump cast_start channel_start channel_end alert garrison_changed transit_start transit_end trigger_fired loaded unloaded cycle_phase traded diplomacy item merged objective dialog camera mission_end learned crew_killed crewed infected submerged trap_fired group_teleport paved morale turn (what unit / other / value mean per event: GameEvent in engine/game/GameCore.h). View scripts get the same names with view.on (read-only). Before-hooks — global functions the engine calls before something happens, in the middle of the tick (so keep them short; they share the tick budget and don't nest: damage dealt from inside a hook doesn't call before_damage again): function called return before_damage(e) every hit, after armor / mitigation: e = {unit, source, player, amount, damage_type} the new amount (fx / integer, >= 0); nothing = unchanged before_command(player, c) every built-in player command: c = {type, units, target, x, z, param, queue} (type as in game.command) false [, reason] drops it can_train(player, type, producer) a train command passed the engine's checks false [, reason] refuses can_build(player, type, x, z, builder) build order / sidebar placement false [, reason] refuses can_cast(caster, ability, target, x, z) an ability is about to fire (commands, autocast, AI) false [, reason] refuses A reason string is shown to that player like game.message. Games without these functions pay nothing (the module checks a flag).

Entities are integer handles. A handle of a dead or removed unit is harmless: queries return nil / false, actions do nothing. Queries (simulation and view scripts): function result game.tick(), game.time(), game.tick_rate() tick, seconds (fx), ticks per second game.players() player slots {1, 2, ...} game.player(p) {slot, team, alive, name, faction, supply, supply_cap} game.player_alive(p), game.team(p), game.hostile(a, b) game.resource(p, "gold"), game.resources(p) fx / {gold = fx, ...} game.units(filter), game.count(filter), game.nearest(x, z, filter) handles sorted by index / count / nearest handle game.unit(h) {id, type, name, owner, x, y, z, hp, max_hp, energy, structure, under_construction, level, garrison, tags, statuses} game.alive(h), game.owner(h), game.type_of(h), game.pos(h) → x, z, game.hp(h) → hp, max game.stat(h, "damage"), game.has_status(h, "slow") effective stat (techs, buffs, statuses) game.type_info("footman"), game.types() {id, name, structure, max_hp, speed, armor, cost, tags, upgrades} (upgrades: type ids of its in-place upgrades) game.map_size() → w, h, game.passable(x, z [, "ground"|"air"|"naval"]), game.level(x, z), game.height(x, z), game.area(name) map game.traffic_light(x, z [, "x"|"z"]) → "green"\ "yellow"\ "red"\ nil signal of the junction at / next to the point (rules traffic, docs/traffic.md) game.traffic_report(kind, x, z [, offender]) → id\ nil, game.traffic_incidents() → {{id, kind, x, z, state}, ...} city incidents ("injured", "crime", "fire", "wreck") and what the services are doing about them (docs/traffic.md) game.traffic_gang() → {state, x, z, car, size, loot}\ nil, {robberies, caught, loot} the gang of citizens that is out robbing now and the totals (rules traffic.gangs) game.traffic_citizen(h) → {state, commute, leg, home, work = {x, z, kind, open}, shift = {from, to}}\ nil, game.traffic_clock() → hour the citizen behind a person on the street or the car he drives (commute: walk / car / bus;
