PRISMA is the name of the full-screen effects and image-processing system. Not to be confused with SpectraFX, the particle/VFX system. Existing game formats do not change.

PRISMA owns post-processing of the final image: HDR/tonemapping, Bloom, color grading/LUT, DoF, Motion Blur, FXAA/TAA/upscaling, screen-space GI/AO/SSR, camera volumes, screen-space Shader Graph (domain postfx), render-pass dependencies and performance budgets. SpectraFX owns world visual effects before post-processing: emitters/particles, smoke, fire, explosions, ribbons, trail streams, CPU/GPU particle simulation, VFX graph authoring and ECS events. SpectraFX produces the scene's HDR contribution; PRISMA may then apply Bloom to the whole scene. The systems do not duplicate each other, do not depend on genre and are not part of deterministic gameplay state. The canonical sources are now engine/render/Prisma.{h,cpp}, PrismaData.{h,cpp}, PrismaShaders.h, PrismaVolumes.h. Editor: apps/editor/core/PrismaOps.{h,cpp} and apps/editor/windows/PrismaWindow.cpp. Legacy PostFx headers forward to PRISMA; the legacy .cpp files contain no implementation. The stable JSON postfx, MCP postfx_* and editor saved id postfx must not be renamed: they are external formats, not code owners.

Main C++ API: #include "engine/render/Prisma.h"; class aiverse::render::Prisma. Compatibility: PostFx and PostFxData are source alias/forwarding includes; the main compilation goes through Prisma.cpp and PrismaData.cpp. The old postfx_* MCP names are kept. Renderer3D requests PostProcess::scenePass and calls resolve(); with HDR/High, ScreenLighting performs screen-space lighting and TAA before the final resolve. Parameters: game.json / map, postfx merged by effect type; the editor panel and MCP operations are already implemented. GPU/RHI: GLSL/MSL, HDR RGBA16F with ACES and sRGB, RGBA8 fallback; the current chain has a fixed order. UI is drawn after PRISMA.

engine/render/PrismaRenderGraph.h is the first RHI-independent implementation of a description of passes and resources. PrismaRenderGraph::addResource/addPass/compile build a stable topological order and check for one writer per resource, identifier errors, feedback read/write within a single pass and dependency cycles. PrismaGraphPlan contains order, resources (first/last use), slots and the number of bytes of allocated internal textures. Transient resources compatible in format and size with non-overlapping lifetimes share one slot; history and resources with allowAlias=false do not share a slot. External input/output/history are supplied by the caller and are not allocated by the planner. Important: for now this is only a dependency graph + lifetime planner, not a GPU executor. The real Prisma::resolve() still executes the current fixed pipeline. Do not claim that the RenderGraph already drives rendering; the next stage is an RHI resource pool and execution callbacks with real pass bindings. Incorrect dependencies are deliberately rejected rather than fixed by an implicit shader blit. Test code: tests/render/prisma_graph.cpp, CTest prisma_graph; with AIVERSE_BUILD_TESTS=ON it is included in the standard CMake ALL build and ./run-tests.sh. A native test run is still required.

PrismaVolumeStack is now used in the game client and in the editor's Scene/Game viewports. At map start the client reads game.json["prismaVolumes"] and map["prismaVolumes"] via parsePrismaVolumes; before Renderer3D::render(...,&prisma) it calls prisma.applyCameraVolumes(stack,camera.eye()), and after resolvePrisma() it resets the settings to the base profile. The editor caches the profile by JSON signature and resolves it separately for each camera; the postfx change is not mutated. Example game.json (the same top-level block can be given on a map): "prismaVolumes": { "volumes": [ { "id": "underwater", "shape": "box", "center": [12, -5, 20], "halfExtents": [15, 6, 12], "blendDistance": 3, "priority": 10, "layerMask": 4294967295, "weight": 1, "profile": { "effects": [ {"type": "colorGrade", "saturation": 0.5, "temperature": -0.3}, {"type": "vignette", "intensity": 0.4} ] } } ] } Shapes: global, sphere (center, radius) and box (center, axis-aligned halfExtents). weight is in [0,1], blendDistance is the fade distance beyond the outer boundary; priorities are processed in ascending order and equal priorities keep insertion order. layerMask filters cameras, enabled disables the volume. The profile inside a volume uses the same existing postfx schema, not a new shader library. Specifying "hdr" or "enabled" explicitly enables the corresponding override; absence of these keys keeps the base profile's value. On a map, a volume with the same id replaces the game one; "replace":true in the map block removes all game volumes before applying the map list. Invalid entries are skipped with issues; authored JSON is not changed. Limitations: the body volume is not yet an oriented box (no rotation), there is no spatial index/priority GPU culling, the camera mask defaults to all bits; the regular GameClient/Editor apply mask all. Interpolation changes only explicitly specified effect parameters (stage 09); other parameters, minQuality and LUT paths keep their base values. For a native C++ profile without masks the legacy full-profile behavior is kept. Discrete settings switch at weight >= 0.5, numeric parameters blend in float on the presentation side. Do not store such a float stack in authoritative ECS state. The new prismaVolumes data is optional and does not affect old projects. Code: PrismaVolumeData.{h,cpp}, PrismaVolumes.h; CPU tests: tests/render/prisma_volume.cpp / CTest prisma_volume (a test run is still required).

PrismaVolumeEffectMask in PrismaVolumes.h and PrismaVolumeData.cpp::authoredEffects map each effect to a bitmask of the parameters explicitly specified in JSON, including color components, the enabled/minQuality flags and the LUT text path. When a volume sets only colorGrade.exposure, the source colorGrade.saturation, contrast, lift/gamma/gain and minQuality are not overwritten. When the base effect is absent, a neutral profile with a smooth entry is added for ColorGrade/Bloom/effects with intensity or amount; for discrete effects the threshold is 0.5. For direct native C++ creation of a volume without effectMasks the old full-profile behavior is kept. The prisma_volume tests are extended to cover preservation of unrelated parameters, but a native run is still required.

engine/render/PrismaGraphDispatch.h adds a header-only, genre-independent dispatchPrismaGraph<Handle>(graph, plan, bindings, callback) contract. PrismaGraphBindings<Handle> contains one entry per graph resource for external handles and one entry per compiled transient slot for physical allocations. PrismaGraphDispatchView::resource(id) resolves a logical resource through the compiled aliasing plan; the host supplies the typed RHI handles, command encoders and texture transitions. Validation completes before any callback: invalid plans, mismatched binding counts, unbound handles, duplicate pass IDs and invalid resource references are rejected without partially drawing a frame. The callback runs in deterministic topological order, and returning false aborts subsequent passes with an error and exact number of completed passes. This is not an RHI executor and does not allocate GPU textures, create encoder barriers, perform render passes or bind PRISMA's current fixed chain. An external integration must first create and retain physical slots, manage external/history resource lifetimes, provide synchronization and connect the existing Prisma::resolve calls. Keep the legacy renderer enabled by default until native Metal/GL validation and image parity tests pass. Tests are appended to tests/render/prisma_graph.cpp / CTest prisma_graph. Native build, CTest and GPU tests have NOT RUN in the GitHub-only agent environment; see docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-11.md.

engine/render/PrismaGraphResourcePool.h provides a host-owned pool of physical render target handles for PrismaGraphPlan::slots. The host creates targets with a create(format,width,height) callback and releases them with release(handle); this header never calls GPU/RHI APIs. prepare(graph, plan, create, release) reuses allocations with identical format/dimensions and matching history resource name, or creates new targets. It never selects the same allocation twice within a single frame. On allocation failure it releases targets allocated during that prepare call and preserves the previous pool entries. markHistoryWritten(name) marks successfully produced temporal pixels valid; invalidateHistory() discards temporal contents on camera cuts/teleports without discarding reusable GPU storage. If prepare returns a false history-valid bit, the caller must avoid reading the old history and use a non-temporal fallback. Resize changes resource descriptors and always allocates a fresh history. pruneUnused(release) frees allocations not selected by the last successful prepare; clear(release) releases all allocations. Call both only after GPU fence completion, not while earlier frames might still reference them. Use one pool instance per independent camera/view/temporal stream, not one global mutable history across cameras. The pool does not allocate external resource bindings, compute barriers, issue render passes or integrate itself into the existing Prisma::resolve. It is an opt-in host contract. Tests for reusable physical slots, valid/invalid history, resize/pruning, allocation rollback and clearing are in tests/render/prisma_graph.cpp. Native build/CTest/GPU screenshot verification is NOT RUN for Stage 12. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-12.md.

h: Stage 13 — Opt-in RHI graph adapter (not yet wired into Prisma::resolve)
x: engine/render/PrismaRhiExecutor.h bridges the GPU-free Stage 11 graph and Stage 12 allocation pool to the existing gfx::Device API. It creates TextureDesc{renderTarget=true} targets, maps RGBA8/RGBA16F/Depth32F to the backend's supported formats, uses copyColor for one-input/one-output matching RGBA8 Copy passes, and executes Raster callbacks inside balanced beginPass/endPass scopes. Compute callbacks run outside render passes only if Device::supportsCompute() reports support. A native host explicitly creates a per-camera PrismaRhiExecutor(device) and calls execute(graph,plan,external,raster,compute,optionalDepth) outside any existing pass. Raster callback signature is bool(gfx::Device&, PrismaGraphId, const PrismaGraphDispatchView<gfx::TextureHandle>&); it binds its own pipeline, uniforms and input textures. Compute has the same callback signature but is responsible for opening/closing any compute encoder it needs. optionalDepth must match raster target dimensions if the chosen Metal backend needs a depth attachment. The adapter never calls endFrame, presents, performs implicit shader conversions, or modifies ECS. Compatibility constraints: currently no RG16F/R32F target formats in gfx::PixelFormat; these graphs fail preflight. The portable copyColor interface only guarantees same-size RGBA8; HDR/other copy operations need explicit raster shader passes. gfx::Device does not expose a universal resource-barrier API. GPU target release and pool reset must happen at a caller-managed safe point after in-flight work finishes. Temporal history is valid only after the host has successfully produced its pixels and explicitly marked it written. Not a complete render pipeline migration. Prisma::resolve() still uses the legacy, shipped fixed pass chain by default, with no automatic RHI graph execution. The header is an opt-in integration point, and the test addition currently covers only RHI format mappings in tests/render/prisma_graph.cpp. Native build, driver smoke, screenshots and numerical parity remain NOT RUN. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-13.md.

The first production call site of PrismaRhiExecutor is an opt-in SDR FXAA prepass in Prisma::resolve(). Set AIVERSE_PRISMA_GRAPH_FXAA=1 to create a two-external-resource graph (scene-fxaa -> fxaa-output) and execute the existing FXAA pipeline, same uniforms and texture bindings, through a single RHI raster pass. The default code path is unchanged. The experimental path is only used when FXAA is active, the scene is RGBA8/SDR, the FXAA pipeline is valid, both color textures exist, and the matching depth attachment was created. If the graph cannot be compiled/dispatched, the original direct draw() path runs instead. Graph preflight happens before any draw submission; the shader uses exactly one full-screen draw and writes the complete destination. The opt-in pass clears neither color nor depth. The graph has no internally allocated targets; it uses the existing Sized per-view resources. It does not switch on graph-rendered HDR, bloom, temporal AA, or the final composite. There is no new JSON schema, editor toggle or change to SpectraFX. This is a guarded runtime foothold, not a whole-chain render-graph migration. GPU parity and native CMake/CTest remain NOT RUN. The test source in tests/render/prisma_graph.cpp checks only graph structure and single-pass binding/dispatch logic, not Metal/GL pixel correctness. For reproduction and outstanding validation, read docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-14.md.

h: Stage 15 — Bloom Prefilter opt-in and legacy clear parity
x: PrismaRhiExecutor::execute now defaults raster passes to the same opaque-black color clear and depth clear as Prisma::draw. An additional clearRasterTargets=false argument is available for explicitly overwrite-only pipelines, but the FXAA and Bloom experimental call sites use the default legacy-compatible behavior. This fixes a known Stage 14 parity risk. AIVERSE_PRISMA_GRAPH_BLOOM_PREFILTER=1 opts only the first Bloom Prefilter raster pass into PrismaRhiExecutor. It uses the existing kPrefilter shader pipeline, uniform block and one source texture; the input/output resources are externally managed Sized targets (full-resolution input, lower-resolution output), and the graph does not allocate transient textures. In HDR mode both resources are declared RGBA16F, otherwise RGBA8. Both are supported by the existing conditional RHI path. The rest of the Bloom downsample/upsample chain remains the original direct renderer; the FXAA experiment still uses its independent AIVERSE_PRISMA_GRAPH_FXAA=1 flag. The default path is unchanged and any preflight/allocation failure falls back to Prisma::draw. The experimental raster callback returns true after a submitted draw; failure after GPU submission cannot be rolled back. No full-frame parity has been established. tests/render/prisma_graph.cpp now has CPU-only graph contracts for SDR and HDR prefilter sizes, bindings, single-dispatch and missing output preflight. These sources have not been compiled or run in this agent environment; Metal/GL screenshots and GPU timings are also NOT RUN. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-15.md.

h: Stage 16 — opt-in full Bloom down/up RenderGraph
x: AIVERSE_PRISMA_GRAPH_BLOOM_CHAIN=1 enables an experimental full Bloom Prefilter → Downsample → Upsample graph inside Prisma::resolve(). The flag is off by default. The graph declares one external Scene input and external per-level down/up targets backed by the existing Prisma::Sized per-view texture cache. Every downsample reads the previous mip; each upsample reads the lower intermediate plus the matching down mip. All passes use the existing kPrefilter, kDown and kUp GPU shader programs, exactly the original size-dependent uniforms, tint/radius normalization, source bindings and texture formats (SDR RGBA8; HDR RGBA16F). The host creates the depth attachments for each output size before execution. The RHI executor now accepts an optional trailing std::function<gfx::TextureHandle(PrismaGraphId)> rasterDepthForPass. When supplied, that attachment replaces the shared rasterDepth for each pass; this is necessary on Metal for different Bloom mip dimensions. Existing Stage 14/15 executor users continue to use the previous optional shared depth and legacy-compatible clear defaults. Scope/limitations: this is real RHI graph scheduling of Bloom raster passes, but it is not yet adoption of Stage 12's transient graph pool: the host supplies externally cached target textures, which already persist per viewport. There is no automatic RHI in-flight retirement queue or resource barrier API. The complete graph is rebuilt on each opt-in frame, and Prisma::resolve() retains the old path as fallback when graph preflight fails. On any unexpected failure after GPU pass submission, the graph is not replayed (partial rendering must not be double-submitted). No effect outside Bloom was migrated during this stage. If both AIVERSE_PRISMA_GRAPH_BLOOM_CHAIN and the Stage 15 prefilter-only flag are set, the full-chain flag takes precedence on success. New GPU-free graph tests check 1/2/4 downsample levels for SDR/HDR, topological order, valid binding resolution, and rejection of missing mip targets before pass execution. Those sources have NOT RUN in a native compiler or on a GPU; see docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-16.md.

h: Stage 17 — per-view compiled Bloom topology cache
x: engine/render/PrismaBloomGraph.h provides a GPU-free PrismaBloomGraphCache. configure(sourceWidth,sourceHeight,format,mips) compiles the complete Bloom topology once per source size, HDR/SDR format and mip shape list. Repeated frames with the same structure reuse graph(), plan() and operations(); changed quality/mip sizes trigger compilation of a replacement graph. Failed reconfiguration leaves the previous valid configuration intact, but the renderer never executes that stale graph for the incompatible current layout. The main Prisma::Sized viewport cache now owns a PrismaBloomGraphCache, so Scene/Game views have separate graph layouts and no cross-view history. The Stage 16 opt-in path AIVERSE_PRISMA_GRAPH_BLOOM_CHAIN=1 uses the cached immutable graph and rebuilds only the frame bindings: threshold/knee/scatter, shader uniforms, source and output texture handles, and per-mip depth attachments. The existing fallback and default-off behavior are preserved. Stage 12 transient target pooling remains a separate future integration; cached topology itself allocates no GPU textures. This is implementation-only work; CMake, CTest and real GPU validation were intentionally deferred at the user's request. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-17.md.

h: Stage 18 — GPU completion-gated retirement and persistent view executor
x: engine/render/PrismaGpuRetirement.h introduces PrismaGpuRetirementQueue<Handle>: retire(handle,submissionFence) transfers an allocation to a pending queue; collect(completedGpuFence, release) invokes the release callback only when the GPU has reported completion through a caller-managed fence/event. drainAfterGpuIdle is valid only after an explicit GPU idle synchronization. A CPU frame counter or gfx::Device::frameSerial() is not a completion fence. PrismaGraphResourcePool::retireUnused/retireAll now transfer allocations to the caller instead of destroying them immediately. PrismaRhiExecutor::retireUnused/retireAll/collectCompleted wires those operations to its queue and calls RHI destroyTexture after the supplied completed fence. resetAfterGpuIdle() also releases all pending and current allocations, but only if the host has ensured the GPU is idle. Every Prisma::Sized viewport now holds a lazy persistent std::unique_ptr<PrismaRhiExecutor>, shared by its opt-in FXAA, Bloom prefilter and full Bloom graph calls. It retains resource pool state across frames rather than creating a new executor on every pass. Lifetime is tied to the existing Sized cache. This does not yet make PRISMA use graph-owned Bloom targets; those remain external RHI textures in Sized, and graph execution stays opt-in. Backend integration constraint: Gfx does not yet provide a portable completed-GPU-fence API. Hosts must pass actual completion signals to collectCompleted. Existing viewport eviction and renderer shutdown still destroy their legacy textures at the current existing release points; they are not automatically made GPU-fence-safe by this opt-in queue. Actual backend fence wiring and transient Bloom pool migration remain future features. Testing/build/GPU verification deliberately deferred at user request. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-18.md.

h: Stage 19 — opt-in graph-owned Bloom mip allocation
x: With both AIVERSE_PRISMA_GRAPH_BLOOM_CHAIN=1 and AIVERSE_PRISMA_GRAPH_BLOOM_POOL=1, the complete Bloom RenderGraph can now allocate its own downsample/upsample targets through PrismaGraphResourcePool in the persistent per-viewport RHI executor. Only the input Scene/FXAA color is external. The graph declares every Bloom mip as an internal resource, enabling the planner to alias identical-format/size GPU textures when their lifetimes do not overlap. Without the new pool flag, the existing Stage 16 graph still uses Sized::targets as external resources. Both experimental flags are off by default. PrismaRhiExecution::resources now maps each logical graph resource to its actual external or pooled RHI texture handle. The final Bloom composite samples resources[cache.outputId()] when pooled mode succeeds. Per-pass depth attachments still come from the established Sized::depths cache; thresholds, scatter, shader pipelines and source UV conventions are unchanged. On graph preflight/allocation failure before GPU submission, the code allocates legacy mip targets and uses the existing Bloom fallback. A failure after GPU submission does not attempt to replay partial passes. Ownership: pooled RHI textures persist with their viewport executor, rather than being released after each frame. Reconfiguration keeps unselected allocations until explicit safe retirement; their eventual release depends on GPU-completion reporting or a confirmed GPU-idle shutdown. No portable completed-fence backend is yet wired, so automatic mid-flight eviction is deliberately not used. Existing view eviction still follows legacy release assumptions, and memory benefits are not quantified. This experimental path needs build/GPU verification before being enabled by default. Implementation-only stage: testing intentionally postponed at user request. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-19.md.

AIVERSE_PRISMA_GRAPH_TILT_SHIFT=1 routes the existing three-pass Tilt Shift (downsample, horizontal Gaussian blur, vertical Gaussian blur) through PrismaRhiExecutor. Four logical SSA resources describe the source, first A target, B target and final A target. The two versions of A are deliberately mapped to the same existing physical texture: they are never simultaneously needed, and the intermediate B is separate. Per-pass uniforms and original pipelines are preserved. The default path remains the legacy three draws. Missing resources or failures before GPU submission fall back to it; partially dispatched passes are not replayed. This stage does not yet migrate physical Tilt targets to the graph-owned pool, nor does it activate Tilt Shift by default. Native/GPU tests deliberately NOT RUN per user request. Handoff: docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-20.md.

AIVERSE_PRISMA_GRAPH_SUN_SHAFTS=1 enables a two-pass graph for the existing sunlight prefilter mask and radial scattering operation. The sun position, offscreen edge fallback, visibility threshold, color, quality tier, sample count and shader uniforms are unchanged. Three externally owned textures represent the source, mask and radial output, with the existing per-size depth attachment. The two-pass graph executes through the per-viewport RHI executor. Failure before any submission uses the legacy two-draw path; a partially submitted graph is never replayed. The path remains off by default and the HUD is still drawn after postprocessing. No new serialised settings or shader variants were introduced. This stage is code-only, intentionally NOT compiled or GPU-tested yet. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-21.md.

h: Stage 22 — experimental depth-based Depth of Field
x: The new depthOfField entry in postfx.effects is handled by the shared PRISMA data catalog (MCP and editor parameter discovery are data-driven). Parameters are focusDepth (0..1 GPU device depth, not metres), focusRange (depth interval), maxBlur (0..16 output pixels) and intensity (0..1). Defaults: 0.5, 0.08, 8, 1 respectively. This entry defaults to High post quality and is classified Heavy in the cost estimation model. The opt-in AIVERSE_PRISMA_DOF=1 activates one full-resolution nine-neighbour blur pass before SDR FXAA and Bloom; it reads the scene color and render-target depth using the existing GLSL/MSL fullscreen-program path and produces a new color texture used as the source by subsequent effects. The hardware depth is deliberately not represented as physical focus distance, since the PostFrame currently lacks a portable inverse-projection/near-far contract. The blur radius follows the distance between sampled hardware depth and focusDepth, with a central sharp interval. The shader is a bounded, approximate defocus, not cinematic hexagonal bokeh, depth-layer separation or physically accurate lens simulation. The pass samples the original scene depth, but uses its own scratch depth attachment of matching dimensions, avoiding read/write feedback on the same depth texture. It can run only when the configured effect, opt-in flag, necessary GPU resources and pipeline are present. Without the flag, existing image processing continues unchanged. DoF is disabled on low/medium quality by its default minQuality=high, unless a project explicitly overrides it. Example game.json postfx.effects entry: {"type":"depthOfField","focusDepth":0.65,"focusRange":0.08,"maxBlur":6,"intensity":0.8} All native compilation, CTest and visual/GPU smoke are intentionally NOT RUN at the user's request. Real Metal/GL depth texture sampling compatibility, reverse-Z behavior and scene-depth interpretation need later validation. The next feature is true world-distance autofocus via camera projection data, followed by multi-resolution CoC separation and physically-inspired bokeh. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-22.md.

h: Stage 23 — HDR Auto Exposure (GPU log luminance + eye adaptation)
x: postfx.effects can now contain {"type":"autoExposure"}. The optional feature remains disabled in rendering unless AIVERSE_PRISMA_AUTO_EXPOSURE=1 is set and the current scene is using linear HDR RGBA16F. On SDR/RGBA8, the effect has no GPU action, because clipped highlights cannot be recovered by metering. The GPU pipeline in Prisma::resolve() is: Read scene-linear RGB and store log2 luminance in a half-resolution RGBA16F target (four color taps with Rec.709 luminance coefficients). Repeatedly average log luminance through a 2x2 pyramid to 1x1. This estimates geometric mean brightness, not a full per-bin histogram. Determine target exposure 2^(clamp(log2(keyValue)-meanLogL+ compensation, minEV, maxEV)). In a dedicated RGBA16F 1x1 ping-pong pass, blend from previous exposure using 1-exp(-speed*deltaSeconds). speedUp controls increasing exposure (dark->bright output); speedDown decreasing exposure. The time delta is clamped at 0.1s to avoid large jumps after stalls. Sample the resulting exposure multiplier as TEX8 in the final composite before HDR tonemapping and sRGB conversion. UI remains unprocessed. ColorGrade's manual exposure/compensation still multiplies the automatic result. Parameters (regular PrismaData catalog and editor/MCP discovery): parameter default range meaning keyValue 0.18 0.01–1 target scene middle grey minEV -6 -12–0 lower automatic EV limit maxEV 6 0–12 upper automatic EV limit speedUp 3 0.01–20 brighten response rate, 1/s speedDown 1 0.01–20 darken response rate, 1/s compensation 0 -5–5 EV bias Example: {"type":"autoExposure","keyValue":0.18,"minEV":-4, "maxEV":4,"speedUp":2.5,"speedDown":1.0,"compensation":0.0} Per-Prisma::Sized temporal history uses two 1x1 HDR textures and a previous timestamp. Explicit native Prisma::resetAutoExposure() invalidates history for camera cuts. Project reconfiguration, postprocess toggle and quality changes reset it; a disabled HDR/auto mode also clears valid history. The first enabled frame snaps to the current measured exposure, avoiding reading an uninitialized history texture. No CPU brightness readback is used. Limitations: the algorithm computes mean log luminance, not a percentile histogram; bright outliers may still influence adaptation, and the measurement is not a physically calibrated light meter. The existing Sized cache is keyed by dimensions rather than stable camera identity, so two viewport cameras of identical size can share their temporal history. A follow-up should add explicit stable view IDs. The fixed exposure sampler uses slot 8, which is also available for the fourth custom ShaderGraph texture (slots 5..8); automatic exposure is skipped for those graphs rather than clobbering user textures. HDR support and blending of 1x1 RGBA16F must be verified on real Metal/GL. This is an opt-in source implementation with NO native/GPU tests run, per the user's features-first request. Do not enable it globally until verified. Handoff: docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-23.md.

h: Stage 24 — independent camera history and weighted GPU metering
x: The presentation-only API Prisma::setViewId(uint64_t id) selects a stable camera/view identifier before rendering. viewId() const returns it. A view's two 1x1 RGBA16F exposure-history render targets, adaptation timestamp, valid bit and ping-pong index now live in Prisma::exposureViews_, keyed by that ID instead of render dimensions. resetAutoExposure(id) invalidates one view; the no-argument overload invalidates every view. The older target caches remain keyed by size for sharing ordinary temporary textures; exposure history no longer cross-contaminates identically sized Scene and Game cameras. The editor sets view IDs 1 for Scene and 2 for Game before applyCameraVolumes; GameClient uses ID 3 within its own PRISMA instance. A native project that renders multiple cameras must assign distinct IDs itself. The default ID remains 0 for legacy native projects. Exposure histories are retained until Prisma::shutdown (no automatic per-camera removal/fence retirement yet). IDs must be stable, not increment every frame. autoExposure has four additional configurable parameters: centerWeight (default 0, range 0..1): 0 = uniform metering, 1 = strongly center-weighted. centerRadius (default 0.35, range 0.05..1): normalized radius for Gaussian center weighting. minMeterLogL (default -10, range -16..0) and maxMeterLogL (default 10, range 0..16): clamp individual pixel log2 luminance in the initial HDR metering pass, reducing extreme brightness influence. This is not percentile-based histogram clipping. The first pyramid pass now outputs two channels: weighted sum of log2 luminance (R) and sum of weights (G); each later 2x2 pass reduces both components identically. The 1x1 adaptation shader divides R/G before computing target EV. No CPU readback, additional fullscreen texture or extra raster pass is required compared with Stage 23. The format stays RGBA16F throughout. Example postfx.effects entry: {"type":"autoExposure","keyValue":0.18, "centerWeight":0.75,"centerRadius":0.35, "minMeterLogL":-8,"maxMeterLogL":6} All rendering remains opt-in via AIVERSE_PRISMA_AUTO_EXPOSURE=1, High-tier HDR only. Existing postfx schema is extended, not migrated. CMake, CTest and real Metal/GL validation are NOT RUN as requested. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-24.md.

h: Stage 25 — HDR camera motion vectors and Motion Blur (experimental)
x: postfx.effects now accepts motionBlur through the shared, genre-independent PRISMA catalog. The new effect defaults to minQuality: "high" and is opt-in at runtime via AIVERSE_PRISMA_MOTION_BLUR=1; it additionally requires an HDR RGBA16F scene (signed RG motion vectors are not representable in the existing RGBA8 path without encoding). Parameters: intensity (0..1, default 0.65), maxPixels (0..64, default 20), samples (2..16, default 8), shutterScale (0..2, default 1). Example: {"type":"motionBlur","intensity":0.6,"maxPixels":20, "samples":8,"shutterScale":1.0} The motion-vector pass samples the current hardware scene depth and reconstructs the world position from the inverse current viewProjection. It projects that position with the previous viewProjection, writing a signed UV velocity currentScreenUV - previousScreenUV into an RGBA16F texture. The next raster pass gathers current-frame scene color along this velocity and blends it with the sharp color. Motion blur is executed before depth of field, FXAA, Bloom and final composite; HUD/UI remains unprocessed. Separate scratch depth attachments avoid sampling and writing the scene depth simultaneously. The previous camera matrix, validity flag and render dimensions are stored in Prisma::motionViews_ per stable setViewId(), using the same camera identity contract as Auto Exposure. The first rendered frame, resize, changed quality, postprocess toggle or explicit resetMotionHistory(viewId)/no-argument reset invalidates motion history and results in an unblurred frame; it then seeds the matrix for the next frame. setSettings also resets history. Optional object velocity bridge: a native renderer may call prisma.setObjectMotionVectors(viewId, velocityTexture) each frame with a borrowed, full-resolution texture whose R/G values are signed current-minus-previous normalized screen UV and B is a valid-object pixel mask (B > 0.5). If present, that velocity overrides camera-only velocity for tagged pixels. The borrowed handle is cleared after each resolve. PRISMA does not yet generate per-object velocity buffers from mesh transforms/skinning; the adapter is an integration contract, not automatic object-motion rendering. These inputs are presentation state, not deterministic ECS. Limitations: this is a camera-reprojection motion blur, not TAA or temporal image accumulation; it does not store previous color, and therefore does not synthesize missing disoccluded samples. Camera cuts must be signaled explicitly to avoid blur across teleports; material transparency and sky (depth≈1) receive zero camera velocity in the basic shader. Neither Metal/GL depth sampling, signed velocity rendering, nor image correctness have been tested. All compilation, CTest and GPU checks remain NOT RUN, per user request. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-25.md.

When HDR motionBlur is active with AIVERSE_PRISMA_MOTION_BLUR=1, Renderer3D now has an optional GPU overlay pass for opaque rigid ModelDraw primitives with a stable persistentId. It runs between the scene pass and Prisma::resolve(), outside any open render pass, then sends the RGBA16F velocity texture to PRISMA through the new generic PostProcess bridge. It does not modify gameplay/ECS, and the existing camera-derived vectors remain the fallback for pixels without valid object velocity. The renderer tracks the previous world transform of each (ModelDraw::persistentId, nodeIndex) in a per-view map. On the first frame or after a camera cut, it records current transforms without drawing a velocity overlay. Once the camera history is valid, it renders each eligible rigid primitive with a dedicated GLSL/MSL shader and ModelVertex position stream. Current and previous model-view-projection matrices produce signed current-minus-previous screen UV motion in RG. B=1 marks visible rigid pixels. A separate scratch depth texture is attached; the shader samples original scene depth and rejects fragments behind the visible surface, so world occlusion/terrain can hide moving objects without writing scene depth. This pass operates on the existing ModelItems after ordinary batching: individual model node transforms are preserved even if the regular opaque pass used instancing/MDI. The velocity overlay currently uses one regular indexed draw per primitive (not an indirect/instanced velocity submission); it reuses the existing model vertex/index GPU buffers. The overlay render target and depth attachment are owned per PostProcess view ID by Renderer3D and released on its shutdown. No resource is shared between cameras with different stable IDs. Only rigid, visible, opaque, non-deformed, stable-ID model primitives are eligible. Missing IDs, transparent/masked materials, skinned or baked animated meshes, morph targets, custom geometry and transient immediate draws are skipped. Their pixels continue using the camera-only motion reconstruction. The scene depth test is an approximate epsilon comparison, not a full material/alpha/deformation replay; fast disocclusions and edge artifacts remain possible. Existing Prisma::setObjectMotionVectors(viewId,texture) stays available for custom native renderers; automatic Renderer3D generation uses the same borrowed-handle bridge via virtual PostProcess::acceptObjectMotionVectors. There is no ECS scheduling or genre-specific integration. Default behavior is unchanged when MotionBlur is not active. NOT RUN: native build, CTest, Metal/GL shader compilation, screen comparisons and profiling, per user's features-first request. A GPU fence-completed retirement path is still required for robust target resizing and teardown while work is in flight. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-26.md.

h: Stage 27 — deformation-aware and instanced object motion vectors
x: The optional HDR motionBlur path now contains two new Renderer3D velocity render variants, both active only with AIVERSE_PRISMA_MOTION_BLUR=1: Rigid velocity instancing. Geometry-equivalent visible opaque rigid ModelItem instances are grouped by source model pointer, first index and index count. A separate 16-instance GLSL/MSL pipeline consumes per-instance current and previous MVP matrices, submitting one drawIndexed(..., instanceCount) per compatible group (up to 16 instances per group). The uniforms occupy at most 2064 bytes; a single item or missing batched pipeline still uses the Stage 26 singleton shader. Matching shader/geometry groups are presentation-only; the existing color draw batching is not altered. Skinned and morph velocity. Palette-skinned objects and morph-target primitives with a nonzero stable persistentId can produce actual deformed vertex velocities. The renderer snapshots the current joint palette and eight morph weights per (persistentId, nodeIndex, geometryPrimitive), retaining the previous frame's values independently for each camera. A separate shader deforms each mesh vertex for both the current and previous pose, computes two clip positions and stores screen UV displacement. Current and previous U3/U4 blocks hold up to 80 joints (3 rows each); U5 contains the two 8-weight morph arrays and morph atlas parameters; tex8 reuses the existing morph delta texture. GPU skinning/morph math is kept separate from the deterministic simulation and is not a CPU-skinned mesh upload. A missing previous pose or changed source model identity causes the deformable primitive to skip object-velocity override rather than invent movement. Depth-edge motion blur. Motion Blur now samples the original scene depth at each color gather position and reduces contributions across large depth discontinuities. This protects foreground outlines against unrelated background colors, although the rejection threshold is based on non-linear hardware depth, so it is a conservative approximation, not physically exact depth-layer motion reconstruction. Prisma::buildProgram supports depth2d<float> for explicitly marked depth samplers on Metal while keeping GLSL sampler2D conventions. Eligibility remains intentionally conservative: visible, opaque non-displaced primitives with stable IDs. Baked animation (whose pose comes from clip textures), material ShaderGraph vertex displacement, transparent/masked models and custom geometry are not yet handled by the new deformed-velocity pipeline. Velocity target resize, first frame and camera cuts seed history rather than extrapolating invalid motion. Renderer3D owns lazy velocity shader/pipeline and target lifetime. Verification deferred by user request: native compilation, Metal/GL shader validation, visual comparison, CTest and GPU profiling have NOT RUN. Do not enable these experimental paths by default before they are validated. Details: docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-27.md.

h: Stage 28 — baked clip motion, alpha-cutout velocity and depth thresholds
x: The experimental motionBlur pipeline now includes a baked-clips vertex velocity shader variant. For a ModelItem with baked=true, the renderer records the current anim values (clip A row, clip B row, blend) and world matrix by stable (persistentId, nodeIndex, geometryPrimitive). The new GLSL/MSL vertex shader reads the original baked bone atlas (tex7) and original per-primitive joint palette. Current and previous clip rows and interpolation are sampled separately to reconstruct both deformed vertex positions. The velocity fragment then writes current-minus-previous normalized screen UV motion. The history snapshot is presentation-only; the animation and authoritative simulation aren't modified. This path intentionally skips baked + morph simultaneous deformation until a mixed permutation is available. An optional alpha-cutout rigid velocity variant now replays the material's base texture alpha cutoff with KHR texture transform (offset/scale/rotation), base alpha and vertex-color alpha (when enabled). Because cutout surfaces contain empty pixels, the dedicated variant samples the base alpha texture and discards rejected fragments before depth-occlusion testing. These materials are kept out of the ordinary opaque instanced velocity draw and rendered separately. ShaderGraph-displaced surfaces and deformable alpha-cutout models are not included, since their visible shape requires matching additional material stages. Fully blended/transparent models remain excluded. The rigid history now stores the source Model identity alongside its world transform, preventing a reused persistentId from picking up a different model's previous transform. Existing per-view reset, initial frame and resize behavior stays intact. motionBlur also accepts depthThreshold (default 0.012, range 0.0005..0.05) for rejecting unrelated depth layers during the directional color gather. The shader falls back to the sharp sample if all gathered samples are rejected instead of blending black into the image. The threshold is in non-linear device depth units, not metres. Example: {"type":"motionBlur","intensity":0.65,"maxPixels":20, "samples":8,"shutterScale":1,"depthThreshold":0.012} All additional paths remain behind the pre-existing AIVERSE_PRISMA_MOTION_BLUR=1 and HDR/quality gates. They use the same masked velocity texture bridge and do not change gameplay ECS or SpectraFX. Baked clip pose and rigid alpha-cutout motion use new GLSL/MSL variants; no backend-specific testing has yet verified their image parity. CPU/GPU builds, CTest, shader compilation, screenshots and benchmarks are NOT RUN at the user's request. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-28.md.

h: Stage 29 — camera-cut epochs, reactive transparency and baked+morph velocity
x: PRISMA's experimental HDR motionBlur path now has three additional presentation-only capabilities, all gated by the existing AIVERSE_PRISMA_MOTION_BLUR=1 runtime flag and configured quality. Explicit camera/view lifecycle. Prisma::resetMotionHistory(viewId) increments a monotonically increasing per-view camera-cut epoch exposed by PostProcess::objectMotionEpoch(viewId). Renderer3D reads this epoch on each opt-in velocity pass and discards prior rigid and deformable transform snapshots when it changes. This keeps the camera reprojection and per-object pose histories in sync across camera cuts, teleports, quality changes and map reconfigurations without modifying gameplay ECS. The renderer also provides resetObjectMotionHistory(viewId) and resetAllObjectMotionHistory() for explicit standalone control. releaseObjectMotionViewAfterGpuIdle(viewId) releases the per-view GPU velocity, reactive and depth textures only after the host has confirmed GPU idle; CPU frame serials are NOT a GPU completion signal. No automatic viewport closure or backend GPU fences are wired yet. A new read-only Renderer3D::objectMotionStats() returns the last velocity pass's view ID, submitted state and rigid instance/draw, cutout, skinned, baked, reactive and rejected draw counters. These values are CPU submission diagnostics, not measured GPU time or performance data. Reactive masks. Renderer3D can emit a separate, current-frame RGBA8 reactive coverage texture for visible rigid, translucent ModelDraw primitives. It samples the final scene depth and uses a dedicated scratch depth attachment rather than modifying scene depth. The red channel is coverage strength, while an all-zero background means no reactive pixels. PostProcess::acceptMotionReactiveMask forwards the borrowed handle to PRISMA. Native renderers can instead provide a borrowed R=0..1 texture through Prisma::setMotionReactiveMask(viewId,texture) before resolve. The motion blur shader samples this mask at texture slot 3 and reduces local blur strength by 1 - reactive * reactiveStrength. A missing mask uses the black fallback, so motion blur remains unchanged. The new optional effect parameter reactiveStrength defaults to 0.85 and has a range of 0..1. The renderer's reactive pass is a conservative geometric silhouette of translucent rigid models: it does not reproduce per-pixel blended texture alpha, alpha-test materials, skinning, particles or water drawn by other renderer modules. False-positive reactive coverage may reduce blur inside glass geometry, which is preferable to inventing object velocities. It remains an experimental approximation. Baked clip + morph. The baked-velocity vertex shader now applies both the current and previous morph weights against immutable morph deltas (tex8) before sampling current and previous baked clip rows from tex7, matching the existing color shader's deformation order. Palette, animation and morph parameters are all per primitive and per view; a missing previous frame or changed model identity still suppresses object-velocity override. This does not add per-vertex CPU readback or change deterministic animation state. LOD transition geometry that requires screen-space dithering is now conservatively excluded from object velocity until a matching LOD fade shader is implemented; camera motion reconstruction remains the fallback there. h: Reactive coverage extension for all renderers

The callback is invoked inside an already open RGBA8 reactive render pass with a separate scratch depth target; it must never call beginPass/endPass. The provider binds its own shader, geometry, texture/constant state and writes red channel R in [0,1] (0 = no reaction, 1 = suppress blur according to the configured strength). Use coverage-union-friendly blending, such as gfx::BlendMode::Screen, so several water/particle/object providers combine rather than erase one another. The current sceneDepth handle may only be sampled: never rebind that texture as a writable depth attachment. The provider must keep any borrowed buffers/textures valid through the callback and cannot modify gameplay ECS state. The generic callback is available for rendering engines and projects implementing water, particles, weather or custom presentation. Stage 30 does not automatically instrument existing water/VFX packages; those owners must register their respective reactive render callbacks to render the correct coverage with their own material/geometry semantics. No callbacks are invoked unless HDR MotionBlur is active and a valid camera history exists; registration by itself cannot force the postprocessing chain to run. The new motionBlur.velocityDilation parameter (default 1.0, range 0..2, 0 disables) samples four neighbouring velocity values at the requested radius, selecting a stronger velocity only when its device-depth closely matches the center pixel. This helps preserve motion around silhouettes without importing motion from clearly different depths. It is a local approximate depth check (hardware depth units, not metres) and costs up to four additional velocity and depth reads per blurred pixel. The cost estimator includes this additional work when enabled. Example: {"type":"motionBlur","intensity":0.65,"maxPixels":20, "samples":8,"depthThreshold":0.012,"reactiveStrength":0.85, "velocityDilation":1} All additions use the existing AIVERSE_PRISMA_MOTION_BLUR=1 opt-in flag, HDR RGBA16F and appropriate quality tier. Reactive mask callbacks are a Renderer3D presentation extension, independent of FPS, RTS, water or SpectraFX ownership. h: Stage 33 — GPU-completed fences for safe PRISMA resource retirement
x: The renderer now exposes a separate GPU-completion timeline in the genre-independent gfx::Device interface: uint64_t submitted = dev.gpuSubmissionFence(); // current GPU frame, 0 if unavailable uint64_t completed = dev.gpuCompletedFence(); // GPU-confirmed completion only The submitted token covers work encoded in the currently active GPU frame and is not the CPU frame counter. It can be attached to a target retirement before that frame is actually submitted; the backend will complete it only after GPU execution. A nonzero gpuCompletedFence() result is a real, contiguous completed GPU timeline token. Unsupported devices return zero. All values are per-device; never compare values from different devices, contexts or GPU queues. Metal: GfxMetal.mm uses the current command buffer's frame token and updates an atomic completed counter in its addCompletedHandler only for MTLCommandBufferStatusCompleted. It does not turn frameSerial() into a completion fence. The asynchronous callback captures shared lifetime-safe state and the graphics owner thread polls it by reading gpuCompletedFence(). GL33 / GLES3 / WebGL2: after the frame's render commands the backend inserts glFenceSync(GL_SYNC_GPU_COMMANDS_COMPLETE,0) and flushes the command stream without waiting. At the next beginFrame, it calls glClientWaitSync(..., timeout=0) on its oldest pending fence, advancing completed tokens strictly in submission order and deleting signalled GL sync objects. The Windows GL33 dynamic loader now loads glFenceSync, glClientWaitSync, glDeleteSync. A failed fence is never treated as successful completion. No per-frame glFinish is added. Vulkan: uses its already existing per-frame VkFence and serial_. gpuSubmissionFence is the currently recording GPU frame's serial; gpuCompletedFence returns only the highest serial whose slot fence has been successfully confirmed by vkWaitForFences. A lost device or unsuccessful wait does not advance the completed fence. This is the existing slot-wait path, not a new polling implementation that blocks extra frames.

Renderer3D::beginScene now calls collectCompletedObjectMotion(dev.gpuCompletedFence()) on the graphics owner thread. When a viewport changes size, queueObjectMotionTexture takes the current dev.gpuSubmissionFence() if available and associates it with the old object velocity, reactive or scratch-depth target. On completion the old targets are destroyed; before then they are retained. retireObjectMotionView and setObjectMotionSubmittedFence remain available for externally managed submission lifecycles. On devices without submission-fence support, old targets remain in the Stage 32 quarantine until explicit GPU idle.

Prisma::sized still keeps three active size entries for Scene/Game views, but when evicting the least-recently-used entry it now moves the whole Sized context — legacy raster targets, depth targets, cached Bloom graph and persistent PrismaRhiExecutor resource pool — into a fence-tagged retirement list instead of releasing it immediately. When the GPU reports that the last referencing submission completed, collectCompletedSizes frees the retired targets and safely resets the graph executor pool. In addition, Prisma::target now fence-retires targets replaced by size/HDR format changes, avoiding immediate destruction of a texture that may be in use by an earlier in-flight GPU command buffer. Prisma::releaseRetiredSizesAfterGpuIdle() is the escape hatch for hosts that have explicitly waited for an idle GPU; the function also drains unfenced/quarantined individual targets. The shutdown path assumes the platform's normal device-teardown GPU-idle condition. This stage is about resource lifetime correctness, not a change to image output, bloom topology, exposed postfx JSON, particle simulation or gameplay ECS. Existing experimental flags remain off by default.

The new timeline only covers commands on the backend's regular graphics submission queue. External GPU queues or devices need their own fence tracking. Metal handles are released after the command buffer completion callback; GLES/WebGL sync capabilities and actual device behavior still require runtime validation. Vulkan may only advance its completion counter when rotating to a frame slot whose fence was waited. Without a GPU-completed token, retired resources are not released opportunistically and quarantine can grow. Auto Exposure per-view 1×1 history, PRISMA LUTs, externally owned Sprite/FX buffers and other unrelated render-resource caches have their own existing teardown policies; they are not all migrated to this queue. RenderGraph internal pool cleanup is deferred together with the evicted Sized context, rather than by assuming every pixel pass finished at the end of the CPU frame. Native compilation, CTest, Metal/GL/Vulkan GPU completion tests, images and memory profiling have NOT RUN, per the user's features-first instruction. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-33.md.

Per-view MotionBlur matrices, validity and borrowed current-frame velocity/reactive handles are discarded without destroying those externally owned borrowed resources. Renderer3D::retireObjectMotionView(id, fence=0) is now callable without a manually supplied fence; the queue first queries the live backend gpuSubmissionFence(). Its separate current-frame GPU velocity, reactive and depth targets are retired independently from PRISMA exposure. Renderer3D::motionRetirementStats() reports retained per-view context count, fenced/unfenced texture count, backend completed GPU fence and known pending bytes. In the editor Editor::frame tracks which view actually rendered postprocess this GUI frame. The API leaves existing postfx JSON, editor configuration, game behavior and ECS unchanged. No new postprocessing effect is enabled by default. Active Prisma::Sized contexts remain keyed by output dimensions, not individual camera IDs, because they contain reusable frame-local targets; only private exposure and motion history is camera-keyed. h: Stage 35 — editor framebuffer GPU retirement and explicit pressure drain
x: The editor's actual Viewport::color and Viewport::depth render targets now use the same GPU-completed-fence principles as PRISMA and Renderer3D. They are not owned by PRISMA: a new apps/editor/ViewportGpuRetirement.h owner lives in the Editor instance and outlives its Scene/Game/FX window objects. Viewport binds that owner during ensure(dev,w,h,owner), and release() / resize / viewport destruction transfer both GPU handles to the owner instead of directly destroying in-flight images. The old color handle may still be in an ImGui draw command even after the window's Viewport::image() returns, so it is only destroyed after gfx::Device::gpuCompletedFence() covers the submission that may reference it. Unfenced resources are quarantined until the host has explicitly verified GPU idle. The owner also clears the viewport's stale drawnFrame / hover state when released. All three editor producers (Scene, Game and FX windows) use this shared owner. They release hidden/closed offscreen render targets without relying on window destruction; the owner retains resources past window lifetime. A hidden/closed tab can later recreate a framebuffer with no stale ImGui texture handles.

ViewportGpuRetirement reports pending fenced/unfenced texture counts, metadata-derived knownPendingBytes, a threshold and an overBudget indicator. The default shared known-pending budget is 128 MiB, configurable through AIVERSE_PRISMA_RETIRE_BUDGET_MB (32..4096 MiB). The editor checks the sum of known pending bytes from Viewport, PRISMA and Renderer3D on the pre-render boundary of Editor::frame, before any new GPU draw submission. It normally collects already GPU-completed resources with no wait. If that known pending memory exceeds the budget, it can call the new explicit gfx::Device::waitForSubmittedGpuWork() hook exactly at that safe point. On successful synchronization it drains the Viewport, PRISMA and Renderer3D GPU retirement queues, including unfenced quarantine. It never releases an in-flight texture based on the number of elapsed CPU frames. This explicit pressure-only wait is implemented with glFinish() on GL33/GLES3 (excluding WebGL), waiting the last actually committed Metal command buffer (never the uncommitted buffer for the current frame), and vkQueueWaitIdle on Vulkan. These waits are not performed every frame; they can cause a visible one-time stall at memory pressure. The WebGL2 backend explicitly returns false because a portable synchronous idle barrier is not promised; resources remain quarantined until an external safe teardown. A positive wait result only covers previously submitted GPU commands, so the editor must call it before it encodes new frame work that uses those resources. The Statistics tab now shows viewport fenced/unfenced resource counts, known pending MiB versus the configured budget, and a "Запросить безопасную очистку GPU" button. That button merely requests a one-shot cleanup at the next frame's pre-render boundary, not while the Statistics window's ImGui pass is active. The threshold is an advisory pressure budget rather than a global hard GPU VRAM cap. Internal RenderGraph allocations, active resources, driver overhead, and unknown/unsupported RHI texture descriptors may not be included in the lower-bound estimate. If a backend cannot synchronize, the editor deliberately retains memory rather than risking GPU use-after-free. The RHI's prior gpuSubmissionFence() / gpuCompletedFence() APIs are unchanged, and the new waitForSubmittedGpuWork() is optional. All postprocessing flags remain off by default; no ECS/gameplay ownership changes. Validation: source-level inspection and GitHub writes only. More than eight pending whole-preview bundles is also a pressure signal for a real pre-render GPU-idle attempt, not permission to assume completion. In unsupported/failed-fence paths, resources are kept alive rather than destroyed early. The Statistics window now reports separately pending pipelines, shaders, buffers, textures, owner bundles, and fenced / unfenced counts. Bundles' underlying GPU memory is not fully known so the budget remains an advisory minimum.

This does not automatically migrate every producer in the engine: a native game, custom rendering module or plugin must opt into a lifetime owner before destroying shaders/pipelines/buffers mid-frame. The Shader Graph and editor FX integrations are concrete paths. Multiple external GPU queues/devices require their own synchronization and owners. A full graphics-device teardown still requires an actual GPU idle guarantee; a pending callback must not dereference an already destroyed gfx::Device. The original postfx JSON, PRISMA visual effects, ECS gameplay, water/VFX feature configurations and default-off experimental flags remain unchanged. NOT RUN at the user's direction: native builds, CTest, Metal/GL/Vulkan driver work, screenshots, FX-preview hot-reload smoke, VRAM profiling and CI. Source-level commits and symbol inspection do not establish runtime correctness. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-37.md.

h: Stage 38 — additional Portrait owners, buffer metadata and GPU device-loss abandonment
x: The editor now uses the existing Stage 37 render::GpuResourceRetirement::retireOwned() API for additional complete Portrait renderer owners in the Model and Materials windows. Those windows previously stored an inline game::Portrait and immediately ran its shutdown() when a panel was destroyed. They now retain the entire old portrait (Renderer3D, generated models, vertex/index buffers, shader pipelines, color/depth textures) in a deferred graphics-owner bundle. Its cleanup runs only after the relevant device's actual GPU completion fence or an explicit host-confirmed GPU-idle drain. On window closure or loss of the selected dock tab, the old portrait is retired; reopening creates a new portrait without reusing the previous in-flight GPU handles. The standalone model-viewer and other clients with different ownership are not modified.

gfx::BufferInfo and the optional gfx::Device::bufferInfo(BufferHandle,BufferInfo&) provide a CPU-only live-resource query. The GL, Metal and Vulkan backends read their own buffer tables without waiting for the GPU or readback. The result contains logicalBytes and versions (dynamic buffer copies can take extra GPU memory). These describe logical buffer allocation size; Metal/Vulkan dynamic snapshots and GPU allocator padding can exceed that amount. GpuResourceRetirement::retire(device,buffer) now automatically uses bufferInfo to estimate the retained bytes if the producer has not supplied them. Retired textures similarly use actual textureInfo width, height and pixel format. This improves the known-pending-memory estimate for Editor FX graph hot reload, model previews and texture caches. It is still not a precise total GPU VRAM counter; shader/pipeline driver allocations and complex preview owner bundles may have unknown size.

GpuResourceRetirement::collect() checks Device::gpuHealthy(); if the device is lost it does not call any destroyShader, destroyPipeline, destroyBuffer, destroyTexture or destroyCompute functions. The new explicit abandonDevice(device) removes pending raw RHI handles without calling dead GPU APIs. Complete owner bundles are more dangerous: destroying a captured ShaderGraphPreview object can transitively call Device in its destructor. Their callbacks are moved to an inert process-lifetime orphan sink with no destructor. This intentionally retains that CPU memory until process exit rather than risking use-after-free after terminal device loss. A normal GpuResourceRetirement destructor also prevents unsafe bundle callbacks from being run implicitly if the host did not first drain at a verified GPU-idle point. The editor's shutdown integrates abandonDevice when gpuHealthy() is false. ClientHost::abandonOnDeviceLoss() provides a similar terminal path for deferred hosted GameClient owners, which otherwise might destroy nested renderers against a dead GPU Device. An archived client's device must match the verified completion source. The Statistics window exposes abandoned handles/bundles for diagnostics. Abandonment is an emergency device-loss/teardown fallback, not ordinary memory reclamation, and does not replace restoring the device, recreating render targets or handling other rendering subsystems' old ownership policies.

The common GPU retirement service remains presentation-only, genre-independent and opt-in for owners that can guarantee the device is alive during normal collection. The Model and Materials windows are additional concrete adopters; the Animation Graph editor, external model viewer and other independent preview owners remain on their own lifetime paths and should be migrated via a similarly self-contained complete owner bundle. No changes to ECS, FPS/RTS gameplay logic, postfx effect schema, HDR shader output, water, or the default-off Motion Blur flag. NOT RUN: CMake/C++/Obj-C++ builds, CTest, GL/Metal/Vulkan runtime GPU fences, editor Model/Materials tab switching, device-loss simulations, memory profiling, screenshots and CI (per user instruction). Static source inspection is not proof of runtime correctness. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-38.md.

h: Stage 39 — Animation Graph/Rig preview bundles and stable editor state
x: The Animation Graph and Rig windows now share a presentation-only GPU-fence-deferred preview lifecycle with the Shader Graph and Model/Materials editors. In apps/editor/animation/AnimationEditor.h, AnimationEditorPanel::release() detaches the old preview's complete owner bundle: the uploaded render::Model, immutable compiled AnimationGraphInstance state that may reference that model, and the game::Portrait with its own Renderer3D, pipelines, textures and color/depth render targets. The previous owner stays alive in GpuResourceRetirement::retireOwned until its actual backend GPU submission fence completes, or a host-confirmed GPU idle. Its cleanup resets the graph before releasing the referenced model's GPU buffers and releases the Portrait's GPU resources at the same safe point. No editor ECS or animation simulation data is exposed to the retirement manager. Both AnimationGraphWindow and AnimationRigWindow call AnimationEditorPanel::suspendPreview() on a hidden or closed dock tab, retiring GPU memory without erasing the editor document. When the tab becomes visible again, a new Model/Portrait is built from the current document. release() intentionally preserves doc_, saved_, undo/redo history, current selected node, graph scope, the user-set playback toggle, ground height, yaw, zoom, camera/canvas layout and animation-control values. When the program is compiled again, numeric and vector preview parameters with matching names are restored from the previous AnimationParameters; new/removed parameters still use the current graph's definitions. The compiled graph's runtime clock and transient per-node state can restart after a model reload/hidden-tab release — there is no unsafe transfer of per-model graph pointers between models. Pure visual graph node position changes no longer invalidate the animation preview's compiled-program key (including nested subgraphs). Dragging nodes does not needlessly restart the current animation playback. The same stage fixes the previously authored ShaderGraphPreview GPU-key loop to use the mutable JSON node iterator (itemsMut()) instead of a const items view; this is a source-level type-correctness fix pending actual compilation. The independent aiverse_modelview Gallery has a different lifecycle: its Portrait and Renderers are normally released when the entire viewer shuts down, not on per-editor-tab hot reload. Its shutdown now attempts Device::waitForSubmittedGpuWork() before destroying Gallery/Portrait and imported model GPU resources. That wait is a shutdown-only best-effort safeguard, not a substitute for the platform's own required GPU-idle teardown contract on unsupported backends. No changes to the FPS/RTS gameplay ECS, animation graph JSON format, animation algorithms, PRISMA effect settings, water rendering or default-off MotionBlur feature flag. h: Stage 40 — GPU-independent preview clock checkpoint (Animation Graph/Rig)
x: When an Animation Graph or Rig editor tab hides or the preview's uploaded model is reloaded, GPU-fenced preview retirement from Stage 39 no longer always restarts simple animation playback from zero. AnimationGraphInstance::snapshotPreviewClocks() provides an optional pointer-free PreviewClockSnapshot with the active state ID, its elapsed time, clip node names and clocks, source clip identities/durations, state IDs, node kind order, and the loaded model's skeleton names/parents. restorePreviewClocks(snapshot) first validates all of those facts against the newly compiled graph and refuses an invalid snapshot without partially mutating the current instance. The editor also requires the same model path and the same authored program key (which excludes visual-only node position changes) before attempting to restore. This is intentionally narrow: a graph with an in-progress transition fade, subgraphs, native operators, rig state, motion matching, controllers, traits, or other stateful nodes will restart rather than rebind potentially model-dependent CPU state. Simple bind/clip/blend/additive/two-bone IK graphs can restore state and clip time, assuming the graph program and skeleton/clip identities are unchanged. Camera, document, controls, playback toggle, and undo/redo remain as in Stage 39. Explicit New/Load/ Discard and Preview Reset clear the saved checkpoint; a changed graph program or incompatible loaded model cannot consume it. Files: engine/render/AnimationGraph.h, engine/render/AnimationGraph.cpp, apps/editor/animation/AnimationEditor.h. This is only preview-presentation state; ECS gameplay, animation graph JSON schema, Prisma GPU shader effects, SpectraFX and the GPU retirement fence policy are unchanged. h: Stage 41 — memory residency by view, shared graph pools, and fenced idle-cache eviction
x: Stage 41 adds GPU-free/read-only diagnostic calls to the Prisma presentation owner without changing shader outputs or game ECS state: Prisma::memoryStats(): reports active size-scoped framebuffer targets, depth attachments, live RenderGraph texture pools, view-private Auto Exposure history, persistent LUT/graph-image inputs and missing RHI metadata. MemoryStats::liveKnownBytes counts each actual size cache once, even when Scene and Game have identical width/height. Repeated per-view ViewMemoryStats::sharedKnownBytes is an explanatory reference to that cache, not an additive view allocation. ViewMemoryStats records the latest successfully allocated postprocessing scene-pass resolution for each stable view ID (Scene=1, Game=2 in the editor; native users may supply their own IDs). Its per-view ownedHistoryKnownBytes is private exposure history, while the RenderGraph pool belongs to Sized and may be shared by multiple view IDs. PrismaRhiExecutor::GpuMemoryStats now differentiates unknown live textures from unknown pending textures. Mips, multisample copies, compression, backend-alignment and shader/pipeline driver allocations are not inferable from the current TextureInfo interface: numbers are lower bounds, not a VRAM budget or GPU-residency certificate. GpuResourceRetirement::Stats separately exposes deferred owner bundles (including ShaderGraph/Portrait preview bundles) with no reliable byte estimate. A zero estimate never means a zero-cost bundle. ViewportGpuRetirement has a non-owning live-framebuffer registry for Scene/Game/FX windows. Viewport::ensure() publishes color+depth handles and size, and Viewport::release() unregisters them before fence-retiring the textures. liveStats() gives a lower-bound per-window memory reading; it does not grant ownership of these RHI handles. StatsWindow now shows active shared postprocessing cache bytes, private per-camera exposure bytes, Scene/Game/FX framebuffer bytes, stale/unreferenced caches, graph pending bytes and missing byte estimates, without summing repeated shared-per-view figures. Idle size cache lifetime: Prisma::retireView(id) removes the stable view's reference but does not destroy shared scene targets. At the end of the editor's viewport work, Prisma::retireUnreferencedSizeCaches() scans up to the small size cache and moves only sizes referenced by no live view into RetiredSized using the graphics submission fence. Resources are actually freed only in the existing nonblocking confirmed-GPU-completion collector or an explicit verified GPU-idle path. When post-processing is disabled for one camera, Editor now marks that view inactive and retires its old reference; it no longer retains a stale cache just because the Game tab continues to render without effects. This may cause fresh allocations on reopen, trading cache warmth for bounded editor idle memory. These diagnostics and retirement paths are opt-in/presentation-only; PRISMA continues to own post-processing. FX emitters remain SpectraFX, and runtime games not using the editor remain free to choose their own cache retention. No gameplay/ECS components, FPS/RTS-specific camera modules or postfx JSON schemas were changed. Verification: GitHub source readback and static call-site inspection only. NOT RUN (features-first): native builds, CTest, GPU fence/driver run, Metal/GL/Vulkan/WebGL smoke, GUI tab-switch/resize and VRAM profiling.
