h: Opt-in physical atmosphere and local volumetric fog (2026-11-20)
x: PRISMA owns PhysicalSky and LocalFog HDR passes. They run before exposure metering and motion/temporal processing, then normal bloom/tonemap. New target roles 200/201 do not overlap DoF (50), metering or motion buffers. Sample scene depth with the existing separate scratch depth attachment; size resources use PRISMA's normal fence-retirement path. Pipelines shut down after its GPU-idle barrier. No second PostFx implementation or SpectraFX emitter ownership. See physical sky/clouds/god rays and local sphere/OBB fog with runtime reveal. The read-only PHYSIS bridge targets Prisma&; the legacy PostFx alias remains compatible. These features are disabled by default. Native region/settings APIs are owner-wide: a multi-camera host must set each view's cosmetic data before its resolve, or use a separate Prisma owner. Camera-volume profile blending does not yet author or interpolate these atmosphere settings. No gameplay changes.

FogVolume::structure optionally shapes local fog with periodic 3D noise, per-axis world scale, height attenuation and wind; Prisma::setLocalFogTime provides a reproducible presentation clock. Default uniform fog is preserved. The existing local fog pass owns this, with no extra history or render targets. See the structured banks section in docs/local-volumetric-fog.md. No terrain sampling, gameplay visibility or PHYSIS state mutation is introduced. Local fog now also supports heightVariation, three-dimensional warp, boundary edgeErosion and optional selfShadow/shadowDistance. Self-shadowing ray-marches all active volumes and reveal holes toward the sun, independently of the existing geometry shadow map. This is bounded single scattering; no new temporal buffers, shadow-map ownership, terrain dependency or authoritative simulation state.

The integrated optional spectra::GpuPoolWorld editor preview contributes through Editor::drawSpectraGpuPreview() in the same open HDR scene pass, immediately before Renderer3D::resolvePrisma(). SpectraFX owns emitters, per-frame simulation and particle GPU resources. PRISMA retains the full-screen resolve, camera volumes, reactive coverage and viewport GPU timing. Main's existing completion timeline is preserved; no new postprocess implementation or renderer default is introduced. See docs/agent-handoffs/inspector-spectrafx-main-2026-11-20.md for integration verification and remaining UI/platform coverage.

The independent lensWater catalog effect is opt-in, configurable and removable without disabling NEREID underwater absorption. See parameters and host contract. NEREID supplies read-only camera immersion; PRISMA owns bounded per-view wetness, post-exit drainage/drying and the shared GLSL/MSL composite. This is a screen-space approximation; see the separate stage handoff for actual GPU/test coverage.

Prisma::setViewDepthOfField(viewId, DepthOfFieldOverride{enabled, focusDistance, focusRangeMeters, maxBlur}) replaces the metric focus plane, sharp interval and maximum blur of the authored depthOfField effect for one stable view, in the same way setViewManualExposure overrides the authored exposure. The override forces the metric (camera-linear) branch and keeps the effect's intensity and occlusionToleranceMeters. enabled=false switches defocus off for that view. Values are clamped to the catalog bounds on ingress; clearViewDepthOfField and retireView remove the override. It still requires the authored effect and AIVERSE_PRISMA_DOF=1; nothing is added to the profile implicitly. LENS drives it from CameraLensComponent::driveDepthOfField through CameraPostFxPool: the thin-lens sharp interval [near, far] becomes focusDistance = (near+far)/2, focusRangeMeters = far-near (an infinite far limit is capped at 500 m) and maxBlur = background disc radius at infinity in render pixels (clamped to 16). This is the same 8-tap screen-space defocus, not a physical bokeh. See docs/handoffs/prisma-stage-96-lens-physical-dof.md. Source on GitHub: docs/prisma.md

SpectraFX is the official name of the universal, genre-independent visual-effects system in AIVERSE. Its design is inspired by the authoring and event-driven workflow of Unreal Niagara, but it is not a copy of Unreal code, asset formats, or editor. aiverse::spectra is the public C++ API namespace. Current scope (2026-11-18): Graph v1 frontend, reusable CPU particle backend, graph-asset variants/hot reload and optional read-only ECS presentation adapter have been committed. A basic graph-v1 node-canvas editor and in-memory CPU preview are committed but unverified; a limited Metal GPU particle prototype is committed but unverified; full GPU/CPU integration, Niagara dataflow and automatic RTS/FPS production integration are not finished. Tests were added but have not yet been run in the authoring environment. Refer to docs/agent-handoffs/universal-niagara-vfx-2026-11-18.md for exact SHA and verification status. 2026-11-22: effects declared in data (rules/map/type/weapon/ability "spectraFx") for every host, and one asset running on the GPU kernel or its CPU twin with Metal parity tests: see spectrafx-entity-effects.md.

SpectraFX is NOT the post-processing engine. It owns emitters, particle simulation, FX graphs (VFX fx/graphs/*.vfx.json), ECS FX sources and transient visual events. PRISMA in engine/render/Prisma.{h,cpp} owns HDR composite/tone mapping, bloom, depth of field, motion blur, temporal AA, screen-space lighting and post-process camera volumes. FX sprites/meshes write scene HDR before PRISMA; the full-screen postfx Shader Graph domain belongs to PRISMA. The common Shader Graph compiler/RHI is shared infrastructure, not a second VFX or postprocess implementation. Never add full-screen frame effects to engine/fx, and never add emitters/particle lifecycle to PRISMA. PRISMA's persisted postfx block and postfx_* MCP commands stay stable for existing projects. See AGENTS.md ownership table and docs/prisma.md. No automatic live binding is implied.

Gameplay ECS (authoritative, deterministic) ├─ typed gameplay events ────────────────┐ └─ data-only SpectraSourceComponent ──┐ │ ▼ ▼ SpectraFX presentation (read-only World + events) │ exposed graph parameters │ graph assets fx/graphs/*.vfx.json │ compileGraph (versioned IR) │ existing fx::EffectDef schema │ CPU fx::ParticleSystem/RHI │ renderer + quality tiers Future opt-in path: GPU simulation/backend + advanced Niagara dataflow nodes No genre-dependent FX engines. An RTS turret, FPS gun, spaceship engine or racing car all use the same source component and event presenter. The host game supplies only the pose resolver and maps its event IDs to effect assets. Graphics state and particle handles never enter deterministic gameplay state/checksums.

engine/fx/SpectraFX.h: aiverse::spectra::Runtime, Effect, Handle, GraphAssets, GraphLoadResult, compileGraph. libraries/include/aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraFX.h: aiverse::spectra::SourceComponent, EventBinding, PresentationSystem. AIVERSE::spectrafx: CMake link target, alias of existing aiverse_fx; the legacy target remains valid for other agents and projects.

Put this file at fx/graphs/engine_fire.vfx.json inside a project: { "version": 1, "parameters": { "color": [[0, "#ffe8a0ff"], [1, "#ff330000"]] }, "nodes": [ {"id": "spawn", "type": "Spawn", "properties": {"rate": 24, "duration": 1, "loop": true}}, {"id": "initialize", "type": "Initialize", "properties": {"life": 0.6, "speed": 1.0, "size": 0.4}}, {"id": "update", "type": "Update", "properties": {"color": {"$param": "color"}}}, {"id": "output", "type": "SpriteOutput", "properties": {"texture": "builtin:smoke"}} ], "links": [ {"from": "spawn", "to": "initialize"}, {"from": "initialize", "to": "update"}, {"from": "update", "to": "output"} ], "outputs": ["output"] } The v1 compiler accepts Spawn → Initialize → Update* → SpriteOutput|MeshOutput|RibbonOutput chains, with output fan-out but no multiple-input node merges. Every node has a properties object whose keys are validated against engine/fx/FxEffect.h. The module chain compiles to the existing fx::EffectDef — it does not execute arbitrary per-particle graph instructions. #include "engine/fx/SpectraFX.h" aiverse::spectra::Runtime particles; particles.init(device); // The native host owns gfx::Device. particles.setFileReader(readGameContent); aiverse::spectra::GraphAssets assets(particles, readGameContent); // Converts a versioned graph asset into a CPU particle effect. auto flame = assets.load("engine_fire"); if (flame.effect >= 0) particles.play(flame.effect, {0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f}); // Overrides produce independent graph variants: auto cold = assets.load("engine_fire", aiverse::Json::parse(R"({"color":[[0,"#aaddffff"],[1,"#0044ff00"]]})")); Runtime loop: call setView(camera, viewProj, width, height), update(dt), then render(fog) after scene rendering while its pass remains open, as described in engine/fx/ParticleSystem.h.

#include <aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraFX.h> using namespace aiverse; auto entity = world.create(); spectra::SourceComponent source; source.effect = "graph:engine_fire:<hash>"; // Better: use GraphLoadResult::runtimeName. source.killOnDetach = false; world.add<spectra::SourceComponent>(entity, source); spectra::PresentationSystem presenter(particles); presenter.sync(world, [](const World& w, Entity e, fx::float3& position, fx::float3& direction) { // Resolve the render transform using YOUR game's component types. // Do not hardcode FPS/RTS into SpectraFX. return gameResolveEffectPose(w, e, position, direction); }); presenter.consumeTickEvents(tick, sim.events(), {{hitEventId, spectra::EventBinding{"impact_flash", 1_fx}}}); Use the actual GraphLoadResult.runtimeName for continuous graph assets after GraphAssets::load; the fx/graphs registry does not automatically initialize all graphs when the game starts. After rollback/new match, call presenter.reset() to discard outstanding presentation handles and reset the presented-tick cursor; GPU/CPU simulation state still belongs to the host.

The new branded Spectra* types were introduced without changing the identity of the old Vfx* aliases. Existing fx/<effect>.json, fx/fx.json, aiverse_fx and compileVfxGraph remain available. Engine runtime files stay under engine/fx during migration. Do not remove compatibility aliases or change persistent binary save identifiers until native project adoption and regression tests pass.

The editor-core registerFxOps also registers universal fx_graph_* operations through apps/editor/core/SpectraGraphOps.cpp. They are available from the GUI Workspace and the standalone MCP server, independent of the project's gameplay genre. No editor GPU context is required to validate graphs. Operation Inputs Result fx_graph_list none All fx/graphs/*.vfx.json, per-file compile diagnostics fx_graph_get name Graph JSON, source text and validation fx_graph_validate graph or text or name, optional overrides Strict compiler errors, emitter count and textures; read-only fx_graph_set name, graph or text Validated file creation/update, Change::Fx notification fx_graph_delete name Deletes only the graph source asset fx_graph_bake name, effect, optional overrides, overwrite Compiles graph into fx/<effect>.json for existing fx_preview and legacy runtime Graph names are limited to lowercase letters, digits and underscores (1–48 characters) for editor compatibility. Graph documents have a 1 MiB input limit. Invalid compilation returns ok:false and does not overwrite a previous valid graph; fx_graph_bake refuses to replace an existing legacy effect unless overwrite:true is explicitly supplied. Example MCP workflow: fx_graph_set {"name":"engine_fire","graph":<graph v1 object>} fx_graph_validate {"name":"engine_fire","overrides":{"color":[[0,"#ffffffff"],[1,"#ffffff00"]]}} fx_graph_bake {"name":"engine_fire","effect":"engine_fire_cpu"} fx_preview {"effect":"engine_fire_cpu","advance":1,"freeze":true} view_screenshot {"window":"scene"} Scope: baking is a CPU-compatible materialization step, not GPU graph execution and not a live reference: editing the graph again does not update an already baked effect until re-baked. Graphs still have no dedicated node canvas in the editor; that is the next authoring stage. The old fx/<name>.json, fx/fx.json and RTS event bindings are unaffected. The new vfx_graph_ops test requires aiverse_editor_core to be built; the test is committed but was NOT RUN in the connector-only environment.

The standard AIVERSE Editor has an optional SpectraFX window in the Графика / Look group, defined in apps/editor/windows/SpectraGraphWindow.cpp. Its source is automatically included by the editor's apps/editor/windows/*.cpp CMake GLOB. Open/create fx/graphs/<name>.vfx.json directly from the project. Add nodes of types Spawn, Initialize, Update, SpriteOutput, MeshOutput, RibbonOutput; drag nodes and pan the canvas with the middle mouse button. Click the source node's output pin, then the target's input pin to link; an input may have one incoming edge. Cycles and invalid endpoint types are blocked; unfinished graphs show compiler errors until connected. Select a node to edit its properties JSON. Edit exposed parameters as a JSON object; undo and redo graph edits. Save through fx_graph_set; compile diagnostics come from the exact spectra::compileGraph implementation used at runtime. Предпросмотр calls the new GUI-only fx_graph_preview command, which compiles graph in memory, defines an ephemeral effect on Editor::gameFx_, and plays it in Scene/Game. No temp FX files are written; screenshots still work via view_screenshot. Graph nodes may optionally include authoring metadata "position":[x,y] (two finite bounded numeric coordinates), validated by the v1 compiler but ignored during CPU effect construction. Existing graph assets without coordinates remain valid; the editor places them in a default left-to-right layout. This metadata does not enter gameplay ECS state or shader runtime resources. This is only a basic v1 editor, not full Niagara parity: there is no arbitrary typed dataflow, function graph, GPU compute execution, depth collision, linked graph preview in shipped clients or complete UE-style module UI. Source-level smoke coverage was added to tests/vfx_graph_compiler_test.cpp for node layout metadata; GUI launch, drag/link interactions and GPU screenshots are NOT RUN in the connector-backed development environment. Manual QA is required.

The canonical public header engine/fx/SpectraFX.h includes it so native projects and the editor use the same types and value bounds. #include "engine/fx/SpectraFX.h" aiverse::Json node = aiverse::Json::parse( R"({"id":"emitter","type":"Spawn","properties":{"burst":8}})"); std::string error; bool changed = aiverse::spectra::applyTypedField( node, "burst", aiverse::Json::number(int64_t(24)), error); // Also available: fieldsForNode("Spawn"), fieldForNode(...), // validateTypedField(...), removeTypedField(...). The SpectraFX visual window now has Типизированные модули above Расширенные свойства (JSON). The typed inspector supports number, integer, boolean, string, choice and 3-component vector properties. Its catalog currently includes: Stage Common fields Spawn burst, rate, perMeter, delay, duration, loop Initialize life, speed, size, direction, spread, shape, radius, gravity Update drag, spin, rotation, speedLimit, stretch, velocity, hidden SpriteOutput texture, blend, align, fps MeshOutput blend, align RibbonOutput hidden All typed field operations are opt-in edits. Validation rejects wrong types, invalid enum choices and values outside declared ranges without mutating the source node. h: Metal GPU particle prototype (stage 10 — source committed, unverified)
x: A new opt-in aiverse::spectra::ComputeParticles class in engine/fx/SpectraGpuParticles.{h,cpp} executes a limited billboard particle subset on the Metal RHI compute path. It is not wired into existing RTS/FPS clients and does not replace the legacy aiverse::fx::ParticleSystem. This subset intentionally contains a single additive soft-textured emitter with configurable burst count, lifetime, initial speed, size, gravity, linear drag and alpha-over-life. Complex attributes, noise, trails, mesh particles, collision, GPU subemitters, Niagara dataflow and user-authored shader graphs remain on the existing CPU emitter backend until separately implemented. #include "engine/fx/SpectraFX.h" aiverse::spectra::ComputeParticles particles; aiverse::spectra::ComputeEmitterDesc params; params.capacity = 1024; params.burst = 16; params.backend = aiverse::spectra::ComputePreference::Automatic; params.quality = aiverse::fx::FxQuality::High; // Initialization can occur outside a frame. Device may be nullptr for // pure CPU/headless tests; RequireGpu fails if compute is unavailable. if (!particles.init(device, params)) { // inspect particles.reason() } // Presentation frame, AFTER Device::beginFrame, BEFORE scene render pass: particles.setView(camera, viewProjection, width, height); particles.burstAt({0,2,0}, {0,1,0}, {1,0.5f,0.1f,1}); if (!particles.step(1.f/60)) { // RHI timing/encoder order error; inspect particles.reason() } // During the scene's existing still-open depth-tested render pass: particles.draw(); // After the render pass: Device::endPass, Device::endFrame. // Before destroying gfx::Device: particles.shutdown(). The headless pure policy chooseComputeBackend(backend, supportsCompute, preference) selects the GPU path only for Metal with compute support. CpuOnly forces CPU; Automatic and PreferGpu fall back on unsupported RHI or failed pipeline allocation; RequireGpu rejects unsupported devices rather than silently running on CPU. Low-quality GPU configurations intentionally choose CPU, respecting the existing particle quality behavior. RHI compute calls must run outside render passes and inside a GPU frame. The caller is responsible for a single presentation owner/device thread and cleanup before device destruction; this module contains no ECS gameplay or deterministic simulator state. Metal implementation: three compute passes per presentation frame (queue accepted births → integrate age/velocity/position → expand camera-facing quad vertices). GPU buffers are persistent: 64 bytes/particle for states and seeds, a 4-byte slot index and 40 bytes per billboard vertex. The compute shader writes a vertex buffer directly sampled by the regular RHI particle vertex shader; normal frames do not read the GPU positions back to CPU. One depth-tested additive draw renders the pool. The current prototype draws the entire capped slot index array (dead slots emit degenerate quads); this is not a compacted or GPU-indirect renderer. Maximum pool is 4096 slots, with a maximum of 64 spawned per call. GLSL source is supplied for future Vulkan compute, but Vulkan gfx::Device::supportsCompute is not implemented in the current RHI. GLES3/GL33/WebGL2 do not run the compute kernel, so the existing CPU particle renderer is used instead. Do not report those platforms as GPU-supported. The dedicated test tests/vfx_gpu_backend_test.cpp checks the selection policy, bounds, headless CPU-fallback emissions and lifetime. It also contains a recording Metal RHI mock that verifies spawn→integrate→expand dispatch ordering and render-pass command sequencing without compiling/launching real GPU shaders. It is not a Metal GPU integration test. CI and native GPU validation are still required. Known limitations: no GPU compaction, no camera culling/LOD for per-particle draws, no GPU-particle soft intersection, no mesh/ribbon GPU rendering, no advanced emitter graphs, no cross-CPU/GPU effect scheduler, no automatic FPS/RTS runtime migration, and no GPU performance measurement

h: Automatic graph-to-backend routing (Stage 11 — source committed, not verified)
x: engine/fx/SpectraGraphRuntime.{h,cpp} introduces a new optional, genre-independent aiverse::spectra::GraphRuntime. It compiles a graph-v1 asset or accepts a precompiled fx::EffectDef and decides whether it can run without semantic loss on the existing Metal compute prototype. Every unsupported graph is executed with the exact same full EffectDef on fx::ParticleSystem; complex modules are never stripped to fit the GPU. #include "engine/fx/SpectraFX.h" aiverse::spectra::GraphRuntime runner; aiverse::spectra::GraphRuntimeOptions options; options.preference = aiverse::spectra::ComputePreference::Automatic; options.quality = aiverse::fx::FxQuality::High; options.capacity = 1024; if (!runner.initGraph(device, graphJson, aiverse::Json::object(), options)) { // runner.reason() and runner.errors() describe the rejection } // After Device::beginFrame, before the scene render pass: runner.setView(camera, viewProj, width, height); runner.burstAt({0, 1, 0}, {0, 1, 0}); runner.step(1.f / 60.f); // While the scene pass is open: runner.draw(fog); // On match change/rollback: runner.clear() outside an active encoder. // Before device shutdown: runner.shutdown(). The schema validator inspectGraphGpuEligibility(effect, options) does not require a GPU and is safe for native modules, headless tests and editor tools. It returns GraphGpuEligibility { eligible, gpu, reason }. GPU v1 is allowed only for one additive builtin:soft camera-aligned point emitter containing one burst of 1–64 particles, constant speed/life/size/drag, zero spread, world-Y gravity, and the default white-to-transparent colour ramp. The current prototype supports only this limited payload. Custom colours/gradients, multiple emitters, random ranges/curves, custom shader graphs, trails/ribbons, noise, force fields, sub-emitters, lights, collisions, texture animation, or any other unsupported module force a full CPU fallback. The validator compares normalized complete effect definitions against a known-supported template and also explicitly checks sensitive unsupported modules and colour keys. ComputePreference::RequireGpu fails if the graph is not eligible, the real device does not expose Metal compute, the quality tier is too low or the shader/pipeline cannot initialize. Automatic and PreferGpu instead use the unchanged CPU asset. CpuOnly never attempts GPU. A GPU health failure inside ComputeParticles can subsequently fall back to its restricted CPU equivalent; GraphRuntime continues to own that instance and reports the actual backend. The editor and MCP fx_graph_validate, fx_graph_get, fx_graph_list responses now add metalGpuEligible and metalGpuReason after successful compilation. These are only asset capability diagnostics, not proof that Metal is present or that GPU execution succeeded. The SpectraFX visual editor shows the same capability verdict under the properties inspector; its in-memory graph preview still uses the established CPU renderer. Important boundaries: This is an opt-in native API. It is not automatically wired into existing FPS, RTS, editor gameplay, ECS authoritative state, file assets or current save protocols. The existing production client renderer stays on CPU. Actual Apple Silicon GPU rendering, MSL compilation, multiple frames in flight and all regression tests remain unverified until run in a real checkout. Source tests: tests/vfx_graph_runtime_test.cpp exercises a supported graph, strict rejections and CPU fallback; tests/vfx_graph_ops_test.cpp checks MCP eligibility diagnostics. CTest name: vfx_graph_runtime (label SpectraFX).

h: Metal lifecycle and sparse draw-range hardening (Stage 12 — source committed, unverified)
x: The opt-in ComputeParticles Metal backend now tracks its occupied slot prefix rather than always updating and drawing all allocated slots. The CPU-owned slot-age bookkeeping determines the greatest currently live slot index; compute integration and quad expansion run through that prefix and the indexed draw is limited to submittedSlots * 6. A pool containing no live particles and no pending births performs no compute dispatch or draw. This is not GPU compaction: gaps between active slots still produce degenerate quads. True GPU stream compaction, prefix sums, indirect draw counts, and thousands of materials are subsequent phases. The hard 4096-slot capacity and original RHI buffer format remain. ComputeStats now exposes: submittedSlots: prefix length actually submitted in the latest GPU draw (may exceed alive when holes exist). gpuFallbacks: automatic runtime transitions to CPU. lostOnFallback: number of GPU-resident particles discarded when the GPU device became unhealthy. Existing stats remain. A runtime device-loss event is not a seamless animation step: ComputeParticles::step reports failure. For RequireGpu, the emitter becomes unavailable, retains its Metal backend identity until shutdown and does not switch to CPU. For Automatic and PreferGpu, the class attempts to initialize a CPU emitter, records the discarded GPU particles and reports false for the transition frame. CPU rendering on a device reported unhealthy is not guaranteed; a real graphics-device recreation may be required. RHI encoder timing errors continue to return failure without silently switching backend. GraphRuntime::step now forwards the actual readiness, backend and error message of its contained GPU/CPU runtime. GraphRuntime::gpuActive also checks the underlying compute emitter, preventing false-positive success reports after RequireGpu device loss. On clear, the sparse range and GPU slot counters reset; attempting clear inside an active GPU encoder leaves state intact and emits a diagnostic. The RHI recording test tests/vfx_gpu_backend_test.cpp has scenarios for active encoder clear protection, sparse draw range, empty-pool zero dispatch, GPU loss with RequireGpu, GPU→CPU transition with explicit lost-particle telemetry and staggered particle expiry over multiple frames. These are mocked host-command tests, not actual MSL execution. A focused workflow, .github/workflows/spectrafx-validation.yml, provides pull-request and manual gates: Linux/macOS build and headless CTest for SpectraFX; Linux additionally builds the editor and tests MCP graph operations. The focused workflow does not validate a real Metal compute shader or GPU image correctness. Actual compilation, CI results, Apple Silicon rendering, screenshots and performance measurements remain NOT VERIFIED until they run.

h: Dense billboard gathering (Stage 13 — source committed, GPU validation pending)
x: The optional Metal spectra::ComputeParticles backend now gathers only live physical particle slots into contiguous GPU billboard vertices. The persistent particle-state pool still uses stable indices for spawn/recycle; one additional 4-byte-per-slot storage buffer maps dense draw ordinal → physical state slot. The CPU already owns lifetime/slot bookkeeping and publishes the live-index list to GPU before the compute encoder starts. The GPU reads each selected particle's position/velocity/tint from its own resident state buffer and writes a contiguous block of four vertices. Motion state is never read back to CPU. The frame order is: upload any new particle states and slot indices → upload the current live slot map → compute births → integrate the physical-slot range that was live before the step → GPU gather and expand exactly the particles still alive after the step → regular RHI indexed draw of alive * 6 indices. The compute kernel uses slot 4 for the live-index buffer and Uniforms.meta.w for the alive count; both MSL and future GLSL sources use the same layout. GPU updates stay between beginFrame and beginPass; draw remains inside the scene render pass. ComputeStats::submittedSlots now equals the densely emitted live count (not the high-water physical slot index). For example, after slots 0–2 expire while slots 3–5 survive, the GPU receives [3,4,5] and submits 18 indices, not 36. The recording-RHI regression verifies this map and the draw count across staggered birth/death frames. The new live-slot upload is 4 * alive bytes each active frame and is tracked under ComputeStats::uploadedBytes. An idle particle pool continues to skip compute and draw. Scope and limitations: This is GPU vertex gathering from a CPU-maintained live-slot list. It eliminates sparse-dead-slot rendering, but it is not a fully GPU-resident atomic/prefix-sum compaction or GPU-authored indirect draw. CPU still scans at most 4096 age records per frame, and live-index uploads incur bandwidth. The fixed 16-bit index buffer still limits the pool to 4096 billboards. The backend is restricted to additive soft sprites eligible under GraphRuntime and is not enabled by default in existing RTS/FPS clients. Metal shader compilation, image output and performance on Apple Silicon remain NOT VERIFIED until native CI/device tests complete. Non-Metal RHI paths continue using the original CPU ParticleSystem.

The Metal subset now has an explicitly opt-in GPU-side compact/draw mode, using the existing optional RHI methods. This does not change the default backend or any existing FPS/RTS runtime: #include "engine/fx/SpectraFX.h" aiverse::spectra::GraphRuntimeOptions opts; opts.preference = aiverse::spectra::ComputePreference::Automatic; opts.gpuIndirect = true; // experimental; default is false // For the standalone billboard emitter: // aiverse::spectra::ComputeEmitterDesc cfg; // cfg.gpuIndirect = true;

The portable gfx::Device adds the default-false capability query supportsGpuAuthoredIndirectDraw(). Metal reports support through its existing plain drawIndexedGpuIndirect path, independently of experimental ICB features. Vulkan/GL/GLES/WebGL continue to return false. A device advertising only supportsCompute() is not enough. Metal compute uses two additional persistent storage buffers: aliveCounter (4-byte atomic uint, compute slot 5) and gpuDrawArgs (20-byte gfx::DrawIndexedIndirectCommand, slot 6). The existing ParticleState and 40-byte expanded vertex formats are unchanged. Mode 3 reset GPU alive counter Mode 0 spawn into persistent physical GPU particle slots Mode 1 integrate physical state / kill expired particles Mode 4 atomic-fetch-add surviving particle -> dense vertex ordinal Mode 5 write GPU indexed draw args (indexCount = alive * 6) Render gfx::Device::drawIndexedGpuIndirect(gpuDrawArgs, 0) Metal's RHI inserts a buffer memory barrier after each compute dispatch, and graphics submission occurs in the following render encoder. Surviving particle order is nondeterministic (atomic allocation), which is acceptable only for the current additive billboard subset. The GPU counter and draw arguments are not read back to CPU during normal rendering. If gpuIndirect=true but the device lacks supportsGpuAuthoredIndirectDraw(), SpectraFX retains Stage 13's CPU-published dense slot gather with regular drawIndexed. If an already-enabled indirect command is rejected during drawing, it reports an error and skips the draw instead of drawing potentially uninitialized/stale vertices with an approximate CPU count. ComputeParticles::gpuIndirectActive() reports actual selection; ComputeStats::gpuCompactDispatches and gpuIndirectDraws track submitted GPU operations. When indirect is active, stats().submittedSlots and stats().alive are host-side lifespan estimates, not GPU-readback measurements. The actual indexed count comes from the GPU-authored 20-byte command.

GPU indirect removes the per-frame upload of the live slot map, and GPU compaction/draw-count calculation no longer relies on that map. The CPU still owns slot allocation and lifetime/free-list bookkeeping, and scans a bounded maximum of 4096 age records. GPU motion and dense quad generation remain GPU-side. This is not a GPU-only allocator, multi-emitter scheduler, sorting system, or complete Niagara simulation.

tests/vfx_gpu_backend_test.cpp: the recording RHI verifies reset/spawn/integrate/atomic compact/args ordering, absence of host live-slot uploads in GPU-driven mode, capability fallback, and rejection without unsafe direct draw. tests/vfx_metal_compaction_smoke.mm: real Metal compute test compiling the MSL cs_main, running GPU passes and reading the counter, indirect arguments and compacted vertex results between frames. On macOS without a Metal GPU it returns 77 and CTest marks it SKIPPED, not PASS. .github/workflows/spectrafx-validation.yml builds and attempts the Metal smoke on macOS alongside the headless suite; Linux still tests portable CPU/recording paths. All of these changes are committed source, not verified execution. At the latest workflow query, the new SpectraFX CI jobs were still queued. No passing MSL compilation, Metal dispatch, offscreen image, timing or GPU visual parity claim is made. A real image-level Metal and multiple-frames-in-flight test is still required before a shipping/default GPU selection.

h: Cross-instance material batching (Stage 14B — source committed, unverified)
x: Multiple GraphRuntime instances previously owned separate fx::ParticleSystem objects and could each submit the same sprite material as a separate GPU draw call. The opt-in spectra::BatchWorld (engine/fx/SpectraBatchWorld.{h,cpp}) puts arbitrary graph/effect definitions into one shared presentation ParticleSystem. This reuses the existing global ParticleSystem::Impl::batchFor and FxRender.cpp render queue, which already groups particles independent of effect and instance IDs. #include "engine/fx/SpectraFX.h" aiverse::spectra::BatchWorld shared; shared.init(device, aiverse::fx::FxQuality::High); aiverse::spectra::GraphRuntime smoke, fire; // smokeJson and fireJson may represent different effects/parameters. smoke.initGraph(shared, smokeJson); fire.initGraph(shared, fireJson); // Each GraphRuntime keeps its OWN handles; no CPU renderer per source. smoke.burstAt({0,1,0}); fire.burstAt({2,1,0}); // ONCE PER FRAME (not once per GraphRuntime): shared.setView(camera, viewProjection, width, height); shared.update(dt); // INSIDE the existing scene render pass, ONCE: shared.draw(fog); // Kill smoke's particles without affecting fire: smoke.clear(); // Full scene/match reset: shared.clear(). smoke.shutdown(); fire.shutdown(); shared.shutdown(); // MUST outlive all attached GraphRuntime instances. BatchWorld::defineEffect caches equivalent fully serialized effect definitions while preserving distinct emitter data. defineGraph compiles v1 JSON through the canonical compiler and registers its effect in the same world. play, move, stop, kill and playing are the underlying ParticleSystem handle operations. The caller can set texture/mesh loaders on the shared world before registering effects, retrieve stats(), call collectLights, and use its existing global quality budget. These APIs are independent of FPS, RTS or any particular game module and live outside authoritative ECS/rollback state. Draw batching key: the actual underlying RHI texture/atlas handle, blend mode, compiled shader-graph identity and primitive kind (mesh vs quad). Effects with distinct animations, sizes, instances or spawn parameters can use the same draw call when these render-state requirements match. Even different sprites in the same atlas can batch because their UVs are encoded independently in vertex data. The same texture with different alpha/additive blending or shader graph must NOT batch. A draw is split at the 16-bit-index limit of 16,384 quads. Alpha sorting still follows the current renderer's existing ordering rules; a single cross-texture globally sorted transparent render queue is a different architectural task. GraphRuntime::initGraph(BatchWorld&, ...) and initEffect(BatchWorld&, ...) explicitly opt the instance into this shared renderer. Its burstAt captures handles and clear()/shutdown() kills only those handles, not all the world's particles. The source handle list is bounded at 65,536: the oldest handle is killed before overflowing the bound. In shared mode, per-source step, setView and draw are no-ops to prevent double updates and duplicate draw calls. The host must call the shared world's methods once per frame. RequireGpu is rejected for shared-world registration, not silently downgraded; current pooling is for the mature CPU-simulated/RHI-rendered emitter path. Existing game apps: RTS/FPS clients already use one central ParticleSystem and benefit from its built-in batching. This feature addresses new native/graph instance contexts that formerly created separate renderers. It does not override individual GPU ComputeParticles instances. Shared Metal GPU-particle pools across multiple independent effects still need a dedicated multi-emitter GPU scheduler and actual device QA. Regression source: tests/vfx_shared_batch_world_test.cpp records RHI indexed draw calls and verifies 5 + 7 particles from distinct effect definitions sharing one atlas texture produce one draw. Different blend modes produce two draws. It also checks independent source cleanup, grap

h: Genre-neutral cue scheduling and ECS source bridge (Stage 15)
x: The opt-in spectra::CueScheduler in engine/fx/SpectraCueScheduler.{h,cpp} coordinates many independent event/attached-effect sources over the already existing BatchWorld. It does not create another ParticleSystem or issue update/draw itself; the owning presentation host still calls BatchWorld once per frame. All scheduling and particle handles stay outside gameplay ECS, deterministic hashes and rollback state. Use the canonical include engine/fx/SpectraFX.h for the pure presentation API, or <aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraFX.h> in native ECS projects to also access syncEcsCueSources and acceptSimCueTick. The ECS adapter reuses SpectraSourceComponent (no new ECS component type or ID). The host supplies the same generic render-pose resolver as the existing SpectraPresentationSystem. Source keys use Entity::packed() so recycled indices with new generations cannot reuse an old effect handle. #include <aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraFX.h> // BatchWorld and CueScheduler must outlive each other's handles in this // order: shared BatchWorld initialized first, CueScheduler destroyed first. aiverse::spectra::BatchWorld shared; shared.init(device, aiverse::fx::FxQuality::High); aiverse::spectra::CueBudgets limits; limits.maxQueued = 512; limits.maxPerTick = 64; limits.maxPerFrame = 128; limits.maxAttachments = 1024; limits.maxTrackedOneShots = 2048; aiverse::spectra::CueScheduler cues(shared, limits); cues.registerEffect("impact", impactEffectDef); // or registerGraph(...) cues.registerEffect("engine_fire", loopingEffectDef); cues.bindCue(72, "impact"); // game-defined event type, not an FPS/RTS enum // On the presentation thread, after a committed gameplay tick: aiverse::spectra::acceptSimCueTick(cues, tick, simEvents); // ONCE per presentation frame, with graphics Device in a valid frame: shared.setView(camera, viewProj, width, height); aiverse::spectra::syncEcsCueSources(world, cues, resolvePose); cues.flush(); // deferred one-shots, bounded per frame shared.update(dt); // exactly once for ALL sources // With the scene render pass open: shared.draw(fog); // exactly once, batches compatible materials // Before replaying restored ticks after rollback/new match: cues.resetForRollback(); // kills only this scheduler's cues/sources // Do not call shared.clear() unless resetting ALL other presentation owners. // Destroy cues BEFORE shared.shutdown()/gfx::Device destruction.

CueBudgets bounds outstanding events, per-tick admissions, per-frame one-shot starts, simultaneous ECS attachments and the rollback-tracked one-shot handle ring. Inputs are clamped to safe hard ceilings; tracked one-shot capacity cannot be zero. CueScheduler::acceptTick(tick, events) ignores duplicate or decreasing ticks until resetForRollback(), but does not advance the underlying particle renderer. flush() starts up to the frame budget and leaves the remaining bounded queue for later frames. The queue stores resolved effect IDs at acceptance time to avoid silent behavior changes during an asset hot-reload. When the tracked one-shot handle ring fills, the oldest effect is killed before its slot is reused, so its particles cannot escape rollback ownership. syncAttachments consumes the complete set of active sources for the current frame, moves existing handles, restarts on effect/revision/scale change and retires absent sources before applying the attachment cap to newcomers. Normal detach uses each component's stop-vs-kill policy; rollback always kills the scheduler's own handles and clears its pending queue, allowing older restored committed ticks to play again. Other producers using the same BatchWorld are untouched. CueSchedulerStats reports accepted/duplicate ticks, accepted and emitted cues, queued/attached counts, budget drops, unbound effects, failed spawns, evicted one-shot handles and source restarts. Call registerGraph/ registerEffect once during setup or asset reload, not every tick; bindCue maps generic unsigned event types to registered effect names. For custom colour, scale or direction per event, call acceptTick directly with CueEvent; acceptSimCueTick uses the default up-direction, scale and tint and converts SimEvent fixed-point positions into presentation floats. This scheduler currently uses the mature shared CPU particle backend plus RHI rendering/batching. It is deliberately not a multi-emitter Metal compute scheduler and does not enable gpuIndirect for ordinary graph assets. Custom GPU per-instance scheduling, automatic native RTS/FPS client migration, full rollback visual parity and actual platform performance remain future verification/work items. Tests: tests/vfx_cue_scheduler_test.cpp, target aiverse_vfx_cue_scheduler_tests, CTest vfx_cue_scheduler with label SpectraFX. Scenarios cover two unrelated ECS genres, generation-safe attachment replacement, committed tick dedup, queue/frame/attachment caps, one-shot eviction, rollback cleanup without affecting an unrelated BatchWorld effect, and graph registration diagnostics. Tests are source-committed but not confirmed executed until native CI results are available.

SpectraFX now accepts "version":2 graph assets through the same fx::compileSpectraGraph / spectra::compileGraph API used by the editor, MCP, GraphAssets, GraphRuntime and shared BatchWorld. All existing "version":1 assets retain their original compilation path; the public spectra::kGraphVersion now reports the newest authoring version (2), with kLegacyGraphVersion=1. V2 adds two distinct types of connections: execution links {"from":"spawn","to":"init"} order Spawn→Initialize→Update modules→Output; typed value-port links {"from":"math","to":"init","toPort":"speed"} bind the value of a data node into one property (dotted property paths are supported, e.g. noise.frequency). Equivalent inline references are {"$node":"math"} and {"$param":"wind"}. Data links can connect math nodes to other math nodes, with cycle validation even for disconnected data branches. The new engine/fx/SpectraValueGraph.h implements a bounded constant-expression DAG of literal values, typed exposed parameters, scalar/vector math, comparisons and Select operations. Representative nodes: Float, Integer, Bool, Vec2/Vec3/Vec4, Color, String, Curve, Gradient, Parameter, Add, Subtract, Multiply, Divide, Min/Max, Clamp, Lerp, Sin/Cos, Pow/Sqrt, Floor/Ceil, Normalize/Length, Dot/Cross, ComposeVec2/3/4, Select, Greater/Less/Equal. Invalid types, nonfinite results, division by zero, excessive graph depth, duplicate node IDs and cyclic references are rejected. Parameter overrides must match their declared JSON type. AgeNormalized is meaningful only inside an explicitly sampled {"$curve":"expression_id","samples":33} reference. It compiles a scalar expression over normalized age to 2–64 keys understood by the existing CPU FxRange/curve system. It is not a per-particle script or general programmable GPU kernel. Math expressions without an age dependency are resolved at graph compile time; sampled curves are evaluated during the already-existing particle lifetime LUT update. The new engine/fx/SpectraGraphV2.h compiler lowers module-stage nodes to existing strict Update module properties: NoiseModule, CollisionModule, TrailModule, LightModule, ForceModule, VelocityModule, SubEmitterModule, TriggerModule, InheritVelocityModule, SpeedLimitModule, ColorBySpeedModule, SizeBySpeedModule, SpinBySpeedModule, LifeBySpeedModule. Flat ShapeModule, FlipbookModule, MaterialModule, SortModule, CustomModule reuse the complete existing FxEffect grammar; unsupported emitter keys are still rejected by fx::parseEffect. SubEmitterModule.properties.items contains the sub-emitter array. Existing sprite/mesh/ribbon outputs remain available. The output is an ordinary fx::EffectDef compiled by the same authoritative v1 parser, preserving native C++/genre compatibility and the mature CPU render path. Any effect with modules outside the limited Metal subset continues to use the full CPU fallback. There is no graph-specific dependency on FPS, RTS or other gameplay modules. Example asset: examples/spectrafx/typed_noise_trail_v2.vfx.json. It combines exposed parameters, multiply nodes, explicit value connections, an age-dependent fade sampled into keys, and noise and trail modules. Explicit limits: V2 is a typed authoring/dataflow frontend for existing CPU effect modules, not arbitrary runtime per-particle bytecode or GPU kernel compilation. Full user-defined functions, variable-length particle attribute buffers and per-particle event graph execution remain separate implementation steps. The code is committed, but no CMake build, test run, screenshot or Metal validation has yet been executed in this stage.

h: Visual authoring and safe drafts for graph v2 (Stage 17)
x: The optional SpectraFX ImGui editor now creates graph version 2 by default. Graph version 1 assets can still be opened and edited, and the v1 → v2 button upgrades a draft in memory without immediately overwriting its source file. The shared pure C++ model engine/fx/SpectraAuthoring.h provides spectra::authoring::nodeCatalog, newGraphV2, addNode, connectExec, connectData, disconnect, inputPorts, node, isData, isOutput and reaches. It lives outside the editor and can be reused by native C++ tooling or agents through engine/fx/SpectraFX.h. Node definitions contain categories, default properties and typed input port names. The editor shows a grouped catalog for value, math, vector, logic, simulation, force, event and renderer nodes. Execution links and typed data links use different canvas colours; the right inspector lets the author choose and connect input properties (including nested paths) to a selected value node. Cycle prevention applies to both link kinds. The right inspector offers fast editors for numeric, integer, bool, vector and colour literal nodes, module-specific field controls for noise, collision, force, trails, light, rendering, sorting and shape settings, and keyframe editing for Curve and Gradient value nodes. A curve can add/remove keys and edit time/value; a gradient can edit RGBA keys. Unknown modules, $node expressions and complex nested fields remain accessible through the existing raw JSON inspector, without lossy coercion.

A graph need not compile successfully at every intermediate authoring step. Draft assets live under fx/graphs/_drafts/<name>.vfx.json and are not enumerated or loaded by the production graph registry. The editor has separate Черновик / Опубликовать actions and a draft list. A draft is saved even while links or modules are incomplete; publishing compiles the exact saved draft and refuses to replace a published graph if the compiler returns errors. Existing fx/graphs/<name>.vfx.json and legacy fx/*.json remain unchanged by saving an incomplete draft. Additional MCP actions: fx_graph_node_catalog: node types, categories, default property JSON, data input port names, and a new default graph. fx_graph_edit: pure in-memory new, upgrade, add, connect/disconnect, deleteNode, setProperty operations. Returns edited graph and compiler diagnostics; no file is written. fx_graph_draft_set, fx_graph_draft_get, fx_graph_draft_list, fx_graph_draft_publish: non-destructive authoring, validation and explicit publication. Existing fx_graph_get/set/list/validate/bake continue working for both graph versions; published graphs always undergo strict compilation. The code is committed; GUI launch, CMake build and CTest are intentionally deferred until functional work is finished. Current advanced editing is still a basic ImGui canvas and raw JSON fallback, not a complete commercial Niagara editor; function subgraphs, custom per-particle attribute debugging, profiler timelines and shader node codegen remain further work items.

SpectraFX graph v2 now supports reusable pure value functions. Function bodies are nested typed value graphs, independent of rendering, gameplay genres and ECS state: { "version": 2, "functions": { "scale_speed": { "parameters": { "base": 1, "gain": 1 }, "returns": "number", "nodes": [ { "id": "a", "type": "Parameter", "properties": { "name": "base" } }, { "id": "b", "type": "Parameter", "properties": { "name": "gain" } }, { "id": "out", "type": "Multiply", "properties": { "a": { "$node": "a" }, "b": { "$node": "b" } } } ], "output": "out" } } } A caller graph references the function with a FunctionCall value node: {"id":"scale","type":"FunctionCall","properties":{ "function":"scale_speed", "arguments":{"base":{"$param":"speed"},"gain":1.5} }} Function signatures declare typed default parameters, an output node ID and an optional strict returns type: number, bool, string, vec2, vec3, vec4. Calls inherit the caller's compile-time or normalized-age sampling context, allowing reusable fade/wind/response functions that compile into existing CPU FxRange curves. Function definitions contain only value DAG nodes, never Spawn/Update/Output stages. The graph compiler rejects unknown functions, wrong argument types, recursion (including disconnected definitions), more than 32 declared functions or more than eight nested calls. No native scripts, reflection or arbitrary executable code are evaluated.

engine/fx/SpectraFunctionAssets.h provides validateFunctionLibrary, mergeFunctionLibrary and FunctionLibraryAssets with an injected file reader and last-known-good reload fallback. Library files use fx/functions/<name>.vfxfn.json: {"version":1,"functions":{"my_function":{ "parameters":{"x":1}, "returns":"number", "nodes":[{"id":"result","type":"Parameter", "properties":{"name":"x"}}], "output":"result" }}} Importing a library into a v2 graph explicitly copies its validated function definitions; existing function names with different bodies reject the import unless replace is explicitly requested. Import works with incomplete editor drafts, and the pure graph compiler still performs no filesystem IO. The native API is available from engine/fx/SpectraFX.h. MCP supports fx_function_list, fx_function_get, fx_function_set, fx_function_import, and fx_function_export. An import returns an edited graph in memory; the user explicitly publishes or saves a draft. The SpectraFX editor has a FunctionCall selector, embedded function JSON editor, plus import/export controls for reusable function-library names. Example assets: examples/spectrafx/common_math.vfxfn.json and examples/spectrafx/function_calls_v2.vfx.json. Status: full code committed, testing deliberately deferred. Functions compile pure values and age-sampled curves into the existing CPU emitter definitions; they do not yet define per-particle mutable attribute bytecode or programmable GPU simulation kernels.

The existing fx::ParticleSystem can now execute an optional EmitterDef::particleProgram: a small compiled, bounded expression program running at individual particle lifecycle stages. It does NOT reinterpret JSON for every particle or run any C++/Lua script from the effect file. The compiler validates opcodes, targets, nesting, finite constants and budgets, and converts the JSON into precompiled instructions in engine/fx/SpectraParticleProgram.h. On every particle step, the VM uses a fixed-size stack with no dynamic allocation. No gameplay ECS state is read or written. Use the ParticleProgramModule pipeline node in a v2 graph before an output, or provide particleProgram in an ordinary legacy emitter definition. Supported named program stages are spawn, update, death, collision, trigger. Each stage contains at most 32 assignments/updates and 256 postfix VM instructions. An expression is a finite number, {"var":"field"}, or a tree of built-in arithmetic, clamp, lerp, comparison and trigonometric operations. Recursion depth is bounded by 16. No arbitrary executable source, network, file access or plugin invocation is allowed. { "version":1, "spawn":[ {"target":"attribute0","value":0.75} ], "update":[ {"op":"addRate","target":"velocity.y", "value":{"op":"multiply", "a":2.2, "b":{"op":"subtract","a":1, "b":{"var":"ageNormalized"}}}}, {"op":"set","target":"tint.a", "value":{"op":"saturate","a":{ "op":"subtract","a":1,"b":{"var":"ageNormalized"}}}} ] } Supported scalar reads include age, ageNormalized, dt, uid, world-space position.x/y/z, velocity.x/y/z, size, rotation, tint.r/g/b/a, and eight independent user-defined attribute0..7 floats stored with each visual particle. Read-only lifecycle fields cannot be written by a program. Actions set, add, multiply, addRate (value * dt per second) apply to writable fields. Output values are finite/bounded, tint channels clamp to 0..1 and size clamps to nonnegative. spawn is invoked after built-in particle initialization and before trails/birth handlers; update runs after existing gravity/forces/integration and before collision and trigger testing; event stages run at the corresponding collision, trigger and death boundaries. The legacy velocity/size/light/noise/trail mechanics still run for any effect lacking a program with no new script evaluation. Dynamic attributes can drive size, rotation, tint and motion through subsequent VM statements. Function graphs v2 remain a separate compile-time subgraph feature; arbitrary graph-to-GPU kernel codegen is not implied. Example: examples/spectrafx/runtime_particle_program_v2.vfx.json uses a custom attribute, age-dependent rising force, alpha fade, variable size and a death handler.
