When switchToCpu occurs after device failure, it attempts recovery only when the checkpoint matches the last submitted GPU frame, has the full physical slot count, and there are no unsent births. Imported particles are counted in ComputeStats::recoveredOnFallback; remaining discarded allocations are reported in lostOnFallback. On stale/missing/invalid snapshots the existing CPU fallback still starts clean and reports losses. RequireGpu continues forbidding an implicit CPU switch. Recovery is opt-in by capture timing: checkpoints are not collected automatically because the available synchronous Metal RHI readback blocks until the GPU finishes. Call checkpoint capture only between completed frames at deliberate safe intervals. An unhealthy GPU cannot be relied on to produce new snapshots. Exact CPU/GPU numerical continuation is not proven: renderer and simulation algorithms differ, imported particles have no original source instance, and a formerly live effect may stop emitting. The term lossless is not warranted until parity, all emitter categories and fault injection are verified. No native compiler, CTest, Metal test or GUI smoke was run for this stage; code remains unverified.

h: Stage 30 — opt-in chunked asynchronous Metal checkpoint capture (source committed, not validated)
x: GraphRuntimeOptions::checkpointEveryFrames (or the direct ComputeEmitterDesc::checkpointEveryFrames) controls a disabled-by-default periodic checkpoint request. Every N successful Metal compute submissions the runtime may enqueue a snapshot after Spawn/Integration/Update/Compaction, without waiting for completion. GraphRuntime::requestGpuCheckpoint(callback) and ComputeParticles::requestGpuCheckpoint(callback) allow explicit manual requests. The callback reports bool complete, not a mutable GPU buffer pointer. A failed scheduling attempt returns false and must not yield a usable partial checkpoint. For each physical GPU slot the snapshot includes 64 bytes particle state, 32 bytes per-particle VM inputs and 32 bytes custom registers — maximum 512 KiB at the current 4096 GPU slots. The Metal RHI now implements readBufferRangeAsync(handle,offset,size,callback) for reads of up to 64 KiB each. The checkpoint splits the three buffers into at most eight small requests, assembles them only after all replies have succeeded, and uses a renderer-lifetime token to cancel callbacks after teardown. At most one checkpoint capture per ComputeParticles instance is pending. A partially queued batch is rejected and never published. The GPU frame revision is incremented on successful compute submission, fixing the earlier non-incrementing freshness token. The async result stores its originating revision; switchToCpu may restore it only if it still matches the latest GPU frame and there are no pending unsent particles. A periodic snapshot from an earlier frame can remain for diagnostics but is not eligible for a supposedly lossless restoration. Missing, incomplete or stale snapshots retain the explicit loss-counting CPU fallback. ComputeStats exposes cumulative checkpointRequests, checkpointCompleted and checkpointFailed. An automatic request never blocks render submission with a synchronous read, but enqueues device copies; the callback and CPU assembly still consume resources. The full 512 KiB capture is opt-in and can be costly on mobile. Captures from complex effects are not guaranteed to reproduce an exact CPU trajectory, since GPU/CPU VM and renderer numerical parity has not been demonstrated. NOT RUN: Clang/CMake, CTest, Metal shader compilation, real GPU checkpoint/recovery, fault injection and performance analysis. This API is experimental and not a production-safe guarantee of recovery.

h: Stage 29 — shared GPU-pool committed-tick cue bridge (functional source, tests deferred)
x: spectra::GpuCueBridge adapts bounded one-shot presentation events to the existing spectra::GpuPoolWorld. It does not create its own particle simulator, GPU group, RHI resources, or gameplay ECS components. The pool continues to coalesce compatible graph/material/VM policy into shared ComputeParticles groups and uses the original shared CPU BatchWorld for unsupported effects. #include <aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraFX.h> aiverse::spectra::GpuPoolWorld pool; pool.init(device); pool.defineGraph("impact", graphJson, aiverse::Json::object(), options); aiverse::spectra::GpuCueBridge cues(pool); cues.bind(42, "impact"); // Once AFTER a committed gameplay simulation tick: aiverse::spectra::acceptSimGpuCueTick(cues, tick, simEvents); // Per render frame, after Device::beginFrame and before its scene pass: pool.beginPresentationFrame(camera, viewProjection, width, height); cues.flush(); // queues are bounded; effects route to GPU/CPU via pool pool.step(dt); // Within the open render pass: pool.draw(fog); // After the render pass: pool.endPresentationFrame(); // On a gameplay rollback: outside GPU render/compute passes, // before replaying any restored committed tick: if (!cues.resetForRollback()) { /* handle cues.reason() */ } GpuCueBudgets controls queued, acceptedPerTick, and dispatchedPerFrame, independently of the pool's global maxBurstsPerFrame. accept(tick, span<GpuCueEvent>) refuses duplicate or decreasing ticks. Accepted cues capture the effect's name at admission time so later rebinding of an event type does not change queued events. The bridge tracks admission, drops, successful launches and world-level rejects. Failures during flush are not treated as emitted and are dropped rather than blocking future frames. GpuCueEvent optionally supplies a source generation key, a direction, tint and a snapshot of eight param0..7 values. resetForRollback() calls GpuPoolWorld::resetForRollback() before clearing queued events and its tick cursor. A rejected reset leaves the bridge's state intact so a safe retry is possible. This reset clears the entire pool, not only the bridge's particles: the host must dedicate the pool to the same presentation rollback scope. Native ECS projects use libraries/include/aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraGpuCueEcsAdapter.h and acceptSimGpuCueTick for the existing SimEvent type. The adapter is read-only and makes no FPS/RTS/genre assumptions. Important functional boundary: This bridge handles only one-shot effects. The pool currently does not expose a per-source GPU particle handle that could selectively stop/kill particles or retarget a continuous emitter. Continuous ECS-attached effects remain with the existing shared-CPU CueScheduler until there is a generation-safe per-source GPU lifecycle API. Do not claim selective GPU source deletion, complete persistent ECS binding, or standalone production migration. Verification: tests are explicitly deferred by the user. CMake/CTest, Apple Silicon Metal execution, screenshot/visual parity, native FPS/RTS host integration and performance have NOT RUN. This is committed source, not confirmed release readiness.

h: Stage 32 — pooled checkpoint readback admission and live telemetry
x: GPU checkpoints are optional and visual-only. Stage 32 adds SpectraCheckpointReadbackBudget.h, a graphics-owner-thread limiter that reserves readback bytes and chunk counts per GPU frame and across in-flight requests. A request exceeding either bound returns false; no partial checkpoint is published. Per-emitter ComputeStats reports checkpointBudgetDenied and checkpointBytesReturned in addition to the existing completed/failed/request counters. The byte counter measures valid callback payload received on CPU; it is not a hardware bandwidth profile. The reservation remains held until callbacks complete or their closures are destroyed, including rejected partial enqueues. using namespace aiverse::spectra; auto limiter=std::make_shared<CheckpointReadbackBudget>( CheckpointReadbackLimits{}); GraphRuntimeOptions options; options.checkpointEveryFrames=15; // 0 disables automatic snapshots options.checkpointBudget=limiter; // share across standalone GraphRuntime objects PoolWorldBudgets poolOptions; poolOptions.sharedCheckpointBudget=limiter; GpuPoolWorld pool; pool.init(device,poolOptions); // now every GPU group uses this same limiter // After any presentation frame / callback deliveries: const PoolCheckpointStats info=pool.checkpointStats(); // info.pendingGroups / staleGroups / freshGroups / missingGroups // info.restoreEligibleGroups / budgetDenied / bytesReturned // info.budget.bytesInFlight / chunksInFlight / frameBytesReserved If sharedCheckpointBudget is omitted, GpuPoolWorld creates one limiter for all its own GPU groups using PoolWorldBudgets::checkpointReadback. The default ceiling is 512 KiB and 16 chunks per frame; 1536 KiB and 24 chunks in flight. The Metal RHI supports only 32 total in-flight ranged reads; the 24-chunk ceiling leaves a margin for VM diagnostics but does not guarantee admission when other readback clients are active. Multiple worlds on the same graphics device must pass the same shared limiter to enforce one device-wide budget; independent worlds otherwise enforce only their local bounds. Standalone GraphRuntime keeps its old independent behavior unless GraphRuntimeOptions::checkpointBudget is supplied. Pooled identical effects are grouped by complete serialized effect, GPU policy, and now checkpoint cadence. The pool rotates its per-frame GPU group submission start to prevent one permanently first group from consuming the entire shared checkpoint budget. This changes presentation-only dispatch ordering, not ECS simulation or authoritative gameplay. PoolCheckpointStats is computed on demand without GPU readback and includes successful callback payload counts plus freshness classification from checkpointStatus(). Budget metrics reflect the entire limiter when intentionally shared with other worlds. A fresh checkpoint is merely current at the last submitted GPU simulation revision and is not proof of completed GPU/CPU numerical parity, source continuity, or lossless recovery. No stale snapshot is imported automatically. NOT RUN: C++/Metal builds, CTest, device-loss injection, partial-enqueue fault simulation, multi-pool stress tests, or performance measurements.

h: Stage 33 — adaptive checkpoint scheduling and source-safe pooled VFX
x: Checkpoint readbacks can now adapt their frequency when GPU submission is backed up. The opt-in AdaptiveCheckpointPolicy is defined in engine/fx/SpectraAdaptiveCheckpoint.h and passed through GraphRuntimeOptions to ComputeParticles. Scheduling counts successful GPU simulation submissions, not wall-clock frames or ECS ticks. using namespace aiverse::spectra; GraphRuntimeOptions o; o.checkpointEveryFrames=15; o.adaptiveCheckpoint.enabled=true; o.adaptiveCheckpoint.maxIntervalFrames=240; o.adaptiveCheckpoint.recoverAfterCompletions=3; o.checkpointBudget=sharedBudget; // optional Stage 32 shared limiter // Runtime accepts the options during initGraph / initEffect. // A budget denial, a pending earlier capture, or RHI rejection doubles // the interval up to maxIntervalFrames; fully completed captures restore // it by halves after the configured number of successes. const auto st=runtime.checkpointStatus(); // st.checkpointIntervalFrames; st.nextCheckpointRevision // runtime.gpuStats().checkpointAdaptiveBackoffs / Recoveries The scheduling state is optional and does not block rendering. It cannot make an old snapshot current or guarantee lossless CPU fallback. A capture completion is counted as a successful transfer even if the simulation has advanced and the snapshot is therefore stale. GpuPoolWorld now supports generation-safe presentation source handles. A source owns a name-bound effect revision and a distinct 8-scalar parameter snapshot. It can pause, resume, retire, and emit multiple bursts through the shared pooled GPU/CPU resources: PoolSourceId source=pool.createSource("impact"); pool.setSourceNamedParameter(source,"speed",2.5f); // if "speed" is declared pool.emitSource(source,position); pool.pauseSource(source); // prevents future emission pool.resumeSource(source); pool.emitSource(source,newPosition); pool.retireSource(source); // invalidates this handle Source handles carry worldEpoch, slot and generation. A retired, reused, post-rollback or reinitialized handle cannot legitimately emit. Redefining a named effect invalidates old handles' binding revisions instead of silently changing the graph used for future bursts. maxSources limits active/reusable slots (default 4096, max 65536). This remains genre-agnostic, ECS-read-only presentation state. Important limitation: pauseSource and retireSource prevent future emissions. Already-born GPU particles continue their natural lifetime and cannot yet be selectively killed or migrated to a different source group. Per-particle GPU slot ownership and fence-safe selective kill are a separate feature. A rollback resets the shared pool and invalidates source handles. PoolWorldStats::activeSources counts active handles, including paused ones. The editor SpectraFX Graph Window has an optional Metal GPU checkpoint — live telemetry panel using PoolCheckpointStats. The host may attach a non-owning pool via Editor::setSpectraGpuTelemetry(&pool) and must detach it before the pool is destroyed. The existing Scene VFX preview is CPU-only and does not automatically create a Metal GPU pool; without an attached pool, the window displays an explicit unavailable message. Diagnostics include fresh/stale/missing/pending, readback budget pressure, bytes returned, adaptive backoffs/recoveries, current maximum interval and active source count. These do not imply completed GPU validation. Verification: GitHub source commits only; NOT RUN CMake/Clang, Metal shader compilation, CTest, native editor launch, fault-injection, render preview, user-facing GPU capture validation or performance benchmark.

h: Stage 34 — source-owned particles, continuous emission and Metal editor preview
x: Stage 34 supersedes Stage 33's limitation that pooled GPU particles cannot be selectively killed. The resource group still owns one shared ComputeParticles instance per unique effect/policy: this is not a separate compute emitter for every game object or a genre-specific VFX system. The presentation-only source API now supports an ordered selective kill, a bounded continuous scheduler, and a host-updated render transform: using namespace aiverse::spectra; PoolSourceId flame=pool.createSource("flame"); pool.setSourceTransform(flame,{10,1,20},{0,1,0},{1,0.5f,0.2f,1}); pool.configureContinuous(flame,PoolContinuousEmission{ .burstsPerSecond=12, .metresPerBurst=0.5f, .lifetimeSeconds=0, .maxBurstsPerFrame=8 }); // Once after gfx::Device::beginFrame and before the scene pass: pool.beginPresentationFrame(camera,viewProj,width,height); // Native scene updates the current transform once or more before pool.step(). pool.setSourceTransform(flame,updatedPosition,forward,tint); pool.step(dt); // emits at configured time/distance gates, then simulates // During depth-tested scene pass: pool.draw(fog); // After render pass: pool.endPresentationFrame(); pool.pauseSource(flame); // future emissions only pool.resumeSource(flame); // resumes bounded scheduler pool.stopSource(flame,true); // also selectively kill current particles pool.retireSource(flame); // invalidate handle/release source slot PoolContinuousEmission defines a rate gate in bursts per second, a distance gate in metres per burst, optional elapsed lifetime (0 means no expiration), and an additional per-source max bursts/frame. Both gates contribute births, limited by global PoolWorldBudgets::maxBurstsPerFrame. Excess is dropped, not queued for unbounded catch-up. PoolWorldStats::continuousBursts and continuousSkipped track both. Attached transforms are renderer-fed values; the engine does not insert graphics state into authoritative ECS. A native ECS adapter may call setSourceTransform from an immutable/committed render-pose snapshot. For GPU groups, ComputeParticles::burstAt(...,sourceToken) marks every physical slot with a source ownership token. The token is unique for a pool lifetime and does not alias a newly recycled source handle. killSourceParticles(token) removes source-matching births which were never submitted, and queues the submitted physical slots for GPU invalidation. On the next step, contiguous killed slots are coalesced into dead-state buffer updates before the compute encoder; only after the ordered GPU submission are those physical slots returned to the free list. GPU indirect compaction subsequently omits invalidated particles. This is a scoped kill, not a global buffer clear. The source's CPU path retains bounded FxHandle ownership and calls the existing shared CPU kill on demand. The selectivelyKilled counter is GPU particles marked/cancelled, not a GPU-side observed count. Pending kills make checkpoints ineligible for CPU restore, and a clear invalidates prior checkpoint revision data. Editor GPU preview (opt-in): SpectraFX Graph Window offers Metal GPU alongside the original CPU Предпросмотр. Equivalent MCP operation is fx_graph_preview {graph:..., gpu:true, loop?:true, instanceValues?:{...}}. Graphs are validated with inspectGraphGpuEligibility and a real Metal-compute capability check: RequireGpu refuses unsupported effects instead of silently dropping features or drawing a CPU approximation. The editor queues the compiled effect, creates a one-group GPU pool in the next pre-pass phase, submits compute before r3d_.render, draws in the open scene pass, and releases the preview after the pass. That live pool attaches automatically to the SpectraFX checkpoint telemetry panel. The default CPU preview path remains available and unchanged in output semantics. GPU preview does not yet replicate the CPU preview's advance/freeze feature and only previews the one-shot strict Metal billboard subset. Important correctness boundaries: source kill and transform attach

h: Stage 35 — completed-frame GPU kill fencing and ECS attachments
x: Main integration status: At the start of Stage 35, main=9ee6ff6fbf390bd45363bc92c838f492dfe92eee was already an ancestor of feature/universal-entity-inspector-fps, whose starting HEAD was 4a50d05329840e713d6179a1519fb2f16a8d8604. No merge or rebase was needed or performed. The feature branch was 450 commits ahead of main; main was zero commits ahead of the feature branch. The Metal-only gfx::Device API now optionally exposes updateStorageBufferChecked(handle,data,size,offset) and completedFrameSerial(). Other RHIs default to unsupported. Checked Metal uploads must be encoded in the active frame outside graphics/compute encoders and report whether the ordered copy was accepted. Metal stores the highest successfully completed command-buffer frame serial in a separate lifetime-safe atomic. A device with an unhealthy GPU or no completion support must never be treated as though a fence passed. ComputeParticles::killSourceParticles(token) still cancels unsent births and uploads dead state into only the physical slots owned by the source. Stage 35 now enqueues the kill writes through the error-reporting RHI method and retains submitted physical-slot IDs in a per-frame quarantine. It returns them to the spawn free list only after completedFrameSerial() >= submittedFrame. If a checked upload fails, the pending slots are retained rather than being reused. The GpuCheckpointStatus::killsAwaitingGpuFence, ComputeStats::gpuKillFencesPending/killedSlotsReclaimed, and PoolCheckpointStats::killedSlotsAwaitingFence/killedSlotsReclaimed diagnostics expose the CPU-side state. While any source kills await completion, fresh checkpoints are not eligible for fallback and blocking or async captures are rejected.

<aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraFX.h> now exports the header-only spectra::GpuEcsAttachmentPresenter, implemented in libraries/include/aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraGpuAttachmentEcsAdapter.h. It reads the existing lib::genre::SpectraSourceComponent from const World& using eachExistingConst. Each source is keyed by Entity::packed(), so recycled ECS IDs cannot inherit another entity's VFX handle. The caller supplies the same genre-neutral SpectraPresentationSystem::ResolvePose used by the CPU path. using namespace aiverse::spectra; GpuPoolWorld pool; pool.init(device); pool.defineEffect("engine_flame",compiledEffect,gpuOptions); GpuEcsAttachmentPresenter ecsFx(pool); PoolContinuousEmission rate{}; rate.burstsPerSecond=15; rate.maxBurstsPerFrame=6; ecsFx.bindEffect("engine_flame",rate); // Once per presentation frame, after Device::beginFrame: pool.beginPresentationFrame(cam,viewProj,width,height); // Only the committed (or immutable copied) authoritative ECS snapshot // is read; renderer pose resolver may interpolate visual positions. if(!ecsFx.syncCommitted(committedTick,world,resolveRenderPose)) { // Handle ecsFx.reason(); never pretend that emission succeeded. } pool.step(dt); // GPU/CPU group simulation once BEFORE render pass. // pool.draw(fog) once INSIDE open render pass. // pool.endPresentationFrame() after render pass. // When a rollback is observed: at a safe point outside active encoders, // before replaying committed ticks or new presentation frames: bool cleared=ecsFx.resetForRollback(); syncCommitted(tick,...) is idempotent for source creation at a repeated tick but can update a render pose multiple times; decreasing ticks are rejected until explicit resetForRollback(). Missing/disabled components are retired; if killOnDetach is set, their existing particles are killed selectively. A temporarily unresolved pose pauses new births and resumes without recreating the handle when valid again. Effect/revision/policy changes detach obsolete sources and create new ones. Policies are explicitly registered with bindEffect; there are no genre-default rules. The adapter exposes detachAll(killLiving) for explicit teardown. No silent scale mismatch: The original SpectraSourceComponent::scale has semantics the current GPU pooled billboard subset cannot fully preserve. This bridge currently requires unit scale and reports an error for any non-unit value. It never mutates ECS components, inserts PoolSourceId into a simulation component, writes gameplay state or uses GPU particles for authoritative collisions. A dedicated pool per rollback scope is required because GpuPoolWorld::resetForRollback() resets all its effects.

The SpectraFX editor window now has Pause GPU/Play GPU, Freeze GPU, Loop GPU and Stop GPU for an explicitly opted-in Metal preview. Pause stops future births while existing particles continue to age; Freeze advances at zero visual delta and does not advance existing particles. Loop repeatedly bursts the same strict Metal-compatible graph. Preview and frame ordering are still presentation-only, and the default CPU preview is not replaced. The live panel now also reports physical slots waiting for GPU completion and those safely reclaimed. Verification: GitHub source writes and branch ancestry inspection only. NOT RUN: local CMake/Clang build, Objective-C++/Metal shader compilation, CTest, full editor launch, GPU screenshots, real frame completion tests, device loss/fault injection, CPU-vs-Metal parity, continuous attachment stress, or visual performance benchmarks. Do not treat source completion as production readiness.

h: Stage 36 — bounded GPU scatter kill and native ECS example
x: Stage 36 completes a source-level optimization, not a new authoritative simulation mode. On supported Metal compute devices, selective GPU source deletion no longer sends a separate full 64-byte dead-particle buffer upload per contiguous range. The ComputeParticles runtime now uploads a compact list of physical kill-slot indices (at most capacity*4 bytes; 16 KiB for capacity into an explicit storage buffer. Shader mode 6 invalidates only those physical indices before the existing Spawn/Integrate/ Compaction passes within the same ordered compute encoder. The MSL implementation is active only on the strict Metal subset; the matching GLSL case is future-backend reference code. On failure of the checked upload, the pending kill slots remain quarantined; the compute pass is not submitted and the physical slots are not recycled. On successful compute submission, their recorded graphics-frame serial is retained. Stage 35's completedFrameSerial() fence check continues to control subsequent recycling. Other source particles remain untouched. This is asymptotically one 4-byte/slot index transfer and one compute dispatch rather than up to capacity separate dead-state blits. No hardware performance numbers or shader compilation have been verified. Telemetry exposes gpuKillScatterDispatches / gpuKillIndexBytes, aggregated through PoolCheckpointStats and the editor.

A new reusable native-project reference header lives at examples/spectrafx/native_ecs_attachments.h with instructions in examples/spectrafx/native_ecs_attachments.md. It demonstrates GpuEcsAttachmentPresenter, the existing SpectraSourceComponent and Entity::packed() generation identity, read-only fixed-point render-pose resolution, frame pass ordering, source retirement, and whole-pool visual reset after a gameplay rollback. This is a host integration example, not a standalone executable or confirmation that a project has been built on a GPU. The host still owns gfx Device, its scene pass, its own game tick and committed World snapshots.

The experimental Metal GPU preview toolbar now offers Step GPU (while Freeze is on, advances only one visual update of 1/60 seconds and does not emit a new burst) and GPU speed clamped to 0.1x..2.0x. The existing CPU preview is unaffected; these parameters never change gameplay time or deterministic ECS state. The diagnostic panel exposes the GPU scatter-kill index bytes and dispatches. This preview still only supports the strict, one-shot Metal billboard subset, not the CPU path's advanced Niagara-style modules. Stage 36 verification: GitHub connector source updates and file reads only. Native C++ compilation, Objective-C++/Metal shader compilation, CTest, editor rendering and Metal hardware verification, source-generation rollback and performance tests have NOT RUN. The source remains unverified for production.

h: Stage 37 — staged ECS source admission, checked rollback reset and forward GPU timeline

x: GpuEcsAttachmentPresenter::syncCommitted(tick,world,resolve) now uses staged source creation. It validates every requested effect policy, unit-scale limitation, and finite resolved pose before modifying existing attachments. It creates/configures replacement PoolSourceId handles in a temporary map and uses GpuPoolWorld::canStopSource(handle,killLiving) as a read-only detach preflight. Any allocation/configuration/preflight failure frees the temporary sources and leaves the existing tracked effects alone. If the old source is still alive but its named effect definition was replaced in the GPU pool, sourceBindingCurrent detects the stale binding even when that source is paused. The presenter prepares a fresh source instead of trying to emit with the wrong definition. For a replacement, the pool needs enough free maxSources headroom to hold both the old source and the staged replacement temporarily. When it cannot, sync fails without silently removing existing sources; the native host can increase PoolWorldBudgets::maxSources or explicitly retire some effects at a safe presentation boundary. The commit phase that retires obsolete GPU sources cannot be made fully transactional against a hardware failure during a later selective-kill operation: a partial detach may still happen. The adapter preserves remaining tracked handles and explicitly returns false so the host can retry. This is not a promise of atomic hardware-level state transitions.

ComputeStats now separately records gpuDeviceUnhealthy, gpuKillUploadFailures, gpuComputeBeginFailures, gpuPassOrderRejections, and gpuResetFailures. PoolCheckpointStats aggregates these counts and reports whether Metal device health is genuinely known (gpuDeviceHealthKnown) and if it is healthy (gpuDeviceHealthy). Unsupported backends show an unknown rather than an invented healthy status. The editor SpectraFX telemetry view surfaces all these statuses and source-kill fence counters. A GpuPoolWorld group that failed its step no longer draws stale vertices from a previous frame; standalone ComputeParticles also invalidates its submission flags on important early GPU step errors.

ComputeParticles::tryClear() is a new explicit success/failure API, while clear() remains a compatibility wrapper. Metal reset requires an active gfx Device frame outside render/compute encoders, not just a completed previous frame. It uses updateStorageBufferChecked for particle state, VM parameter, and custom attribute reset writes. It does not commit the CPU free-slot/age mirror until all three ordered transfers have been accepted. On a partial failure gpuResetDirty_ blocks future GPU births, simulation and checkpoint capture until a successful reset is retried; it never reports stale state as an exact recovery. These checked uploads still confirm command encoding, not successful hardware completion. Later GPU failure must be handled using device health and completed frame telemetry. GpuPoolWorld::resetForRollback() calls tryClear() for all GPU groups before clearing the shared CPU effect world or releasing ECS presentation sources. If a group fails, it returns false and preserves CPU/source tracking for a retry. An earlier GPU group may already have cleared successfully; the operation is therefore best-effort across multiple GPU groups, not an atomic multi-group transaction. Source clients must not replay presentation ticks until the reset succeeds. // At a rollback boundary: finish the old scene/graphics frame first. device.beginFrame(width,height); // active RHI command buffer required bool resetOk=attachmentPresenter.resetForRollback(); device.endFrame(); if(!resetOk) { // Do not claim visual reset. Retry at a subsequent safe frame. } The Stage 36 native integration example has been updated to show this required frame ordering.

The editor's opt-in Metal GPU graph preview now displays Visual simulation time (accumulated only from successful presentation steps). While Frozen, the user can request forward advancement in 1/60-second increments; at most 300 frames may remain queued at once and one frame is consumed for each rendered preview frame. The Restart GPU control schedules a checked whole-pool visual reset at the next safe pre-pass phase. No reverse seek or restoration of historical GPU frames is claimed. The preview loop cadence now follows simulated visual time instead of editor wall time, so GPU preview speed/freeze settings do not silently change the repeat rate. Advanced frames while frozen only evolve existing particles and do not create new bursts. A failed GPU step does not increase the displayed time; the panel reports the last preview error. Actual verification: GitHub source writes and source/ancestry inspection only. NOT RUN: local CMake/Clang compilation, Objective-C++ or MSL compilation, CTest, Metal hardware tests, editor UI launch/screenshots, GPU reset fault injection, multi-group atomicity stress, source staging under capacity pressure, or CPU/GPU parity. Implementation is unverified executable source; do not enable it by default for production.

h: Stage 38 — retryable GPU-group reset, Device recovery and interpolated ECS presentation
Explicit recovery state for pooled Metal VFX
x: A SpectraFX GpuPoolWorld now has a read-only PoolResetReport resetReport() and presentationBlocked() gate. A rollback attempt remembers a per-GPU-group accepted-reset mask, rather than resetting already prepared groups repeatedly. If group number N rejects its checked reset uploads, resetForRollback() returns false, records groupsAccepted, groupCount and failedGroup, and blocks new source creation, bursts, GPU frame submission and drawing. A later safe presentation-frame retry skips groups whose uploads have already been accepted. The CPU effect world and renderer-source handles are not invalidated until ALL GPU groups accept their ordered reset commands. This is restartable preparation, not a hardware-atomic reset. groupsAccepted means the RHI encoded the reset uploads; the GPU may not have finished. If a subsequent Metal command buffer fails, the host must handle device health/loss and reinitialize the graphics stack. A lost Device latches resetReport().deviceLost; the pool does not falsely resume merely because a health flag later becomes true. A new CPU-only definition catalog, PoolRecoveryManifest, allows a native host to reconstruct effects on a new, healthy graphics Device. It preserves effect names, compiled original EffectDef, graph options, declared runtime-parameter schema and effective default values. It does NOT contain renderer source IDs, graphics handles, particle buffers, emitter timing or GPU checkpoints. using namespace aiverse::spectra; PoolRecoveryManifest snapshot=oldPool.exportRecoveryManifest(); // Keep OLD graphics Device alive until oldPool.shutdown() finishes. oldPool.shutdown(); GpuPoolWorld recovered; bool ok=recovered.importRecoveryManifest(&newHealthyDevice,snapshot); // Recreate the ECS attachment presenter against recovered and re-sync // the latest committed ECS World only if ok == true. Import fails without publishing a usable partial pool if a RequireGpu effect is unsupported on the new backend. The old readback limiter is not reused across the Device boundary: a new checkpoint budget is created. GPU particles are deliberately lost; the goal is safe re-creation of effect definitions and native presentation attachments.

The public native header <aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraFX.h> exports GpuEcsPoseInterpolator from libraries/include/aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraEcsRenderPose.h. The native host supplies the same ResolvePose callback used by GpuEcsAttachmentPresenter. The interpolator stores at most two renderer-side pose snapshots, captured once per committed ECS tick through const World iteration, and samples them with alpha in the range 0..1. GpuEcsPoseInterpolator poses; poses.captureCommitted(committedTick,world,resolvePose); pool.beginPresentationFrame(camera,viewProj,width,height); presenter.syncCommitted(committedTick,world,poses.resolver(renderAlpha)); pool.step(dt); // draw scene + VFX, then end presentation frame // On rollback: presenter.resetForRollback() at safe frame; // only when it succeeds: poses.resetForRollback(); Only consecutive committed ticks and identical Entity::packed() identities interpolate. New/recycled entities snap to their current pose, avoiding history leaks across ECS generations. Nonfinite poses, excessive source counts or decreasing ticks are rejected without replacing a valid pose history. If a pose is unavailable, the attachment presenter pauses new emission; the interpolator never writes float positions into authoritative ECS. The updated examples/spectrafx/native_ecs_attachments.h shows this integration and explicitly rebuilding after device loss.

h: Read-only diagnostic history in Metal GPU preview
x: The optional editor Metal GPU preview records the last 180 rendered preview attempts as a CPU-side timeline with deviceFrame, successfully accumulated visual time, estimated GPU particle count, checkpoint fresh/stale/pending counts, source kills awaiting a completion fence, GPU health and whether the simulation step was accepted. The SpectraFX editor shows a small history plot and can copy these records as JSON through spectraGpuPreviewHistoryJson(). The history is intentionally not a restorable GPU snapshot: no particle positions, VM registers or arbitrary framebuffer content are saved. Reverse seeking is still unsupported; the Stage 37 forward-only step/restart model remains intact. Device recovery/partial rollback status appears in the same editor diagnostics without asserting that accepted GPU commands have already completed. Verification: GitHub source writes, tree/branch readback and manual API/source inspection only. NOT RUN: local CMake or Clang compilation, Objective-C++/MSL shader compile, CTest, editor startup, actual Metal device-loss recovery, multi-group partial rollback fault injection, ECS pose interpolation tests, image parity or GPU performance benchmarks. Do not enable these experimental features by default in production based only on source code presence.

h: Stage 39 — recovery host events, bounded fresh GPU exports and fair VFX pressure
Native GPU recovery notifications and explicit Device replacement
x: The genre-neutral native presentation header <aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraFX.h> now exports GpuPoolRecoveryHost from libraries/include/aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraGpuRecoveryHost.h. This object holds references only to an initialized GpuPoolWorld, the presentation-owned GpuEcsAttachmentPresenter and optionally a render-pose interpolator. It does not take ownership of the platform's gfx::Device or perform background work. GpuPoolRecoveryHost recovery(pool,ecsPresenter,&poseHistory); recovery.onChange([](const PoolRecoveryEvent& e) { // e.phase/e.next: Ready, retry rollback in an active gfx frame, // recreate Device, inspect unknown failure or initialize the pool. // e.resetGroupsAccepted, e.resetGroupsTotal, e.resetAttempts, e.reason }); auto status=recovery.poll(); if(status.next==PoolRecoveryAction::RetryResetInGraphicsFrame) { // Only after Device::beginFrame, BEFORE any active encoder: if(!recovery.retryPresentationReset()) { /* do not render VFX */ } } if(status.next==PoolRecoveryAction::RecreateGraphicsDevice) { // Host/platform explicitly creates a healthy replacement Device. // OLD Device remains alive through old-pool shutdown. bool restored=recovery.replaceDevice(newHealthyDevice); // Compiled effect definitions survive; live GPU particles do not. } poll() reports only phase/progress/health transitions to its callback, and never invents successful recovery. The host must perform actual platform device reconstruction. replaceDevice() exports the CPU-only recovery manifest, releases old graphics resources, invalidates presentation-owned source handles and interpolated pose history, then imports effect definitions into a freshly initialized pool. No GPU-resident particle buffers, authoritative ECS data, network state or previous renderer source generations are resurrected. The standalone native integration example at examples/spectrafx/native_ecs_attachments.h now uses this controller for rollback and new-Device recreation.

h: Strict and bounded GPU checkpoint binary diagnostics
x: engine/fx/SpectraCheckpointExport.h defines a 40-byte GpuCheckpointExportHeader with magic SPFX, format version, slot count, captured GPU revision, graphics frame serial and raw payload length. The capture body consists of the existing 128-byte per-slot GpuCheckpointParticle state plus a 4-byte-per-slot CPU lifetime mirror. At the existing 4096 physical-slot limit the maximum is 512 KiB GPU state + 16 KiB mirror + 40-byte header. The encoding is a native ABI diagnostic blob, not a portable savegame, stable cross-version serialization, screenshot, or restorable GPU timeline. ComputeParticles::exportFreshCheckpoint(bytes,maxBytes) and GpuPoolWorld::exportFreshCheckpoint(groupIndex,bytes,maxBytes) only copy existing completed GPU checkpoint data when all of these are true: Metal GPU is active and healthy, the retained checkpoint's captured revision is exactly the current GPU revision, the snapshot is complete and the correct slot count, there are no unsent particle births or kill slots awaiting a GPU fence, no incomplete GPU reset, and no concurrent pending checkpoint read. The encoded buffer is swapped into the output only after all preflight/size validations; failure leaves the caller's old output intact. These methods never initiate GPU readback. PoolCheckpointStats::exportReadyGroups counts groups that currently satisfy these conditions. The SpectraFX editor now shows the count and offers Save fresh GPU checkpoint only when a group is eligible. It saves one bounded .spfx file under platform::userDataDir()/spectrafx-diagnostics/ using a temporary file and then renaming it. If an async readback is stale at UI time, the button is disabled or a clear error is returned; there is no fake snapshot or blocking synchronous readback. This feature requires the host to have opted into actual checkpoint cadence or to have completed a manual checkpoint; by default, no checkpoints are automatically captured.

PoolLoadSheddingPolicy is available inside PoolWorldBudgets::loadShedding and via GpuPoolWorld::setLoadShedding(policy) between presentation frames: PoolLoadSheddingPolicy policy{}; policy.enabled=true; policy.maxContinuousBurstsPerFrame=64; policy.reserveManualBursts=16; policy.estimatedParticleSoftLimit=8000; // previous frame's estimate policy.maxReadbackBytesInFlight=1024u*1024u; pool.setLoadShedding(policy); The scheduler rotates its starting source slot every frame, so a consistently busy low-index emitter cannot permanently starve higher-index emitters. The enabled policy caps automatic births while preserving the existing global limit and an explicit allocation of capacity for manual one-shot bursts. Particle pressure is based on the previous rendered step's estimated CPU + GPU particle count; readback pressure uses the existing Stage 32 scheduler's reserved bytes in flight. This is not a GPU performance measurement or hard memory-residency guarantee. Excess automatic bursts are discarded, not queued into an unbounded catch-up backlog. Disabling the policy preserves the old overall emission behavior (other than fair rotation). PoolWorldStats reports continuousFrameBudget, pressureActive, pressureSkipped and sourceCapacity; the editor renders these values when a GPU pool is attached. Stage 39 verification: GitHub source commits and source API inspection only. NOT RUN: native C++/ObjC++/MSL compilation, CTest, editor launch, on-device Metal simulation, complete/fresh checkpoint export at various revisions, GPU reset/device loss fault injection, pressure/starvation validation or performance benchmarks. The implementation is not production-verified.

h: Stage 40 — frozen-revision GPU snapshots, checked input staging and VFX hysteresis
GPU Freeze retains the particle revision without freezing the camera
x: Stage 39 async checkpoint captures were often obsolete by the time Metal delivered the readback callback because ComputeParticles::step(0) still dispatched the Update VM, even though the emitter was frozen. Stage 40 adds gpu_pipeline::plan(...,bool integrate=true). When dt==0 and there are no pending births, source kills or live VM parameter edits, a GPU step skips Update VM mode 1, but still executes camera-facing vertex gather/atomic compaction and indirect-argument publication. The particle state revision is not incremented during this graphics-only redraw. An existing complete checkpoint can therefore remain fresh across several frozen rendered frames, even while the editor camera moves. The new GpuPoolWorld::requestGpuCheckpoint(groupIndex,callback) forwards a bounded asynchronous capture to a valid GPU group. It never performs a blocking GPU read. The editor's Freeze & capture GPU state button sets Freeze, cancels queued visual-time steps, then requests the GPU capture at the next safe pre-render phase. It tracks Queued / InFlight / Ready / Failed; a pending or stale capture does not enable binary export. Only once a complete snapshot of the currently retained particle revision arrives can the editor save the checkpoint diagnostic. If an earlier scheduled capture is already in flight, the editor waits for it rather than enqueueing an overlapping GPU readback.

h: Checked Metal input staging with safe retry
x: The Metal compute emitter now uses gfx::Device::updateStorageBufferChecked() for its per-frame VM diagnostic reset, per-slot VM parameters, spawn states, spawn-slot IDs, spawn VM parameters and CPU-authored live-slot gather map. A rejected checked upload or compute-encoder submission retains pending births and slot ownership, sets gpuStagingDirty_, invalidates previously captured checkpoint data/revision and suppresses stale GPU drawing. The next accepted ComputeParticles::step retries the complete set of input transfers; only after a successful compute submission are dirty upload flags and CPU birth queues consumed. This is an intentionally conservative strategy against partially accepted Metal blits. Any already accepted graphics commands remain ordered in the device's command buffer; it is not an atomic rollback of earlier GPU DMA operations, and hardware completion still requires the RHI's Metal command-buffer health/fence contract. GpuCheckpointStatus::stagingRecoveryPending, ComputeStats::gpuStagingUploadFailures and PoolCheckpointStats::stagingRecoveryGroups / gpuStagingUploadFailures expose the state in the editor. No gameplay ECS data is affected.

h: Diagnostic checkpoint format V2 (supersedes Stage 39 V1)
x: engine/fx/SpectraCheckpointExport.h now writes an explicit 48-byte V2 header containing a CRC32 over the payload. The bounded raw-body size remains 512 KiB of GPU particle/VM state plus 16 KiB of CPU lifespan mirrors at 4096 slots. The validateGpuCheckpointDiagnostic() function checks header magic, version, exact byte count, slot count and CRC32 without touching graphics hardware. The editor uses this validator before writing a .spfx file. The earlier 40-byte V1 export is historical and superseded by V2; validateGpuCheckpointDiagnostic intentionally validates only the current V2 format. Neither V1 nor V2 is a portable savegame, stable across arbitrary compiler ABIs, replayable GPU history or authoritative ECS serialization. The binary can be inspected for integrity but does not provide a GPU state import.

The native GpuPoolRecoveryHost retains its CPU-only PoolRecoveryManifest if importing effects on a newly created graphics Device fails. The host can supply a different healthy replacement Device and retry without requiring the original GPU pool to remain alive. Failed imports remain visibly in DeviceRecreationRequired state; live GPU particles and renderer-owned source handles are never resurrected. The optional PoolLoadSheddingPolicy::recoverBelowPercent (default 85, range 1..100) introduces hysteresis for estimated particle-count pressure and Stage 32 readback bytes-in-flight pressure. Once automatic bursts are throttled, they stay throttled until the corresponding estimate reaches the lower recovery threshold. This avoids frame-to-frame on/off oscillation near a soft limit. Updating the policy between frames clears both hysteresis latches. Metrics include particlePressureLatched, readbackPressureLatched and pressureHeldFrames. The policy still does not apply to manual one-shot VFX, never queues skipped bursts, and is disabled by default. Actual Stage 40 verification: GitHub source edits, source re-fetch and manual callsite/contract inspection only. NOT RUN: native C++/Objective-C++ compilation, Metal shader compilation, CTest, editor startup/screenshots, checkpoint CRC corruption/fault tests, real GPU readback, device-loss recovery and load-pressure benchmarks. New features are source-implemented but not production-verified.

h: Stage 41 — offline V2 checkpoint inspection and safe native capture requests
V2 checkpoint inspector: no graphics Device required
x: The new pure header engine/fx/SpectraCheckpointInspector.h provides inspectGpuCheckpointDiagnostic(bytes) and gpuDiagnosticErrorString(error). It validates one bounded same-build .spfx V2 diagnostic capture without accessing any Metal resources, rendering code, ECS state, or GPU readback API. The inspector distinguishes invalid magic, unsupported V1/other versions, truncated headers/payloads, invalid header/physical slot counts, mismatched declared sizes, unexpected trailing bytes and CRC32 mismatch. Only after the complete bounded structure and checksum pass does it read individual 128-byte particle records and 4-byte CPU lifespan mirrors. A structurally valid file can still carry semantic warnings: NaN/nonfinite particle values, invalid ages, inconsistent CPU remaining-life mirrors or unusual lifetimes. It reports estimated live/dead physical slots and bounding coordinates for finite live positions. A structural success does NOT certify numerical CPU/Metal parity or a correct gameplay state. The reusable offline CLI tools/spectrafx/inspect_spfx.cpp requires only a native C++20 compiler and the repository headers: c++ -std=c++20 -O2 -I. tools/spectrafx/inspect_spfx.cpp -o inspect_spfx ./inspect_spfx path/to/checkpoint.spfx ./inspect_spfx --json path/to/checkpoint.spfx The CLI checks disk file size before allocating and reading, caps memory at kGpuCheckpointExportMaxBytes (540,720 bytes at the current 4096-slot maximum), detects files that change while being read and emits plain or JSON diagnostics. It returns exit 0 for a structurally valid V2 file (even if it contains semantic warnings), exit 1 for invalid V2 format/integrity, and exit 2 for invalid invocation or I/O. Full usage and the same-build limitations are documented in tools/spectrafx/README.md. The V2 checksum covers the checkpoint payload. The header and packet layout still depend on the native build's ABI and endianness; V1 conversion, arbitrary-version migrations, serialization portability, GPU buffer import and reverse GPU rewind are intentionally unsupported. Diagnostics may include world positions and graph parameters and should be treated as project data.

h: Native owner-thread capture and callback lifetime
x: A new public <aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraFX.h> integration spectra::GpuPoolCaptureHost (implemented in libraries/include/aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraGpuCaptureHost.h) provides a bounded one-at-a-time request API: GpuPoolCaptureHost captures(pool); // Between frames: one requested GPU group with an explicit byte cap. captures.request(0); // Each frame, AFTER Device.beginFrame delivers earlier readbacks and // BEFORE any new pool.step(dt) can invalidate the captured revision: auto status=captures.pollBeforeStep(); // Between pool.step(0) and the scene render pass, on the same owner thread: if(captures.status().phase==GpuCapturePhase::Queued) captures.submitAfterStepBeforePass(); // Once Ready, bytes are already copied and validated (no new GPU read). std::vector<uint8_t> bytes; if(captures.takeReady(bytes)) { /* offline diagnosis only */ } // Always cancel before pool rollback, shutdown or graphics-Device recreation. captures.cancel(); The controller maintains an exact GpuPoolWorld::lifecycleEpoch() and request ID, discards results from a recycled/recreated pool, retains at most one bounded byte vector, and permits up to 600 owner-thread graphics-frame polls before returning a timeout. Asynchronous RHI callbacks hold only weak references to the request's shared completion state; they do not capture a dangling host object or force a second graphics owner. Cancellation invalidates publication but cannot forcibly cancel already submitted Metal work; Stage 32 shared checkpoint budget and RHI callback settlement still apply. The status distinguishes Idle, Queued, InFlight, Ready and Failed, with a concrete error when a complete GPU readback has become stale before export. The sample examples/spectrafx/native_ecs_attachments.h now embeds the capture controller into the single native render-frame lifecycle. It freezes VFX progression and defers read-only ECS source/pose synchronization while the capture is Queued/InFlight/Ready. Each frame continues drawing the current particles via pool.step(0); the host takes or cancels the result before normal presentation resumes. On rollback or device loss, the capture is cancelled before the Stage 38/39 recovery workflow, with no lost/old GPU particle state published as authoritative ECS data. Recovering a valid GPU state still requires the host's existing explicit new-Device reconstruction; captured V2 bytes are not imported.

GpuPoolWorld::boundToDevice(device) allows the recovery controller to explicitly reject an attempted graphics Device replacement that supplies the SAME old Device object even if it temporarily reports healthy. A true recovery requires a different healthy gfx::Device, disposal of old GPU resources while the old Device still exists, import of the CPU-only effect manifest and fresh generation-safe ECS source reattachment. No callback, offline parser or checkpoint diagnostic may bypass this protocol. Verification performed: source inspection, SHA-guarded GitHub source writes and file existence/readback only. NOT RUN: native C++/ObjC++/MSL builds, CTest, execution of the offline inspector CLI, actual corrupted-payload parsing, Metal readback completion/cancellation, editor launch, host recovery/fence tests, CPU/GPU parity or performance measurements. Stage 41 is source-implemented, not production-verified.

h: Stage 42 — privacy-redacted diagnostics, per-group capture and explicit recovery requests

x: Stage 41's read-only inspector exposed world bounds and GPU frame identifiers in its JSON/console output. Stage 42 introduces engine/fx/SpectraDiagnosticReport.h and GpuDiagnosticReportPrivacy. The new gpuDiagnosticReportJson(inspection,privacy) returns a fixed aggregate-only schema, without original file paths, per-particle positions, VM scalar values or raw GPU binary data. By default it also redacts scene-coordinate bounds, GPU serial/revision and CRC-based content fingerprints. Each sensitive category requires its own intentional opt-in: auto inspected=inspectGpuCheckpointDiagnostic(checkpointBytes); GpuDiagnosticReportPrivacy privacy{}; // all sensitive categories OFF std::string redacted=gpuDiagnosticReportJson(inspected,privacy); // Only when a developer specifically requires bounds: privacy.includeWorldBounds=true; // Similarly, frame serial/revision/CRC fingerprints are opt-in: privacy.includeGpuIdentifiers=true; tools/spectrafx/inspect_spfx.cpp now defaults to redacted text and --json. The explicit --report <safe.json> argument creates one local JSON report, never auto-uploads or automatically includes the raw checkpoint. The optional --include-coordinates and --include-identifiers CLI flags enable only their respective aggregate fields. No CLI option ever prints the original per-particle VM parameter arrays. The editor adds Save safe JSON report and an intentionally separate Save RAW GPU checkpoint (sensitive). A safe report contains aggregate inspection counters and at most 180 privacy-filtered GPU preview samples (sample ordinal, estimated particles, step result, fresh/stale/pending counts and pending kill count). It excludes exact RHI frame serials, authored graph names, filenames and per-particle positions and VM inputs. Checkboxes permit optional world-coordinate BOUNDS and GPU identifiers, but never raw state inside a safe report. Saving is a direct, local user action under platform::userDataDir()/spectrafx-diagnostics; the system does NOT upload diagnostics or create recurring jobs.

h: Group selection across a pooled GPU world
x: GpuPoolWorld::gpuGroupCount() and gpuGroupSummary(index,out) expose a read-only PoolGpuGroupSummary: active state, estimated particle count, GPU buffer bytes, pending/fresh checkpoint revision status, most recent step/reset acceptance and whether a complete, current checkpoint can be exported. These APIs do not expose serialized effect graph keys or the source effect code. An invalid group index leaves the output unmodified. The editor displays a bounded index selector for up to the existing 64 GPU-group maximum and scopes both binary saveFreshSpectraGpuCheckpoint(out,index) and saveSafeSpectraGpuReport(out,index,...) to the chosen group. The old one-argument binary-save API still auto-selects the first eligible group for compatibility. Only the editor-owned Metal preview group 0 can be captured directly by the editor; a separately attached external renderer pool remains non-owning telemetry and must run its own GPU capture between safe RHI passes. It is never driven out of render order by a diagnostics UI. The native GpuPoolCaptureHost::requestNext(policy) selects one currently active group via GpuCaptureTargetPolicy::{RoundRobin,LargestEstimatedGroup, MissingOrStalestCheckpoint}. RoundRobin rotates starting group; the other modes use the previous CPU-estimated active count or the checkpoint's missing/stale revision. Groups already reading back are skipped. Exactly one capture remains queued/in flight per native host and the shared Stage 32 bytes/chunk budget is still authoritative. Requests are owner thread operations, with no background polling, extra GPU contexts or direct synchronous buffer reads.

h: Native reset and graphics recreation events
x: GpuPoolRecoveryHost::requestPresentationReset(purpose) now explicitly schedules a visual reset without submitting GPU commands. On the next safe graphics frame, outside active encoders, the host calls retryPresentationReset(). PoolRecoveryPhase::ResetRequested is distinct from ResetRetryRequired (a failed/incomplete GPU-group reset) and DeviceRecreationRequired (lost GPU or failed new-device import). PoolRecoveryEvent now includes a stable monotonic transitionSequence that changes only when an observable phase, progress, health or error detail changes. It also reports host reset-request and Device-replacement attempt counters, whether a reset was explicitly queued, and whether a CPU-only recovery manifest is being retained for retry. No event handler recreates a Device itself. A real platform host must construct a distinct healthy gfx::Device and keep the old Device alive until old pooled GPU resources have been released. The updated examples/spectrafx/native_ecs_attachments.h exposes both explicit per-group and automatic policy-based capture, safe summary retrieval, and a queued reset/status workflow. VFX capture bytes and GPU physical-slot identifiers remain outside authoritative ECS, and lost GPU particles are never falsely reconstructed. Verification: Stage 42 source changes and GitHub content readback only. NOT RUN: CMake/C++/ObjC++/MSL compilation, CTest, offline redacted-report CLI, actual editor report export, Metal multi-group capture, fault-injected device reset, UI screenshots, CPU/GPU parity or performance benchmarks. These are experimental source APIs pending executable validation.

h: Stage 43 — explicit local safe ZIP bundles, native capture mailbox and bounded GPU recovery retries
Safe local ZIP support package (no raw GPU state)
x: A new header engine/fx/SpectraDiagnosticBundle.h provides makeSafeGpuDiagnosticZip(inspection,frames,output). This creates one bounded, deterministic ZIP STORE archive containing only three fixed filename entries: manifest.json checkpoint_summary.json preview_timeline.json No zlib or other compression library is required: each ZIP member contains strictly generated JSON and a CRC32. Only a structurally valid V2 inspection and up to 180 renderer-side aggregate GpuSafeTimelineFrame values are accepted. The total ZIP size is capped at 128 KiB, and invalid/oversized requests return false without modifying the caller's output. The manifest declares the privacy restrictions explicitly: redacted=true, containsRawCheckpoint=false, containsWorldCoordinates=false, containsVmScalars=false, containsGpuIdentifiers=false, and uploadedAutomatically=false. The ZIP builder deliberately has no input argument for raw SPFX bytes, authoring graph paths or arbitrary ZIP entry names. Calling the builder cannot package a raw GPU snapshot accidentally. Even when a developer enables world bounds or GPU identifiers for a separate Stage 42 JSON report, the ZIP remains fully redacted. This is a local support artifact, not an ECS save, GPU replay or cross-build SPFX importer. The editor's Save SAFE ZIP bundle action creates one .zip under platform::userDataDir()/spectrafx-diagnostics/ only after the user presses the button and an eligible current-revision V2 checkpoint is ready. It uses a local safe-bundle-group-N-M.zip filename, not a GPU frame serial, and refuses to overwrite an existing safe bundle. The related safe JSON report also uses serial-free filename numbering. Only when the report belongs to the editor's own GPU preview are its last 180 sanitized sample counters included; external GPU pools do not inherit unrelated editor preview history. The offline tools/spectrafx/inspect_spfx.cpp utility now also supports: ./inspect_spfx --bundle /path/to/support.safe.zip /path/to/checkpoint.spfx The offline ZIP has an empty preview timeline. The binary SPFX source is never added as an archive entry. There is no implicit upload, email, issue creation or external sharing. The existing Save RAW GPU checkpoint (sensitive) button is deliberately a separate user action.

The public <aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraFX.h> includes GpuCaptureRequestMailbox from libraries/include/aiverselib/mechanics/SpectraGpuCaptureMailbox.h. The mailbox is a same-owner-thread intent/status holder with states Idle / Requested / Claimed / InFlight / Ready / Failed / ReleaseRequested. It stores one requested group index, a monotonically increasing sequence and bounded failure information; it performs no GPU commands and carries no particle data, graphics handles, ECS mutation or background scheduling. The native render host may expose a non-owning mailbox pointer to the editor through Editor::setSpectraGpuCaptureMailbox(mailbox). The UI can call Editor::queueSpectraExternalGpuCapture(groupIndex) or Editor::releaseSpectraExternalGpuCapture() on that mailbox, but cannot access gfx::Device or run readBufferAsync itself. The native presentation owner claims a request in its next safe pre-render phase, uses the existing one-at-a-time GpuPoolCaptureHost, keeps VFX state frozen while an async checkpoint is pending, and publishes the same request's state back to the UI. Release is consumed by the native host on the next presentation frame, not during ImGui drawing. examples/spectrafx/native_ecs_attachments.h now demonstrates this integration and exposes captureMailbox(), poolTelemetry() and recoveryHost(). The application must detach all non-owning pointers from the editor before destroying the native host/graphics Device. If the pool is reset, recovered or shut down, the native host clears the mailbox and cancels the capture; late Metal callbacks cannot reattach to an obsolete source generation.

GpuPoolRecoveryHost::serviceQueuedResetAtSafeFrame(ownerFrameOrdinal) adds an optional owner-thread reset retry pump. The host calls it only after gfx::Device::beginFrame, outside render/compute encoders. On a recoverable failed reset, the next attempt is spaced by a bounded exponential number of host frames (max 32); this avoids busy reset writes every frame. The returned PoolRecoveryServiceResult distinguishes NoWork, Deferred, ResetSucceeded, ResetFailed and NeedsNewDevice. A lost Device must be rebuilt by the native platform host; it is not retried as an ordinary reset. The existing PoolRecoveryEvent adds consecutiveResetFailures and retryNotBeforeOwnerFrame, making retry/cooldown status visible without timers. Its transition counter changes on observable recovery state changes rather than spinning duplicate callbacks during the same recovery service call. The updated native example invokes this bounded service in its safe frame before beginning normal presentation and cancels any pending capture before GPU rollback. An optional non-owning Editor::setSpectraGpuRecoveryHost() attachment lets the editor show this status and enqueue a VFX-only reset intent. The editor never executes the actual GPU reset.

The editor resets both sensitive report opt-ins when the selected GPU group or GPU telemetry pool changes, preventing consent from carrying over to a different renderer. A safe ZIP never includes raw particle state or exact GPU device serials. Raw SPFX still contains scene positions/VM values and remains a deliberately sensitive export. Verification performed: SHA-guarded GitHub source commits and source readbacks. NOT RUN: native C++/ObjC++/MSL compilation, ZIP validity extraction, CLI output/privacy/corruption tests, CTest, editor UI launch/screenshots, real Metal capture and owner thread callback/device-loss tests. This stage is source-implemented, not production-verified.

MotionWeave is the canonical name for AIVERSE's modular, genre-independent animation subsystem: AnimationGraph, clips, blend trees, IK, Motion Matching, Montages, root motion, ragdoll poses, inertialization and animation LOD/GPU crowds.

Use the new CMake target and the branded public header in native projects: target_link_libraries(my_game PRIVATE AIVERSE::MotionWeave) #include "engine/animation/MotionWeave.h" // Separate client presentation ECS World; never Simulation::world(). aiverse::World presentation; // Configure animation asset, player and output pose components first. aiverse::motionweave::MotionWeave::update(presentation, frameDt); This is the same implementation as the existing library, not a second engine: Recommended new symbol Compatible existing symbol AIVERSE::MotionWeave AIVERSE::animation_ecs AIVERSE::motionweave AIVERSE::animation_ecs aiverse::motionweave aiverse::lib::animation MotionWeave::update(world,dt) stepAnimationPresentation(world,dt) "engine/animation/MotionWeave.h" "engine/animation/EcsAnimationSystems.h" All specialist libraries still have their historical <aiverselib/animation/...> paths. Existing render::AnimationGraph, render::Animator and Pose names are deliberately unchanged.

Presentation: floats, AnimationGraph instances, IK and skinning reside in a dedicated visual ECS World. FPS opts into actor.visual.model, configurable Graph or baked crowd animation, preserving cube fallback. Existing RTS view continues using its original animation path until migrated deliberately. Gameplay: fixed-point, authored root motion enters the authoritative simulation only through a collision-aware motor. Cosmetic AnimationGraph and Montage notifies cannot trigger authoritative damage, reloads or hits. Authoring: visual editor windows, Humanoid Avatar profiles, Ragdoll descriptors, Montage and root-motion baking operations share Workspace/MCP. Persisted asset schemas and editor IDs do not change with branding.

New standalone test tests/animation/motionweave_api.cpp is registered as motionweave_api (target aiverse_motionweave_api_tests). NOT RUN: the user requested to defer tests, CMake builds and visual QA. Naming changes do not imply the large animation PR is feature-complete. Before further implementation read AGENTS.md and the latest entry in docs/agent-handoffs/animation-universal.md. Every implementation stage must be followed by its own committed, append-only handoff.

For a game with many animated characters, create a persistent host-owned scheduler once and pass it to the three-argument MotionWeave update: #include "engine/animation/MotionWeave.h" aiverse::motionweave::MotionWeaveScheduler scheduler; auto stats = aiverse::motionweave::MotionWeave::update( presentationWorld, frameDt, scheduler); The existing two-argument MotionWeave::update(world,dt) is still sequential for compatibility. The scheduler owns a persistent, bounded work-stealing thread pool (up to seven background threads plus the frame thread). Each frame it classifies models/compiled graphs, separates independent clip, blend, controller, motion-matching and compatible IK work into cost-weighted chunks, then executes them in parallel. Native/Lua callbacks, animation traits, environment contacts, and callback-sensitive rig operations always run on the frame thread after the workers have finished. A mainThread=true AnimationWorkHintComponent forces this lane explicitly. MotionWeaveScheduleOptions exposes minimum entity count, minimum estimated work and chunk sizing. AnimationWorkHintComponent also supports a per-character cost multiplier. Graph safety/cost plans are memoized per frame, while dense work-list allocation capacity is reused. Invisible characters with an already valid pose carry reduced estimated work. Caller code must not change World structure or snapshot it until MotionWeave::update returns. MotionWeaveScheduleStats provides eligible/parallel/serial actor counts, batches, worker count, estimated work, unique graph count, offscreen actor count and safe/serial phase times. These measurements are non-authoritative presentation diagnostics; they never affect gameplay lockstep/checksums.

FPS supports actor.visual.animationMode: "auto" | "cpu" | "gpu" and legacy bakedCrowd: true. With an eligible simple imported, skinned model, auto mode enters GPU baked instancing at 24 visible remote characters and exits at 12, avoiding frequent toggling. Complex custom graphs, IK/controller requirements and graphFile stay on CPU; the FPS client lazily constructs the persistent scheduler when 16+ palette characters are present. actor.visual.animationStats: true enables optional HUD diagnostics. GPU scene draws and uploads remain on the graphics thread. The fast crowd path reuses AIVERSE's existing baked skinning and Renderer3D instancing; MotionWeave does not claim a new GPU compute skinning backend. Test status: all new worker/scheduler/backend CTest fixtures are committed but NOT RUN (user-requested deferral). Verify compilation, TSAN, macOS FPS screenshots, FPS save/network parity and real FPS/RTS benchmarks before declaring production readiness.

Build the standalone (no GPU/model files) benchmark after configuring AIVERSE_BUILD_TOOLS=ON: cmake --build build/ecs-test --target aiverse_motionweave_bench ./build/ecs-test/aiverse_motionweave_bench --actors 1000 --frames 120 ./build/ecs-test/aiverse_motionweave_bench --actors 5000 --frames 120 --ik It creates identical serial and persistent-worker Worlds, warms both, measures average CPU frame times and verifies one output pose for parity. The benchmark intentionally is not registered in CTest because timings are machine-dependent. It must be run together with ThreadSanitizer, real-model Metal screenshots and a representative RTS/FPS frame trace before changing production worker thresholds. NOT RUN.

MotionWeave must NEVER depend on or inspect FPS/RTS/RPG modules. Dependency direction is one-way: Any game module / game simulation / editor ↓ generic animation model and named parameters MotionWeave reusable presentation ECS ↓ generic Pose / Notifies / Root delta Host rendering, audio/VFX and host-owned gameplay motor The core doesn't know what "fire", "attack", "move", "cast", "reload" or another action means. Authors select parameter/event names in their own graphs; clients project their state into the same reusable API. Generic "engine/animation/MotionWeaveSourceBridge.h" exposes AnimationSourceFrame {sourceId,generation,model,graph,inputs} and MotionWeaveSourceBridge::sync(presentationWorld, sources). A bridge maintains visual ECS entity identity, resets visual players on source replacement, copies graph-defined scalar/vector parameters and removes missing sources. It neither evaluates animation nor commits gameplay state. Call the normal MotionWeave scheduler after all input projection and optional view budget configuration. The original FPS event adapter has been moved out of the animation library to engine/view/ActorAnimationEvents.h. The shared "engine/animation/AnimationActionEdges.h" now processes only opaque named counters/boolean state transitions, with no FPS/RTS/action-type semantics. playAnimationSlot lives beside the generic ECS AnimationMontageSlotsComponent definition.

The canonical scene/view type is aiverse::View (also aiverse::view::View) in engine/view/View.h, linked through AIVERSE::view. Host code supplies aiverse::view::Object records containing stable IDs, generic render::ModelDraw packets, optional AnimationGraph and named parameters. The generic View manages independent presentation ECS states, animation LOD budgets, worker scheduling and pose-based scene submission. Use View::update(span,dt) before View::submit(renderer,span) or View::submitOne(renderer,object). A packet may contain a model with no animation graph. View does not depend on RTS, FPS, camera controller, game rules, network, combat, map or terrain modules. A transition adapter still exists in engine/view/game/GameView.cpp and GameViewDraw.cpp: it projects only simple, eligible compiled animation graphs into the generic View and delegates their final ModelDraw submission to View::submitOne. Complex RTS procedural animation, contact IK, genre-specific attachments/FX/fog/terrain remain in the game host until each has a generic render contract. The compatibility class game::GameView remains for older game code; it is not the canonical engine View and should not be used in new projects.

Both existing game frontends now send at least their supported animated-model draws through the universal engine aiverse::View::submitOne: The legacy game-side game::GameView delegates a strictly eligible subset of pure AnimationGraph pose evaluation and the final styled model draw. The FPS reference client projects its existing CPU Graph / GPU Baked render::ModelDraw through View::submitOne, preserving the precomputed pose. Its replicated gameplay state never enters engine View. The common CMake name AIVERSE::View (legacy lowercase AIVERSE::view also works) and public <engine/view/View.h> describe the preferred engine API. The old aiverse_game_view/RTS-specific presentation remains compatibility code during migration; it is not identical to the new generic View yet. Shared camera/culling/terrain/lighting composition and full legacy game adapter removal require further refactoring. No source-level genre dependency is allowed inside engine/view.

MotionWeave graph and pose state does not own GPU Model allocations. Generic native hosts can use aiverse::render::ModelResourceCache (engine/render/ModelResourceCache.h) with a separate presentation World/aiverse::View. The cache owns the model map and shared texture leases. On model/graph replacement, hosts must detach affected AnimationSourceFrame and pose/graph players before moving the old model to the cache's deferred retirement queue. At the next safe host frame boundary, collectRetired(device) invokes the explicit gfx::Device::waitForResourceIdle barrier and releases only resources whose previous GPU submissions are complete. Never derive completion from frameSerial() or a fixed number of frames in flight. Legacy game::view_adapter::GameModelResourceCache and GameModelPreparationService are aliases to the universal render classes. Material preview sphere/box resources in game::Portrait are the first independently owned real editor consumer. The complete RTS scene compatibility adapter is not yet retired. Deferred GPU/backend and animation parity tests are NOT RUN.

Model and texture GPU lifetime is independent of MotionWeave player state. A native host can own render::ModelAssetProvider (from engine/render/ModelAssetProvider.h) without loading RTS/FPS headers, then submit its borrowed model through aiverse::View::submitModel or the generic ordered ScenePacketBatch. After graph/source invalidation, detach the owning presentation ECS sources before moving models into render::ModelResourceCache retirement. Only one animation owner evaluates each graph; packet submission must not tick its graph a second time. Stage 100 adds asynchronous per-batch retirement markers via gfx::Device::beginResourceRetirement, resourceRetirementComplete, and endResourceRetirement. ModelResourceCache::collectRetired polls rather than waiting for the whole GPU on supported backends. The old synchronous wait is only a fallback or explicit shutdown barrier. Never use a frame counter, fixed delay or time-since-last-use as a GPU completion condition. The new game::Portrait::renderStaticModel is a direct native-model preview consumer using the canonical View, with no game-side owner required for that code path. Dynamic RTS models still use compatibility presentation and rendering. NOT RUN: deferred native/Metal/Vulkan/GL/WebGL2 build, runtime, GPU-lifetime, sanitizer and visual parity checks.

h: Stage 101 — async model source preparation and GPU retirement pressure
x: Animation graphs remain separate from render-resource loading. Native project hosts can use render::ModelAssetProvider::requestAsync(path) for bounded, single-worker CPU model import, then call publishReady(device, maxCount) on the owning render thread before constructing aiverse::View packets. The CPU queue records source revisions: invalidating a model source makes any older worker result unpublishable even if the CPU task completes later. MotionWeave source identity/generation and any live pose/graph players must still be detached before replacing a resident Model. render::ModelResourceCache now exposes model-count-based retirement pressure telemetry and a soft admission limit for NEW generic model loads. Existing graph sources continue to render; a saturated backlog must never force early GPU destruction. The default is 128 retired Model objects, NOT a byte-accurate GPU memory budget. Editor's Statistics panel reports pending GPU model retirements and fence fallbacks. The editor Model window provides an opt-in native-source preview for static unskinned models, using an independently owned render::ModelAssetProvider and game::Portrait::renderStaticModel.
